text:
順天府鄉試錄序
今年已卯順天復當鄉試士
提調官府丞臣庭梧以
請
上命諭德臣思育洗馬臣子義充
考試官旣
陛辭入院則同考官同知臣汝
===
爲教諭臣桐臣泮臣國宗臣
官臣如蘭臣養湛臣可久臣
子洛訓導臣文明臣文皆以
聘至相與毖飭從事而御史
臣煥臣祥暨臣許一德臣于
應昌譏防唯謹於是進諸曹

punctuated:
順天府鄉試錄序
今年已卯，順天復當鄉試士。提調官府丞臣庭梧以請，上命諭德臣思育、洗馬臣子義充考試官。旣陛辭入院，則同考官同知臣汝爲、教諭臣桐、臣泮、臣國宗、臣官、臣如蘭、臣養湛、臣可久、臣子洛，訓導臣文明、臣文，皆以聘至，相與毖飭從事；而御史臣煥、臣祥，暨臣許一德、臣于應昌，譏防唯謹。於是進諸曹六館，暨提學御史臣賀一桂、
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination

This year, the jimao year (1579), it was once again time for Shuntian to examine scholars in the Provincial Examination. Upon the request of the Proctor, Vice Prefect Your Servant [Jia] Tingwu 庭梧, His Majesty commanded the Admonisher Your Servant [Gao] Siyu 思育 and the Librarian Your Servant [Chen] Ziyi 子義 to serve as Examiners. Once they had taken leave of the throne and entered the examination compound, the Associate Examiners—the Vice Prefect Your Servant Ruwei 汝爲; the Instructors Your Servants Tong 桐, Pan 泮, Guozong 國宗, Guan 官, Rulan 如蘭, Yangzhan 養湛, Kejiu 可久, and Ziluo 子洛; and the Assistant Instructors Your Servants Wenming 文明 and Wen 文—had all arrived by invitation, and together they attended to their duties with caution and diligence. Meanwhile, the Censors Your Servants Huan 煥 and Xiang 祥, along with Your Servants Xu Yide 許一德 and Yu Yingchang 于應昌, maintained strict vigilance in inspection and security. Thereupon, there were admitted [the students] from the various bureaus and the Six Halls [of the Directorate of Education], as well as those [selected by] the Education-Intendant Censors Your Servant He Yigui 賀一桂…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
臣商為正先後選士四千有
竒三試之得雋者百三十五
人并錄其文以
獻臣竊惟帝王之興莫不以得
士為急務而士者居嘗自待
誰不思表建以徼尺寸之功
於當世哉然弗值其時雖有
===
志無以自樹者豈少也臣閱
古傳記見士所遭時之難輒
掩卷嘆之使其得當論報詎
泯泯若此哉以方
今日則何如也蓋教化翔洽乆
矣
上復加意文學歳下求賢
alt_text:
奇三試之得儁者百三十五
人并錄其文以
獻臣竊惟帝王之興莫不以得
士爲急務而士者居嘗自待
誰不思表建以徼尺寸之功
於當世哉然弗值其時雖有
===
志無以自樹者豈少也臣閱
古傳記見士所遭時之艱輙
掩卷嘆之使其得當論報詎
泯泯若此哉以方
今日則何如也蓋教化翔洽久
矣
上復加意文學歲下求賢
punctuated: 臣商為正，先後選士四千有竒，三試之，得雋者百三十五人，并錄其文以獻。臣竊惟帝王之興，莫不以得士為急務；而士者居嘗自待，誰不思表建，以徼尺寸之功於當世哉？然弗值其時，雖有志，無以自樹者，豈少也？臣閱古傳記，見士所遭時之難，輒掩卷嘆之。使其得當論報，詎泯泯若此哉？以方今日，則何如也？蓋教化翔洽乆矣，上復加意文學，歳下求賢
translation_en: …and Your Servant Shang Weizheng 商為正, numbering four thousand and more, and tested them in three sessions. We obtained one hundred and thirty-five outstanding men, and have recorded their essays to present to the throne. Your Servant privately reflects that when emperors and kings arise, none fails to regard obtaining worthy scholars as an urgent priority; and as for scholars, in what they ordinarily expect of themselves, who among them does not wish to distinguish himself and achieve even a modest measure of merit in his own time? Yet when they do not meet with the right era, even if they possess high aspirations, how could those who have no means to establish themselves be few? When Your Servant reads ancient biographies and records and sees the difficulties of the times that scholars encountered, I always close the book and sigh over them. Had they been given the opportunity to prove their worth and repay their sovereign, how could they have vanished into obscurity like that? If we compare that with the present day, how does it stand? Moral transformation has long spread far and wide, and His Majesty moreover pays special heed to literature and learning, annually issuing edicts seeking worthy men…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
詔書士束髮通一經有司則已羅
而薦之
闕下雖遐壤僻隅咸獲登遂矧
茲
京師首善地乎夫其地邇則被
服必深其化深則振奮當異
固宜有卓茂之才嚮用矣且
===
業已稱
王國士人方屬目而求之厚焉
儻其才無以大異於人或又
不逮令四方猶得以藉口則
安所副國士之望不惟多士
也即今校士之役
□□暫輟

punctuated: 詔書。士束髮通一經，有司則已羅而薦之闕下，雖遐壤僻隅，咸獲登遂，矧茲京師首善地乎？夫其地邇，則被服必深；其化深，則振奮當異。固宜有卓茂之才嚮用矣。且業已稱王國士，人方屬目而求之厚焉。儻其才無以大異於人，或又不逮，令四方猶得以藉口，則安所副國士之望？不惟多士也，即今校士之役，□□暫輟
translation_en: …edicts. As soon as a scholar binds up his hair in youth and masters a single classic, the authorities already gather him in and recommend him to the foot of the palace gates. Even those from distant lands and remote corners are all able to advance and fulfill their ambitions—how much more so in this Capital, the foremost place of moral excellence? Indeed, since its location is near, its embrace of royal influence must be deep; and since its transformation is deep, the rousing of its spirit ought to be extraordinary. Surely there should be men of outstanding and flourishing talent coming forward for employment. Moreover, once they are already acclaimed as scholars of the royal domain, people fix their eyes upon them and expect much of them. If by chance their talents are in no way greatly superior to those of others, or perhaps even fall short, allowing the four quarters still to find grounds for criticism, how then could they live up to the expectations placed in the scholars of the realm? And this applies not only to the many scholars: for the present task of examining the scholars, [His Majesty? (□□)] has temporarily suspended…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
講事以徃誠重之矣以臣至愚
若品隲不明使才者不獲進
將
明命之謂何故竭殫心力庶幾其
遇之而多士又逢時厚幸非
復如昔賢所患乃以答希曠
之遘何術哉臣竊疑焉語有
===
之天下無害聖人無所施才
上下和同賢者無所立功此
謂需士于治時難也今
上睿聖耆賢濟濟而復際九服晏
如之盛即爾多士之才者並
錄特韋布後進耳輒望以能
奉驅策可不謂難哉臣又聞

===
之天下無害聖人無所施才
上下和同賢者無所立功此
謂需士于治時難也今
上睿聖首賢濟濟而復際九服晏
如之盛即爾多士之才者並
錄特章布後進耳輙望以能
奉驅策可不謂難哉臣又聞
punctuated: 講事以徃，誠重之矣。以臣至愚，若品隲不明，使才者不獲進，將明命之謂何？故竭殫心力，庶幾其遇之。而多士又逢時厚幸，非復如昔賢所患，乃以答希曠之遘，何術哉？臣竊疑焉。語有之：「天下無害，聖人無所施才；上下和同，賢者無所立功。」此謂需士于治時難也。今上睿聖，耆賢濟濟，而復際九服晏如之盛，即爾多士之才者並錄，特韋布後進耳，輒望以能奉驅策，可不謂難哉？臣又聞
translation_en: … Classics-mat lectures to go forth, showing how truly important He considers this task. Utterly foolish as your servant is, if my evaluation and ranking lack discernment, causing men of talent to fail to advance, how then could I answer to His Illustrious Command? Therefore, I have exhausted my heart and strength, hoping that I might find them. And now that the many scholars have met with the great good fortune of a propitious age—no longer suffering what the worthies of old lamented—by what means will they respond to this rare and extraordinary encounter? Your servant privately wonders about this. There is a saying: "When the realm is free of harm, the sage has nowhere to exercise his talent; when superiors and inferiors are in harmony, the worthy has nowhere to establish his merit." This means that making use of scholars in an era of good governance is difficult. Today, His Majesty is wise and sagely, veteran worthies fill the court in abundance, and we moreover enjoy a flourishing era in which the nine domains are at peace. Even though the talented among you many scholars are now selected together, you are merely junior scholars from humble cloth-clad origins; yet if one immediately expects you to be capable of answering the call to service, can this not be called difficult? Yet your servant has also heard…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之士者非患有難稱之時而
常患無自盡之心夫其修之
窮居也豈沽名已哉將適於
用也其出而從政也豈干祿
已哉將抒所學以報
上也今
上尊則
===
天也以爲才而登進之
恩不啻猶親也仁人不以天之高
明而忘有相孝子不以親之
燕翼而忘克家奈何際
主聖時清而竟退讓邪未遇既遭
時難得時又圖報難則士所
期以自樹者無時而可矣臣

punctuated: 之：「士者非患有難稱之時，而常患無自盡之心。」夫其修之窮居也，豈沽名已哉？將適於用也。其出而從政也，豈干祿已哉？將抒所學以報上也。今上尊則天也，以爲才而登進之，恩不啻猶親也。仁人不以天之高明而忘有相，孝子不以親之燕翼而忘克家。奈何際主聖時清而竟退讓邪？未遇既遭時難，得時又圖報難，則士所期以自樹者無時而可矣。臣
translation_en: … it: "What scholars should worry about is not encountering an age in which it is difficult to live up to expectations, but rather constantly lacking the resolve to give the utmost of themselves." Now, when they cultivate themselves in humble retirement, is it merely to fish for a reputation? It is so that they will be suited for practical service. And when they come forth to participate in governance, is it merely to seek an official emolument? It is so that they may put forth what they have learned in order to repay the Sovereign. Today, in His exaltedness, the Sovereign is like Heaven; and in deeming them talented and promoting them, His grace is no less than that of a parent. A benevolent person does not forget to assist because Heaven is lofty and bright; a filial son does not forget to sustain the household because his parents have provided comfort and protection. How, then, upon encountering a sage ruler and a tranquil age, could they end up shrinking back in deference? If before finding an opportunity it is difficult to meet with the right times, and once the right times are attained it is again difficult to endeavor to repay the dynasty, then there would never be a moment when scholars could hope to establish themselves! Your servant …

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
願多士盡此心耳大抵士之
才器所受不同而心則無不
可盡者意有所注即精祲金
石且爲之變況以濟時供職
莫非吾分内事邪此見心易
盡矣盡心云者純然于中之
謂非有二用也以爲義而知
===
有其利心不謂盡以爲實而
知有其名心不謂盡有一于
此是爲不忠故曰臣事君以
忠此盡其心之說也士誦孔
氏言豈不願忠即今操觚而
書又不甚辨哉而於論報猶
然難之豈誠難哉難在心不

===
有其利心不謂盡以爲實而
知有其名心不謂盡有一于
此是爲不忠故曰臣事君以
忠此盡其心之說也士誦孔
氏言豈不願忠即令操觚而
書又不甚辯哉而於論報猶
然難之豈誠難哉難在心不
punctuated: 願多士盡此心耳。大抵士之才器所受不同，而心則無不可盡者。意有所注，即精祲金石且爲之變，況以濟時供職，莫非吾分内事邪？此見心易盡矣。盡心云者，純然于中之謂，非有二用也。以爲義而知有其利，心不謂盡；以爲實而知有其名，心不謂盡。有一于此，是爲不忠。故曰：「臣事君以忠。」此盡其心之說也。士誦孔氏言，豈不願忠？即今操觚而書，又不甚辨哉？而於論報猶然難之，豈誠難哉？難在心不
translation_en: …wish that the many scholars would simply devote their hearts to the utmost. On the whole, the talents and capacities with which scholars are endowed differ, yet there is no heart that cannot be devoted to the utmost. When one's intent is focused upon something, even ethereal vapors, metal, and stone will transform in response to it—how much more so when aiding the age and fulfilling one's official duties are nothing other than matters within our own proper lot! From this we can see that it is easy to devote the heart to the utmost. What is meant by "devoting the heart to the utmost" is being pure within, without any divided purpose. If one considers something to be righteous yet remains conscious of its profit, the heart cannot be said to be devoted to the utmost; if one considers something to be substantial yet remains conscious of its fame, the heart cannot be said to be devoted to the utmost. To have either of these is to be disloyal. Therefore it is said: "A minister serves his ruler with loyalty." This is the meaning of devoting one's heart to the utmost. When scholars recite the words of Confucius (Kongshi), how could they not wish to be loyal? Even now, as they take up their writing tablets to compose, do they not argue this most eloquently? Yet when it comes to discussing how to repay the ruler's grace, they still regard it as difficult. Is it truly difficult? The difficulty lies in the heart not…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
盡耳第以誦法之心而供職
何職不供以明於脩辭之心
而濟時何時不濟乎此士能
自盡則難稱非所患臣敢以
多士進矣雖然臣猶懼焉不
聞匠氏用木乎材者收之其
不材與材而未中度棄弗收
===
矣此可以引尺尋也若外堅
而中折質惡而膚美者豈一
時目力所及哉必斵削乃見
耳臣持有司尺度索爾多士
於曲直纖鉅之間既知爲良
矣異日斵削之果清廟明堂
之任則梁棟材也上也次之

而中折質惡而膚美者豈一
時目力所及哉必斲削乃見
耳臣持有司尺度索爾多士
於曲直纖鉅之間旣知爲良
矣異日斲削之果清廟明堂
之任則梁棟材也上也次之
punctuated: 盡耳。第以誦法之心而供職，何職不供？以明於脩辭之心而濟時，何時不濟乎？此士能自盡，則難稱非所患，臣敢以多士進矣。雖然，臣猶懼焉。不聞匠氏用木乎？材者收之，其不材與材而未中度，棄弗收矣，此可以引尺尋也。若外堅而中折，質惡而膚美者，豈一時目力所及哉？必斵削乃見耳。臣持有司尺度，索爾多士於曲直纖鉅之間，既知爲良矣。異日斵削之，果清廟明堂之任，則梁棟材也，上也；次之…
translation_en: …not being wholly devoted. If one simply brings the mind with which one recites and models oneself on the classics to the performance of one's official duties, what duty will go unfulfilled? If one brings the mind that is clear in crafting literary expressions to the task of aiding the times, what age will go unaided? Thus, if scholars can give the utmost of themselves, then the difficulty of living up to expectations is nothing to worry about, and I, your servant, dare to present this multitude of scholars on these grounds. Even so, your servant still feels apprehension. Have you not heard how the master carpenter uses timber? That which is good timber he accepts; that which is unfit timber, or timber that does not meet the standard measurements, he discards and does not accept. This much can be determined by applying the foot-rule and the eight-foot measure. Yet as for wood that is firm on the outside but cracked within, or of poor substance beneath a fine surface—how could that be within the reach of a single moment's eyesight? Only when it is hewn and planed will this become apparent. Holding the measuring stick of the authorities, your servant has sought out you many scholars amid the crooked and the straight, the slender and the massive, and has already recognized you as fine material. On a future day, when you are hewn and planed, if you truly prove equal to the service of the Pure Temple and the Hall of Light, then you are timber for ridgepoles and beams—that is the highest grade. Next to that,…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
榱桷終不失為可用脫或蠹
敗反荆榛不若焉旋棄之矣
奚貴於都人士哉嗟乎此不
盡心之過耳士未必然臣不
厭覆說其意者誠念自設科
取士以来
國家實以是孜孜求之也誠念
===
古来賢士之感時論報者未
嘗外是也多士勉之豈獨使
臣釋于懼即士所酬素志而
塞厚望者尚亦有賴哉
左春坊左諭德兼翰林院侍
讀陳思育謹序

3. 奚貴於鄙人士哉嗟乎此不
4. 盡心之過耳士未必然臣不
5. 厭覆說其意者誠念自設科
6. 取士以來
7. 國家實以是孜孜求之也誠念
Center: 鄉試錄序 八
1. 古來賢士之感時論報者未
2. 嘗外是也多士勉之豈獨使
3. 臣釋于懼即士所酬素志而
4. 塞厚望者尚亦有賴哉
5. 左春坊左諭德兼翰林院侍
6. 讀陳思育謹序
樸桷終不失爲可用脫或蠹
敗反荆榛不若馬旋棄之矣
奚貴於鄙人士哉嗟乎此不
盡心之過耳士未必然臣不
厭覆說其意者誠念自設科
取士以來
國家實以是孜孜求之也誠念

古來賢士之感時論報者未
嘗外是也多士勉之豈獨使
臣釋于懼即士所酬素志而
塞厚望者尚亦有賴哉
左春坊左諭德兼翰林院侍
讀陳思育謹序
punctuated:
榱桷，終不失為可用。脫或蠹敗，反荆榛不若焉，旋棄之矣，奚貴於都人士哉？嗟乎！此不盡心之過耳，士未必然。臣不厭覆說其意者，誠念自設科取士以来，國家實以是孜孜求之也；誠念古来賢士之感時論報者，未嘗外是也。多士勉之！豈獨使臣釋于懼，即士所酬素志而塞厚望者，尚亦有賴哉！
左春坊左諭德兼翰林院侍讀陳思育謹序。
translation_en:
… serve as rafters and purlins, never failing to be of use. Should it happen to be worm-eaten and rotted, however, it becomes worse than brambles and thorns, and is promptly cast aside—what worth would there then be in the scholars of the capital? Alas! Such would merely be the fault of not devoting one's whole heart; it need not be so with you scholars. That I, your servant, do not tire of repeating this message is because I truly reflect that ever since the institution of the civil service examinations for selecting scholars, the dynasty has in truth sought them tirelessly on this very basis; and I truly reflect that the worthy scholars of old who were moved by their times and spoke of repaying the state never departed from this principle. Strive hard, all you scholars! Not only will this relieve your servant of his trepidation, but the means by which you scholars fulfill your long-cherished ambitions and satisfy the high hopes placed in you may also depend upon this!

Respectfully prefaced by Chen Siyu 陳思育, Left Admonisher of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent and concurrently Expositor-in-Waiting in the Hanlin Academy.

《禮記》：
「德產之致也精微，觀天下之物，無可以稱其德者。」

"In winter, in the eleventh month, on the day gengwu, the Marquis of Cai, leading the Viscount of Wu, fought a battle with the men of Chu at Boju, in which the army of Chu was utterly defeated" (Fourth year of Duke Ding); "The Duke met with the Marquis of Jin and the Viscount of Wu at Huangchi" (Thirteenth year of Duke Ai).

"The workings of productive virtue are subtle and minute; observing all the things in the world, there is none sufficient to match its virtue."
"Now music is that whereby the former kings gave expression to their joy; armies and battle-axes are that whereby the former kings gave expression to their anger. Therefore the joy and anger of the former kings both found their proper counterparts. When they rejoiced, the world harmonized with them; when they were angry, the violent and rebellious stood in awe of them. "The loyal minister in serving his ruler, and the filial son in serving his parents—their root is one."

策〔五道〕

問：《易》稱「天地交，泰」，又曰「上下交而其志同也」，則君臣之交，等于天地，古今言致理者，未有不繇斯者矣。虞廷賡載之歌，周人矢詩之雅，于今誦之，其盛可想焉。漢以下，有朝而問相，且懇款於郎署之詢者；有日昃罷朝，數引公卿郎將講論經理者；有令學士更日宿直，引入內殿講論商榷者；有侍從陳言，温顏訪問，且御天章咨得失者，亦可方於古否歟？我聖祖神武天縱，虛懷下賢，一時文武之彥，雲合景從，攄籌效績，泰交之盛，焜燿前古矣。載惟孝皇光紹祖烈，數延大臣面議章奏，商度政機，于時致理之效，亦迥軼古初焉，可得而揚厲歟？
translation_en:
Repairing bridges and roads.

Third Session

Policy Questions (five items)

Question: The Book of Changes (Yi) states: "Heaven and earth are in communion: Peace (Tai)," and further says: "Above and below are in communion and their wills are the same." Thus the communion between ruler and minister is equal to that of heaven and earth; from antiquity to the present, none who speak of achieving good governance have failed to proceed from this. The songs of continued composition at the court of Yu [Shun], and the Odes (Ya) in which the men of Zhou set forth their poems—when we recite them today, their flourishing state can be imagined. From the Han dynasty onward, there was one who held court and questioned his Counsellor-in-Chief, and moreover made earnest inquiries in the offices of the Court Gentlemen; there was one who dismissed court only when the sun inclined to the west, and repeatedly brought in Excellencies, Ministers, Court Gentlemen, and Generals to expound and discuss the principles of governance; there was one who ordered Scholars to take turns on night duty, bringing them into the inner palace halls to lecture, discuss, and deliberate; and there was one who, when attendants presented their words, inquired of them with a gentle countenance, and furthermore repaired to the Tianzhang Pavilion to consult on successes and failures. Can these also be compared to antiquity or not? Our Sacred Progenitor [Emperor Taizu], divinely martial and heaven-endowed, humbled his heart to condescend to the worthy; at that time civil and military talents gathered like clouds and followed like shadows, unfolding their plans and rendering meritorious service—the flourishing of peaceful communion (taijiao) shone brightly beyond former antiquity. Furthermore, our Filial Emperor [Emperor Xiaozong] gloriously continued the ancestral achievements, repeatedly inviting Grand Ministers to discuss memorials face to face and deliberate on the pivotal affairs of governance; the efficacy of achieving good order at that time also far surpassed early antiquity—can you set this forth and extol it?

請遵祖法者或以識治體稱之是矣又
punctuated:
皇上緝熈聖學，孜孜治理，綸扉政本，時厪訪納。頃歲輔臣以聖齡日茂，請停罷書翰，講議章奏，上欣然報可，獻歲之始，首舉行焉。一時臣工欣欣喜色，謂祖宗徽烈，奕世載光，泰道之亨，即《詩》、《書》所稱無殊已。夫宣揚懿鑠，臣子之分；顧聖心無窮，設有忠藎可以仰裨萬分一者，尤宵旰所亟欲聞也。幸悉陳之，毋讓。

問：自昔談致理之務者，大凡在議法矣。《詩》不云乎：「率由舊章。」《易》又有「通其變，使民不倦」之訓，何也？抑法非變通不可為治歟？甞觀漢、宋人臣，持議濟時，亦各不同：有好觀故事、條奏施行者，有復起為相、請遵祖法者，或以識治體稱之，是矣；又
translation_en:
His Majesty continually illuminates his sagely learning and works untiringly at bring about good governance; toward the Grand Secretariat, the root of administration, he constantly devotes his earnest attention in consulting and accepting advice. In recent years, because His Majesty's sagely age was daily maturing, the Grand Secretaries requested that calligraphy practice be suspended in favor of lecturing on and discussing memorials. His Majesty gladly approved this, and at the beginning of the new year it was put into practice first of all. At the time, all the officials wore joyful expressions, declaring that the splendid achievements of the imperial ancestors are glorified across the generations, and that this flourishing of the Way of Peace (Tai) is no different from what is praised in the Classic of Poetry (Shi) and the Classic of History (Shu). Now, to proclaim and extol such illustrious virtue is the duty of subjects and sons; yet the sagely mind is boundless in its aspiration, and should there be loyal and devoted counsel that might offer even a ten-thousandth part of assistance on high, that is especially what His Majesty, in his tireless pre-dawn and late-night diligence, most urgently wishes to hear. Please set it all forth in full, without holding back.

Question: Since antiquity, those who have discussed the business of achieving good governance have generally focused on deliberating over laws and institutions. Does not the Classic of Poetry say, "Following the old statutes"? Yet the Classic of Changes (Yi) also has the teaching, "By carrying through changes, they keep the people from growing weary." Why is this? Or is it that unless laws are adapted to changing circumstances, one cannot achieve order? If we examine the ministers of the Han and Song dynasties, the proposals they upheld to rescue their times also differed from one another: there was one who was fond of examining precedents and submitting itemized memorials to put them into effect, and there was one who, upon being recalled as Grand Councilor, requested adherence to the ancestral laws. Some praised them for understanding the substance of governance, which is right indeed; yet…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
有上治安之疏多欲匡建者陳時弊十
事批答手詔者亦何以明非過計歟
國家熈平之日久矣法立弊生漸有廢墜而
不舉者抑沿襲之後人心玩愒勢必至
於此歟若仍其故習法將安飭曩時諸
臣集議思爲拯民捄弊之術所籌畫至
詳而計慮甚遠矣今者効固可睹也豈
保泰持盈其體不得不然而者歟或者拂
情違衆之議蓋不必卹也抑與時宜之
===
無失立法之意要於善守焉不相悖歟
夫法患不飭耳飭之而俾無遺慮其究
乃有不盡在法者歟願悉言之庶議法
者采焉
問六經遭秦火闕佚學者多病其難通而
春秋彌甚今學春秋者率本胡氏次則
稱左氏公穀三家後先出往往齟齬不
合可一斷以胡氏歟且三傳去孔氏差
近昔人猶有以意增損之疑胡氏去三

事批答手詔者亦何以明非過〔譽〕〔餙〕

不舉者抑治襲之後人心玩愒勢必至
於此歟若仍其故習法將安餙曩時諸

情違衆之議蓋不必卹也抑與時宜之
===
無失立法之意要於善守為不相悖歟
夫法患不餙耳餙之而俾無遺慮其究
乃有不盡在法者歟願悉言之庶議法
者采焉
問六經遭秦火闕佚學者多病其難通而
春秋彌甚今學春秋者率本胡氏次則
稱左氏公穀三家後先出往往齟齬不
合可一斷以胡氏歟且三傳去孔氏差
近昔人猶有以意增損之疑胡氏去三
punctuated:
有上《治安》之疏、多欲匡建者，陳時弊十事、批答手詔者，亦何以明非過計歟？國家熈平之日久矣，法立弊生，漸有廢墜而不舉者，抑沿襲之後，人心玩愒，勢必至於此歟？若仍其故習，法將安飭？曩時諸臣集議，思爲拯民捄弊之術，所籌畫至詳而計慮甚遠矣，今者効固可睹也。豈保泰持盈，其體不得不然而者歟？或者拂情違衆之議，蓋不必卹也；抑與時宜之，無失立法之意，要於善守焉不相悖歟？夫法患不飭耳，飭之而俾無遺慮，其究乃有不盡在法者歟？願悉言之，庶議法者采焉。

問：六經遭秦火闕佚，學者多病其難通，而《春秋》彌甚。今學《春秋》者率本胡氏，次則稱左氏、公、穀。三家後先出，往往齟齬不合，可一斷以胡氏歟？且三傳去孔氏差近，昔人猶有以意增損之疑；胡氏去三
translation_en:
…there was one who submitted a memorial on "Order and Peace" (Zhi'an) wishing to make many rectifications and establishments, and another who set forth ten current abuses and received a personally written imperial rescript in reply—how can it be shown that these were not overly anxious calculations?

Our Dynasty has enjoyed peace and prosperity for a long time. Once laws are established, abuses arise, and gradually some fall into disrepair and are no longer enforced. Or is it that after long routine, people's minds grow lax and indolent, so that the trend must inevitably come to this? If we continue in these old habits, how will the laws be put in order? In recent times, various officials gathered to deliberate, seeking ways to rescue the people and remedy abuses; their planning was most detailed and their foresight very far-reaching, and today the results can indeed be seen. Is it not that in preserving peace and maintaining fullness, the fundamental principle cannot but be thus [?]? Perhaps objections that go against popular sentiment and oppose the multitude need not be heeded; or is it that by adapting to what is appropriate for the times without losing the original intent of establishing the laws, it is after all not incompatible with preserving them well? Now, the worry with laws is only that they are not kept in order; yet when they are put in order so as to leave nothing overlooked, does the ultimate outcome perhaps not lie entirely in the laws themselves? I wish you to speak of this in full, so that those who deliberate on the laws may select from your views.

Question: The Six Classics suffered gaps and losses from the Qin fires, and scholars have mostly been troubled by the difficulty of comprehending them, with the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) being even more so. Today, those who study the Spring and Autumn Annals generally base themselves on Mr. Hu [Hu Anguo 胡安國], and next cite Mr. Zuo [Zuo Qiuming 左丘明], Gongyang, and Guliang. These three schools appeared one after another and are often at odds and in disagreement; can everything be decided solely by following Mr. Hu? Moreover, the Three Commentaries were relatively close in time to Confucius, yet scholars of the past still suspected them of making additions and deletions according to their own views; Mr. Hu was separated from the three…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
家又千餘載其言顧可盡信歟夫聖人
作經之意簡易明白要以仍人道達王
事如斯而已也必若傳者之說將聖人
以微詞深文疑誤後世可乎可畧剖其
事歟說者謂春秋為尊王而作韙矣廼
又曰夫子託二百四十二年南面之權
以誅賞人也此何名為尊王哉將其義
別有在歟夫六經將與天地無終極而
存非一人一世之私論也今羣言紛如
令學者奚適而可故願與諸士揚搉疑
義以求厥衷焉
問聖王知人則哲能官人自昔論之矣考
諸書以堯薦舜可自信不疑者必待羣
臣推引已復試歷諸艱若此其兢兢焉
何哉夫聖哲知人猶然難矣乃後世又
何以易之也有問相而知能安劉者有
知緩急為可任將者有悟上書之詐而
獎其忠者有因告變而勞以守益州清

以微詞深文疑誤後世而乎可畧剖其
事歟說者謂春秋爲尊王而作避矣廼

臣推引已復試歷諸艱若此其兢兢焉
何哉夫聖哲知人猶然難矣乃後世又

知緩急爲可任將者有悟上書之詐而
獎其忠者有因告變而勞以守益州清
punctuated:
家又千餘載，其言顧可盡信歟？夫聖人作經之意，簡易明白，要以仍人道、達王事，如斯而已也。必若傳者之說，將聖人以微詞深文疑誤後世，可乎？可畧剖其事歟？說者謂《春秋》為尊王而作，韙矣；廼又曰「夫子託二百四十二年南面之權以誅賞人也」，此何名為尊王哉？將其義別有在歟？夫六經將與天地無終極而存，非一人一世之私論也。今羣言紛如，令學者奚適而可？故願與諸士揚搉疑義，以求厥衷焉。
問：聖王知人則哲、能官人，自昔論之矣。考諸《書》，以堯薦舜，可自信不疑者，必待羣臣推引，已復試歷諸艱，若此其兢兢焉，何哉？夫聖哲知人猶然難矣，乃後世又何以易之也？有問相而知能安劉者，有知緩急為可任將者，有悟上書之詐而獎其忠者，有因告變而勞以守益州清
translation_en:
… three schools by more than a thousand years; can his words then be completely trusted? Now the Sage's intent in composing the Classic was simple, easy, and clear—in essence, to follow the way of humanity and carry through the business of the true king, and nothing more than this. If it must be as the commentators claim, would the Sage have used subtle phrasing and abstruse wording to confuse and mislead later generations? Can these matters be briefly analyzed? Commentators say that the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) was composed to honor the king, which is right; yet they also say, "The Master assumed the south-facing authority of a ruler over two hundred and forty-two years in order to punish and reward men." How can this be called honoring the king? Or does its meaning lie elsewhere? The Six Classics will endure without end alongside heaven and earth; they are not the private discourse of one man or one age. Today the multitude of opinions is in utter confusion—where are scholars to turn? Therefore I wish to discuss and weigh these doubtful points with you gentlemen, so as to seek the proper middle ground.

Question: That a sage-king shows wisdom in knowing men and is thus able to place men in office has been discussed since antiquity. Examining the Book of Documents (Shu), when Yao recommended Shun—something in which he could have trusted himself without doubt—he still waited for the assembled ministers to recommend him, and afterward tested him through various hardships. Why was he so cautious as this? Now if knowing men was still so difficult even for the sage and wise, why did later ages treat it as so easy? There was one who, upon asking about chief ministers, knew who could keep the Liu clan secure; one who knew who could be entrusted with a generalship in an emergency; one who perceived the fraud in a submitted memorial and praised the man's loyalty; one who, upon receiving a report of rebellion, comforted the governor of Yizhou for his purity and…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
正者有聞焉將而决才非破賊者有見
容儀安雅而信非為惡者不識數君者
果可稱知人之明否歟抑古今人才不
同故知有難易歟昔之觀人者有謂五
視九徵又稱十二流之業及稽以八計
舉以十科者詳哉其言之矣今果足為
準歟或尚有一二可議指也至宋大儒
獨推陰陽剛柔之理辨君子小人心術
論者稱深得易書之微㫖以視諸說孰
為要歟今
國家需才甚切乃名實相貿或猶議焉當何
道以辨抑宋儒之說有可推廣而言之
者歟諸士試悉陳之以備
今日知人之助
問漢志稱周禮冢宰制國用量入以為出
三年耕必餘一年之食至三登而稱太
平蓋教民地著力本之效爾未嘗言利
也中世興利者出於是有官山海務積

正者有闢爲將而决才非破賊者有見
容儀安雅而信非爲惡者不識數君者
果可稱知人之明否歟抑古今人才不
同故知有難易歟昔之觀人者有謂五
視九徵又稱十二流之業及稽以八計
舉以十科者詳哉其言之矣今果足爲
準歟或尚有一二可議指也至宋大儒
獨推陰陽剛柔之理辨君子小人心術
論者稱深得易書之微旨以視諸說孰
===
爲要歟今
國家需才甚切乃名實相貿或猶議焉當何
道以辨抑宋儒之說有可推廣而言之
者歟諸士試悉陳之以備
今日知人之助
問漢志稱周禮冢宰制國用量入以爲出
三年耕必餘一年之食至三登而稱太
平蓋教民地著力本之效爾來嘗言利
也中世興利者出於是有官山海務積
punctuated:
正者，有聞焉將而决才非破賊者，有見容儀安雅而信非為惡者。不識數君者，果可稱知人之明否歟？抑古今人才不同，故知有難易歟？昔之觀人者，有謂五視、九徵，又稱十二流之業，及稽以八計、舉以十科者，詳哉其言之矣！今果足為準歟？或尚有一二可議指也。至宋大儒，獨推陰陽剛柔之理，辨君子小人心術，論者稱深得《易》、《書》之微㫖，以視諸說，孰為要歟？今國家需才甚切，乃名實相貿，或猶議焉。當何道以辨？抑宋儒之說有可推廣而言之者歟？諸士試悉陳之，以備今日知人之助。

問：《漢志》稱《周禮》冢宰制國用，量入以為出，三年耕必餘一年之食，至三登而稱太平，蓋教民地著力本之效爾，未嘗言利也。中世興利者出，於是有官山海、務積
translation_en:
… integrity; there was one who heard someone had been made a general [焉將; for 為將?] and judged that his talent was not up to defeating the rebels; and there was one who saw a man's calm and refined demeanor and trusted that he would not do evil. I do not know whether these several rulers can truly be praised for having the discernment to know men? Or is it that men of talent in ancient and modern times are different, so that knowing them varies in difficulty? Among those in the past who observed men, there were those who spoke of the "Five Observations" (wushi) and "Nine Verifications" (jiuzheng), or cited the "Professions of the Twelve Streams" (shi'er liu zhi ye), as well as examining by the "Eight Assessments" (baji) and recommending by the "Ten Categories" (shike)—how detailed were their words! Are they truly sufficient to serve as standards today, or are there still one or two points open to criticism? Coming to the great Confucians of the Song dynasty, they alone inferred from the principles of yin and yang, firmness and softness, to distinguish the mental dispositions of the gentleman (junzi) and the petty man (xiaoren). Commentators praise them for deeply grasping the subtle purport of the Book of Changes (Yi) and the Book of Documents (Shu). Compared with the other theories, which is more essential? Today the State needs talent most urgently, yet reputation and reality are confounded with one another, and some still criticize this. By what way should we distinguish them? Or can the theories of the Song Confucians be extended and elaborated upon? Let you gentlemen set this forth in full, to serve as an aid to knowing men today.

Question: The Treatise in the Book of Han (Hanzhi) cites the Rites of Zhou (Zhouli) as saying that the Grand宰 (Minister of State, zhongzai) regulates the state's expenditures by measuring income to determine outlays; three years of ploughing must leave a surplus of one year's food, and when there have been three such accumulations of abundant harvests (sandeng), it is called Great Peace. This was simply the effect of teaching the people to settle on the land and exert themselves in fundamental agriculture; there was never any talk of profit. In the middle ages, promoters of profit emerged, and thereupon there were those who put the mountains and seas under official control, devoted themselves to accumulating…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
著筦鹽鐵置平準者然言利愈析而治
彌不古曾不若節儉化民者收人給家
足貫朽粟腐之效也然則約泰之間固
盈縮之原歟我
國家以仁儉造邦取民制用具有
成憲蓋遠法成周而不泥於跡者迺邇者度支
費鉅率一歲之出踰歲入以數十百萬
計夫度賦非益寡計民不加給又寓內
乂寧邊燧希尠而直此廩廩也是曷故
===
歟脫有災警又將何以處歟議者謂諸
邊之供饋非額
宗藩之制祿日繁軍職之耗蠹無已然歟抑
或別有指歟又謂兵屯弛廢宜理鹺政
開中宜復河以北水利稼政宜修然歟
抑又別有術歟夫經費
國家大計
天子宰臣所軫念講求者諸生倘有便計長策
幸熟陳之將以備主計者擇焉

彌不古曾不若節儉化民者收人給家
足貫朽粟腐之效也然則約泰之間固
盈縮之原歟我

又寧邊燧希儆而直此廩廩也是曷故
===

邊之供饋非額
宗藩之制祿日繁軍職之耗蠹無已然歟抑
或別有指歟又謂兵屯弛廢宜理鹺政

抑又別有術歟夫經費
國家大計
天子宰臣所軫念講求者諸生倘有便計長策
幸熟陳之將以備主計者擇焉
punctuated: 著、筦鹽鐵、置平準者，然言利愈析而治彌不古，曾不若節儉化民者收人給家足、貫朽粟腐之效也。然則約泰之間，固盈縮之原歟？我國家以仁儉造邦，取民制用，具有成憲，蓋遠法成周而不泥於跡者。迺邇者度支費鉅，率一歲之出踰歲入以數十百萬計。夫度賦非益寡，計民不加給，又寓內乂寧，邊燧希尠，而直此廩廩也，是曷故歟？脫有災警，又將何以處歟？議者謂諸邊之供饋非額、宗藩之制祿日繁、軍職之耗蠹無已，然歟？抑或別有指歟？又謂兵屯弛廢宜理、鹺政開中宜復、河以北水利稼政宜修，然歟？抑又別有術歟？夫經費，國家大計，天子、宰臣所軫念講求者。諸生倘有便計長策，幸熟陳之，將以備主計者擇焉。
translation_en:
… reserves, monopolized salt and iron, and established bureaus of equalization and standardization. Yet the more minutely they calculated profit, the further governance fell short of antiquity; they never matched those who transformed the people through frugality and achieved the result of every person being provided for and every household self-sufficient, with strings of cash rotting and grain decaying in the granaries. If this is so, does the difference between restraint and extravagance not truly lie at the root of surplus and deficit?

Our Dynasty founded the state with benevolence and frugality; in drawing revenue from the people and regulating expenditures, it possesses established institutions that emulate the distant model of the flourishing Zhou without being bound to its literal traces. Recently, however, fiscal expenditures have become enormous, and a single year's outlay generally exceeds its revenue by several hundred thousand or even several million. Now, measured taxes have not grown smaller, nor are the people when reckoned any better supplied; moreover, the realm within is peaceful and secure, and border beacon-fires are rare. Why, then, do we face such precarious straits? Should natural disasters or military alarms suddenly arise, how would we deal with them?

Commentators say that supplies sent to the various frontiers exceed the fixed quotas, that the statutory stipends for imperial clansmen and princely establishments grow daily more numerous, and that the waste and peculation of military officers are endless. Is this so, or does the explanation point elsewhere? They also say that the neglected and abandoned military state farms should be put in order, that the border grain-for-salt exchange system (kaizhong) in the salt administration should be restored, and that water conservancy and agricultural administration north of the Yellow River should be repaired. Is this so, or are there other methods?

Regular expenditure is a great affair of state, over which the Son of Heaven and his chief ministers anxiously deliberate and investigate. If you students have convenient plans and long-term strategies, pray set them forth thoroughly, so that they may be ready for the fiscal officials to choose from.

First Session
Four Books
"Duke Ai asked You Ruo, 'In a year of famine, expenditures are insufficient; what is to be done?' You Ruo replied, 'Why not apply the tithe (che)?' The Duke said, 'Even with two-tenths, I still do not have enough; how could I manage with the tithe?' You Ruo replied, 'If the hundred surnames have enough, with whom will the ruler have too little? If the hundred surnames do not have enough, with whom will the ruler have enough?'"

Feng Jiayu 馮嘉遇

Associate Examiner and Instructor Hui 惠 comments: He expounds the doctrine that ruler and people form a single body in a precise, incisive, and well-rounded manner, deeply grasping the meaning of You Ruo's reply to Duke Ai.
Associate Examiner and Instructor Xiao 蕭 comments: The conception is dignified and fitting, the phrasing elevated, ancient, and extraordinary, and the intent of enriching the state and bringing abundance to the people shines forth warmly—a fine scholar indeed.
Associate Examiner and Instructor Xu 徐 comments: That enriching the state lies in enriching the people, and enriching the people lies in practicing the tithe—this idea is developed clearly and thoroughly; moreover, the brushwork is crisp and pure, and the style solemn and elegant. It ought to be recorded as a model.
Examiner and Librarian Zhou 周 comments: The essay addresses matters of vital import, and its diction is moreover solemn and grand.
Examiner and Left Admonisher Chen 陳 comments: The words and meaning are clear and exhaustive; select it.

Twice the worthy answered the ruler of his time on the way to enrich the state, the essence of which lies simply in enriching the people. Profound indeed is it that the ruler and the people form a single body! Seeing that state expenditures depend upon the people, what further doubt can there be that the tithe ought to be practiced? title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
上下相通之義焉魯自徹法廢而民困矣民困
而國告匱矣故哀公以年饑用不足爲問而有
若對曰天菑流行何代無之君患國用不足意
者取民無制耳盍亦行徹乎中公外私無收分
田之舊民什君一惟循薄斂之規如是而猶患
不足者否也夫徹者一今則二矣二不足而損
之爲一故公復問焉蓋欲以加賦而百姓之足
與不足若不相關者乃復對曰君與民一體也
盈則俱盈縮則俱縮者也使徹行而百姓足矣
===
未有百姓充然其有而上之所需猶弗給者何
也百姓者君之百姓也借曰不足其孰與之使
徹不行而百姓不足焉未有百姓索然其無而
上之所需猶能供者何也君者即百姓之君也
借曰足又孰與之然則君毋務足國也足民耳
已毋憂國不足也憂民耳已徹行而民足則凶
荒不能累賦稅不必加而財恒足矣不然費愈
滋而斂愈急豈惟二猶不足哉嗟乎後之君當
粟紅貫朽畝棲野被之時庶幾哉稱富足矣侈

punctuated: 上下相通之義焉。魯自徹法廢而民困矣，民困而國告匱矣。故哀公以年饑用不足爲問，而有若對曰：「天菑流行，何代無之？君患國用不足，意者取民無制耳。盍亦行徹乎？中公外私，無收分田之舊；民什君一，惟循薄斂之規。如是而猶患不足者，否也。」夫徹者一，今則二矣。二不足而損之爲一，故公復問焉，蓋欲以加賦，而百姓之足與不足若不相關者。乃復對曰：「君與民一體也，盈則俱盈，縮則俱縮者也。使徹行而百姓足矣，未有百姓充然其有，而上之所需猶弗給者。何也？百姓者，君之百姓也；借曰不足，其孰與之？使徹不行而百姓不足焉，未有百姓索然其無，而上之所需猶能供者。何也？君者，即百姓之君也；借曰足，又孰與之？然則君毋務足國也，足民耳已；毋憂國不足也，憂民耳已。徹行而民足，則凶荒不能累，賦稅不必加，而財恒足矣。不然，費愈滋而斂愈急，豈惟二猶不足哉！」嗟乎！後之君，當粟紅貫朽、畝棲野被之時，庶幾哉稱富足矣。侈
translation_en:
… the meaning of mutual communication and sharing between high and low. In Lu, ever since the universal tithe system (che) was abandoned, the people had fallen into distress; once the people were in distress, the state reported exhaustion of its resources. Thus Duke Ai (Ai Gong 哀公) asked about the harvest being afflicted by famine and state expenditures being insufficient, and You Ruo (有若) replied: "Natural calamities occur in succession—what era is without them? If Your Lordship worries that state expenditures are insufficient, perhaps it is simply because your exactions from the people lack regulation. Why not implement the universal tithe? With public fields in the center and private fields on the outside, do not alter the old system of dividing the land; with the people keeping nine parts out of ten and the ruler taking one, simply follow the rule of light taxation. That one could act thus and still worry about insufficiency—no, that could not be."

Now, the universal tithe was one part in ten, whereas at that time they took two. Because two parts were insufficient, reducing it to one prompted the Duke to ask again—for he wished to increase taxes, as though whether the hundred surnames had enough or not had nothing to do with him. You Ruo therefore replied again: "The ruler and the people are a single body: when there is abundance, both enjoy abundance; when there is scarcity, both suffer scarcity. Suppose the universal tithe is practiced and the hundred surnames have enough: there has never been a case where the hundred surnames possess abundant wealth and yet the needs of the ruler above remain unsupplied. Why is this? Because the hundred surnames are the ruler's own hundred surnames; even if one were to say the ruler has not enough, with whom could he share that lack? Suppose the universal tithe is not practiced and the hundred surnames do not have enough: there has never been a case where the hundred surnames are utterly destitute and yet the needs of the ruler above can still be supplied. Why is this? Because the ruler is none other than the ruler of the hundred surnames; even if one were to say the ruler has enough, with whom could he enjoy that sufficiency? This being so, let Your Lordship not strive to enrich the state, but simply enrich the people; let him not worry that the state has not enough, but simply worry about the people. When the universal tithe is practiced and the people have enough, then famine and dearth cannot burden them, taxes and levies need not be increased, and wealth will constantly suffice. Otherwise, as expenditures grow ever more profuse and exactions ever more urgent, how could even two parts in ten be enough!"

Alas! Among rulers of later ages, in times when grain rotted in the granaries and strings of cash decayed in the treasuries, when sheaves piled in the acres and covered the open fields, they could very nearly be called rich and well-supplied. Yet once an extravagant…

心一生累世之積不保則聚歛之臣繼進而民

恭儉之主知上天立君意在爲民於其未足能
養之既足能節之茲所以固本而長治也歟
誠身有道不明乎善不誠乎身矣誠者天
之道也誠之者人之道也

translation_en:
… truly possessed within the self is none other than sincerity. Sincerity and goodness are originally one in principle, while the efforts of understanding and of attaining sincerity mutually depend on each other. Therefore, one's understanding is the means to illuminate this sincerity; yet if one's observation and recognition are not precise, subtle incipiencies will remain unanalyzed and falsity and delusion will intrude—if one then wishes to cast out falsity in order to manifest sincerity, how could that be achieved? One's attaining sincerity is the means to make this understanding sincere; yet if one's discernment and choice are not careful, personal opinions will remain unharmonized and hollow artifice will take advantage of it—if one then wishes to guard against depravity in order to preserve sincerity, how could that be achieved? This is why understanding goodness is the way to make the self sincere. Yet this sincerity, though endowed in man, actually originates in Heaven. Thus, when the Supreme Lord sends down the moral nature, the complete substance of the Supreme Ultimate is fully sufficient in each person at the initial moment of bestowal; the Way of Heaven is originally like this. What is bestowed by Heaven may be muddled by man; therefore, skilfully returning to it constitutes learning, and through the people's holding fast to their constant nature, they are able to restore the original state of their Heaven-bestowed nature—the Way of man ought naturally to be like this. Since Heaven brooks no falsity, turning from delusion back to freedom from delusion is our human task; proceeding from understanding to arrive at sincerity—how could such effort be allowed to cease? Since Heaven brooks no adulteration, coming to rest in the highest good is our human responsibility; uniting the human with Heaven—how could this Way be shirked? For this reason, the gentleman prizes the attainment of sincerity. Moreover, this is Heavenly virtue, and the governance of emperors and kings truly hinges upon it. The pure virtue of King Wen was the Way of Heaven itself; as for the reverence of King Wu, it is said that he embodied it in his person—is this not like what is called "making it sincere"? The government of Wen and Wu is recorded on wooden and bamboo tablets, and it truly had this as its root. How should those of later times who study to become sages proceed? I say: the effort lies in choosing the good and holding fast to it, and its essential point lies in being watchful over oneself when alone.

translation_en:
… rousing himself to action must first wait upon something before he rises up, then when he stops, he will likewise excuse himself on the grounds that he is still waiting. Although such a person differs from one who does not become good even when instructed, in the end he is still unworthy of esteem—is he not merely of the same class as the ordinary folk?

With an outstanding scholar (haojie zhi shi), however, it is not so. Possessing talent that surpasses others, whatever he undertakes is right; holding wisdom that transcends the age, he is able to find his own teacher within himself. Should he be fortunate enough to encounter a King Wen, his rousing himself to vigorous effort is naturally just like this—it is not that because King Wen exists, he relies upon him in order to rise up. And even if he is unfortunate and does not encounter a King Wen, his pressing bravely and directly forward is still just the same—it is not that because there is no King Wen, he still waits for one. For Heaven does not give birth to such a person by mere chance; thus, in a day when the Way of the world has already declined, he stands forth alone and returns to his original nature. Such a person does not hold himself lightly; thus, in an era after moral teachings and customs have long been submerged, he rises above and does not herd with the vulgar. An outstanding man is inherently like this—how does he compare to the ordinary folk?

Now, rising up toward goodness is one and the same, yet insofar as waiting for instruction makes one an ordinary person, one is far removed from the outstanding man; and insofar as not waiting for instruction makes one an outstanding man, one is far removed from the ordinary folk. A person's character depends upon how he rouses himself. Will a scholar be an ordinary person, or will he be an outstanding man? One has only to reflect upon oneself to grasp it.

Moreover, during the Warring States period, the learning of human nature was obscured and heterodox doctrines arose in competition. Because there were those who claimed that only when Kings Wen and Wu arose did the people love goodness, Mencius worried about this and put forward a discourse to awaken the world, wishing through learning to seek the full realization of human nature—was this not also an implicit expression of his taking the responsibility upon himself? Even so, in encouraging, drawing in, correcting, and straightening the people, a sage age is ever earnest and attentive. Moral transformation through teaching is indeed the great foundation for making people good and perfecting customs—how could it be entirely dispensed with? If the world can promote teaching, then by strengthening themselves even ordinary folk can become outstanding men; and this, too, is the intention of the sages and worthies in establishing instruction.

text:
曠然與天下共綱紀之不諭而知者也故天下
咸守其法而不離其獨焉於深宮者昭然與天
下共彝倫之不言而信者也故天下又信其心
而不悖此所謂顯比之吉也九五何以致此哉
蓋以居陽爻之正當上體之中則是帝德淵微
渾乎太極之全體王心純一粹然乾德之至精
本之無為以守正而萬邦之度貞焉故遠近親
疎之分以心觀之本非有二而曷嘗置輕重于
其内也會之精一以執中而四方之極建焉故
===
去来順逆之際以道觀之復通為一而曷嘗介
欣戚于其間也所以致顯比之吉者以此彼求
治太急而以有心迎之憂民太勤而以有心留
之不亦憧憧乎小哉吁此王道也王者施不期
博濟不期衆猶天地於萬物乎一無容心而天
下自不外也是故有苗弗率無損於大防風後
至何累其功惟自昭明德耳自談者必以兼覆
遠届為功而失其精於是乎務勤遠略而廣其
心夫廣其心者必有隱行矣胡以云王道也

punctuated: 曠然與天下共綱紀之，不諭而知者也，故天下咸守其法而不離；其獨焉於深宮者，昭然與天下共彝倫之，不言而信者也，故天下又信其心而不悖。此所謂顯比之吉也。九五何以致此哉？蓋以居陽爻之正，當上體之中，則是帝德淵微，渾乎太極之全體；王心純一，粹然乾德之至精。本之無為以守正，而萬邦之度貞焉，故遠近親疎之分，以心觀之，本非有二，而曷嘗置輕重于其内也；會之精一以執中，而四方之極建焉，故去来順逆之際，以道觀之，復通為一，而曷嘗介欣戚于其間也。所以致顯比之吉者以此。彼求治太急而以有心迎之，憂民太勤而以有心留之，不亦憧憧乎小哉！吁，此王道也。王者施不期博，濟不期衆，猶天地於萬物乎！一無容心，而天下自不外也。是故有苗弗率，無損於大；防風後至，何累其功？惟自昭明德耳。自談者必以兼覆遠届為功而失其精，於是乎務勤遠略而廣其心。夫廣其心者，必有隱行矣，胡以云王道也？
translation_en: …openly shares the fundamental laws with all under heaven, which are understood without needing to be proclaimed; therefore, all under heaven abide by his laws and do not depart from them. What he practices alone within the deep palace clearly shares the constant moral relationships with all under heaven, which are trusted without needing to be spoken; therefore, all under heaven also trust his mind and do not rebel. This is what is called the good fortune of illustrious union (xianbi). How does the Nine in the Fifth place achieve this? It is because he occupies the correctness of a yang line and stands in the center of the upper trigram. Thus the imperial virtue is profound and subtle, whole as the complete substance of the Supreme Ultimate; the kingly mind is pure and unified, unmixed as the utmost essence of the virtue of Qian (Heaven). Grounding it in non-action to maintain correctness, the standards of the myriad states are rectified therein; therefore, when distinctions of distant and near, intimate and estranged are viewed through the mind, they are originally not dual, and how could he ever place differing weights upon them within himself? Uniting it in subtle singleness to hold fast the mean, the supreme standard of the four quarters is established therein; therefore, when occasions of leaving and coming, compliance and defiance are viewed through the Way, they again merge into one, and how could he ever harbor joy or sorrow between them? This is whereby he achieves the good fortune of illustrious union. As for those who seek order too anxiously and welcome people with deliberate calculation, or worry over the people tooassiduously and retain them with deliberate calculation—is this not wavering and petty indeed! Ah, this is the Kingly Way! The true king bestows without aiming at breadth and aids without aiming at multitude, just like heaven and earth toward the myriad things! Being utterly without deliberate intent, all under heaven naturally do not remain outside. Therefore, that the ruler of Miao did not submit did no harm to [Shun's] greatness; that Fangfeng arrived late—how could it blemish [Yu's] merit? They simply made bright their own illustrious virtue. Once commentators insisted on taking universal shelter and reaching the distant as merit, losing its essence, rulers thereupon strove after distant schemes and sought to broaden their minds. Now, one who seeks to broaden his mind will necessarily have hidden motives; how then can one speak of the Kingly Way?

It is as if the Great Treatise were saying: The Way of Changes is fully encompassed in Qian and Kun, and Qian and Kun are made manifest in generating things. translation_en:
…and as form comes into being, inner nature is complete; the myriad things are all brought about by Qian and Kun, and are not capable of bringing themselves about. So great is their achievement! Yet Qian has no difficulty, and Kun has no trouble. For to initiate things one by one would be difficult; but Qian is vigorous and active, so when the bellows of vital force slightly open, those that meet their season experience no obstructed mechanism—it knows them simply through ease. To bring things to completion one by one would be troublesome; but Kun is compliant and tranquil, so the crafting mind does not toil, and those that encounter their birth take on no aberrant shapes—it is capable through simplicity alone. Without speaking, things are born; without conscious intent, transformation is accomplished. Qian and Kun both act through ease and simplicity, while in reality doing nothing at all. So numinous is their virtue! Thus, their marvelous functioning communicates through images, while the master tally lies hidden without a trace; the mechanism of transformation is inwardly secluded, while daily renewal manifests itself inexhaustibly. Vast indeed is the mystery of Qian and Kun as spoken of in relation to the myriad things—how supreme are their flourishing virtue and great enterprise! Therefore, the sage models himself on Qian and Kun, having neither deliberate knowledge nor deliberate capability. Why is this? Because the world fundamentally requires no deliberate knowledge and no deliberate capability; he merely follows what knows of itself and is capable of itself, and responds to it. Thus, he dwells deep in the numinous ultimate, the six directions converge upon him like spokes at a hub, and yet no action of his is seen. Here, the single vital force is hidden beyond names and words, and the Two Modes operate marvelously of their own accord: yin and yang are already generated, cold and heat already proceed, wind and dew are already formed—what further need is there for deliberate action? Occupying the pivot of the jade sighting-tube to observe the great cycle, and grasping the essential nexus to oversee the four extremities, the universe itself does not go against him—how much less do human beings!

下有勢若甚嚴而實則可愛者矣可愛者何非
君乎天下有勢若甚微而實則可畏者矣可畏
者何非民乎蓋君也者衆所仰以治也匪后罔
戴是故有愛道焉而所以孚厥愛者則居若位
者責矣民也者邦所藉與守也匪民罔使是故
有畏道焉而所以祇厥畏者則臨若民者事矣

… is worthy of desire."

Fang Shide

Associate Examiner and Instructor Jiang comments: The phrasing is pure and elegant, and the meaning is moreover harmonious and fluent; this is an exposition on the Book of Documents worthy of being passed down.

Associate Examiner and Instructor Wu comments: He has deeply grasped the original intent of Great Shun's charge to Yu. Furthermore, the composition is orderly, clear, and refined, thorough from beginning to end; it can serve as a model for the many scholars.

Examiner and Librarian Zhou comments: The wording and meaning are gentle and complete.

Examiner and Left Admonisher Chen comments: The words are not verbose, yet the meaning is comprehensive.

By observing the mutual dependence of ruler and people, one sees that the Way of the ruler must be fulfilled to the utmost. Now, reverently cultivating what is worthy of desire is the Way of the ruler; knowing the mutual dependence of ruler and people, how could this Way not be fulfilled to the utmost?

When Emperor Shun charged Yu, it was as if he said: The Way of governance lies in nothing other than a single Equilibrium, and fulfilling the Way rests upon a single Reverence. If we examine the relationship between ruler and people, there is especially that which must not be neglected. Why is this so? In the world, there is that whose position seems exceedingly stern, yet in reality is lovable. What is lovable? Is it not the ruler? In the world, there is that whose position seems exceedingly slight, yet in reality is to be feared. What is to be feared? Is it not the people? For the ruler is the one to whom the multitude look up for governance; without the sovereign, they have no one to revere and support. Therefore, there is a way of loving him, and that by which one inspires confidence in their love is the responsibility of the one who occupies such a position. The people are those upon whom the state relies to be preserved; without the people, there is no one to employ. Therefore, there is a way of fearing them, and that by which one respectfully attends to that fear is the business of the one who presides over such people.

translation_en:
Be reverent! Bear in mind that the position of supreme sovereign is not one in which to dwell in ease and pleasure, and thus exercise cautious care upon ascending the throne; reflect that the multitude cannot be governed through indolence and neglect, and thus maintain strict vigilance when presiding over those below. That centrality be preserved in the mind—is this not your inherent desire? Then reverently cultivate the effort of refinement and single-mindedness, so that what is preserved as master within is entirely central, and nothing unwholesome arises in the mind—only then will it suffice. That centrality be manifested in affairs—is this not the shared desire of all? Then reverently cultivate the reality of heeding and employing advice, so that every response to circumstances is entirely central, and nothing unwholesome is enacted in governance—only then will it suffice. Thus you will be able to recognize the difficulty of being sovereign: above, you will truly be a ruler worthy of affection, whom the multitude will constantly support; able to attend to the reverence due the people, below there will be no populace to be feared, and the state will be constantly secure. Will you not then have been truly cautious regarding your position! Ah, Emperor Shun’s charge to Yu was earnest indeed! If we examine the Way of the sage-emperors and kings, it goes no further than centrality; yet that he added reverence to it is because reverence is the very pivot of holding fast to and applying centrality. Without reverence there is negligence—how then could the mind be preserved, and how could affairs be examined? Therefore Emperor Shun was especially earnest about reverent respect. Moreover, "reverently following" and "respectfully bestowing" are recorded in the Canon of the Emperor (Didian); truly, he had received this transmission from before.

"The many rulers of the six domains all acknowledged his virtue. Having returned to the ancestral capital of Zhou, he supervised and rectified the governing officials. The King said: 'In accordance with the grand plans of antiquity, regulate governance before disorder arises, and preserve the state before danger appears.'"
By Wang Dengcai 王登才.

…the spirit of preserving good governance; it can serve as a model for the many scholars.

Associate Examiner and Instructor Wu comments: Throughout the piece, his comprehension of the meaning of preserving good governance is extremely penetrating, and he expresses it in antique, elegant, and vigorous language. None without superiority in both learning and insight could achieve this; let it be recorded.

Examiner and Librarian Zhou comments: Dignified and weighty, like the words of a person of the Zhou dynasty.

Examiner and Left Mentor Chen comments: Profound and refined, worthy of serving as a model.

The King of Zhou achieved a governance of great harmony, and thereupon instructed his officials in order to preserve that governance. Now, for the six domains to comply with his virtue is great harmony; yet in instructing his officials to preserve good governance, he earnestly took antiquity as a mirror—he may truly be said to have understood the essentials of governance. Moreover, in the governance of the world, its outward manifestation always lies on the outside, while its root always lies within. When the King of Zhou went on inspection tours and punitive expeditions to pacify the people, he already diligently employed his illustrious virtue. Because of this, among all the rulers of the six domains, there was none who did not embody his affectionate benevolence and respectfully comply with his virtuous intentions, or obey his commands of awe and reproof and reverently conform to the royal excellence; the world was nearly in a state of order and peace. When the King returned to ancestral Zhou, how could he be without concern for the fundamental root? Only because subduing the distant always begins with the near, and when the exterior is peaceful there may be internal worries, he therefore solemnized the official regularities to cultivate internal administration, selecting the fine statutes of the state and reiterating them; and he clarified the hierarchical system to instruct all the officials, taking up the duties of the entire court and rousing and rectifying them. Thus, discipline was established and good governance was further extended, the interior was tranquil and the exterior became ever more reverent. This was the King of Zhou's intention in not forgetting disorder in times of order, and not forgetting peril in times of peace. His words were: In the eras of great counsels in antiquity, laws and measures were well-ordered and clear, and the administration was already well-governed; yet they still feared that order is where disorder lies concealed. Therefore, they always planned before events arose; even though the world did not yet show any sign of disorder, by regulating it…

translation_en:
… from within, there was the means to eradicate its buds. The imperial enterprise was consolidated and the state was already secure; yet they still feared that security is what peril leans upon. Therefore, they always prepared for it ahead of time, so that even before any sign of peril appeared in the realm, by safeguarding it from within, there was the means to guard against its gradual onset. Indeed, because they established control before disorder arose, their good governance was ever enduring; because they safeguarded the state before peril appeared, their security was easy to maintain. This is why the grand counsels of antiquity were praised for the longevity of their righteous rule. Now, although the six domains have submitted to our virtue, if internal governance is not kept in order, disorder will thereby find its stepping-stone—why not take the affairs of antiquity and observe them?”

If we examine ancient and modern times, days of order have always been few, and days of disorder have always been many. In the beginning, rulers never failed to firmly consolidate the foundation, yet in the end it sometimes fell into gradual decline and decay. There is no other reason for this: in an age of preserving the achievements of predecessors, superiors and inferiors alike indulge in lazy ease, and official duties fall into neglect and waste; consequently, internal strife and external rebellion arise, and disorder and ruin follow. This is why the “Officers of Zhou” (Zhouguan) was composed. Alas! Even with this as an admonition, there were still those whose resolve grew lax after pacifying Wu, or whose achievements were ruined after conquering Cai.

觀唐人之相戒其憂深而其思切也蓋民逸則
淫而思則善心生也以太康為戒而以居職為
思唐風之厚也至矣賦蟋蟀者之意以為難得
===
而易失者時也難制而易溺者情也惟吾與子
感蟋蟀之依人時若可自娛矣然流連者多玩
時而職之所居者易忽也是得無有之而不覺
矣乎念日月之舍我情若可自適矣然荒湛者
多蕩情而職之所居者易忘也是得無有之而
莫返矣乎欲不可縱而修其職者亦以防其欲

思唐風之厚也至矣賦蟋蟀者之意以爲難得

觀唐人之相戒，其憂深而其思切也。蓋民逸則淫，而思則善心生也。以太康為戒，而以居職為思，唐風之厚也至矣。賦《蟋蟀》者之意，以為難得而易失者時也，難制而易溺者情也。惟吾與子感蟋蟀之依人，時若可自娛矣；然流連者多玩時，而職之所居者易忽也，是得無有之而不覺矣乎？念日月之舍我，情若可自適矣；然荒湛者多蕩情，而職之所居者易忘也，是得無有之而莫返矣乎？欲不可縱，而修其職者，亦以防其欲者也。盍亦慮始於終，而小民之依謀之也惟預？樂不可極，而盡其職者，所以保其樂者也。盍亦圖難於易，而民事之急理之也必周？天時有生，

Associate Examiner Instructor (jiaoyu) Zhang comments: The conception is complete and the diction ancient. In bringing out the people of Tang's intent to moderate pleasure and be diligent in their affairs, nothing surpasses this piece.
Associate Examiner Vice Prefect (tongzhi) Yu comments: The phrasing is classic and elegant, and the mutual admonition is incisive and earnest—vividly evoking the lingering customs of Tao Tang [Yao].
Examiner Librarian (xima) Zhou comments: Measured and dignified, worthy of recitation.
Examiner Left Mentor (zuo yude) Chen comments: A pure and elegant piece.

Observing how the people of Tang admonished one another, how deep was their concern and how earnest their thought! For when the people are at ease, they fall into excess, whereas when they reflect, good intentions arise. Taking excessive pleasure as a warning and taking the duties of their station as their focus of thought, the richness of the customs of Tang reached perfection. The intent of the poet who composed "Cricket" (Xishuai) was that what is hard to obtain and easy to lose is time, and what is hard to restrain and easy to drown in is emotion. Only you and I, moved as the cricket seeks the warmth of human dwellings, might feel that the season allows us to amuse ourselves; yet those who linger in indulgence mostly waste time, and the duties of one's station are easily neglected—could we not fall into such excessive pleasure without even realizing it? Mindful that the days and months are leaving us behind, our feelings might incline us to take our ease; yet those steeped in dissipation mostly let their passions run wild, and the duties of one's station are easily forgotten—could we not fall into such excessive pleasure and be unable to turn back? Desires must not be indulged, and cultivating one's duties is also the means to guard against desires. Why not consider the end at the very beginning, and plan beforehand for what the common people depend upon? Pleasure must not be taken to extremes, and fulfilling one's duties is the means to preserve one's pleasure. Why not tackle what is difficult while it is still easy, and attend with utmost thoroughness to the urgent affairs of the people? The seasons of Heaven bring forth life, …

而所以順天之時者，吾職焉，則吾思焉，庶耕鑿之常，不改夫唐風之舊也。地利有養，而所以因地之利者，職在是，則思在是焉，庶作息之業，想見夫堯天之遺也。至是，則懼其康，可以不至于康矣；思其居，可以永安其居矣。吁！唐人之憂深而思切也如此，不可以觀聖人流風之遠乎？抑天下之事，敗於宴樂而成於憂勤者，豈特民事然哉？《書》紀《無逸》，《易》著「復隍」，怠荒之戒，古帝王所爲兢兢也。夫子刪《詩》，而繫《蟋蟀》于《唐風》之首，其旨深矣。以此爲訓，猶有以豐亨豫大之說導其君者。

鳳凰于飛，翽翽其羽，亦集爰止。藹藹王多吉士，維君子使，媚于天子。鳳凰于飛，翽翽其羽，亦傅于天。藹藹王多吉人，維君子命，媚于庶人。

translation_en:
…and as for that whereby we conform to the seasons of Heaven—where our duty lies, there too must our thoughts lie, so that the constant routines of plowing and digging wells may not alter the ancient ways of the customs of Tang. The advantages of the earth provide nourishment, and as for that whereby we avail ourselves of the earth's advantages—since our duty resides in this, our thoughts must reside in this as well, so that in the occupations of daily toil and rest one may envision the surviving legacy of the days of Yao. When it comes to this, by fearing excessive ease, one can avoid falling into such ease; by being mindful of one's station, one can forever rest secure in that station. Ah! That the people of Tang were so deep in their concern and so earnest in their thought—can we not see in this how far-reaching was the lingering influence of the Sage? Moreover, that the affairs of the world are ruined by indulgent pleasure and brought to success by anxious diligence—how could this be true only of the affairs of the common people? The Classic of History (Shu) records "Against Luxurious Ease" (Wu yi), and the Classic of Changes (Yi) sets forth the warning of "the city wall collapsing back into the moat"; precautions against indolence and neglect were what made the ancient emperors and kings so cautiously attentive. When the Master edited the Odes (Shi) and placed "Cricket" (Xishuai) at the head of the "Airs of Tang" (Tang feng), his meaning was profound indeed. Even with this as an instruction, there were still those who misled their rulers with doctrines of "abundance, prosperity, pleasure, and greatness" (feng heng yu da).

"The phoenixes fly about, their wings rustling, and they settle in their resting place. Numerous are the king's fine officers; by the lord they are employed, showing love for the Son of Heaven. The phoenixes fly about, their wings rustling, and they soar up to heaven. Numerous are the king's fine men; by the lord they are commanded, showing love for the common people." [Ode 252, "Juan A"]
By Pang Jinxian 龐進賢.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor (xundao) Tang: Concise, pure, and elegant, while the intent of admonition is gently and richly conveyed—is he not one who takes the heart of the Duke of Shao as his own heart?

詩人兩興賢才之效用，有爲上爲德者，有爲下爲民者。夫致君澤民，賢者之素志也。舉而用之，有不自效者哉？宜召公托興以諷王也。若曰：君德之成就，在賢才固也；然今日之賢才，夫豈無可用者？王知夫鳳凰乎？彼鳳凰于飛，則翽其羽而集爰止，物之來儀則然矣。况藹藹王多吉士，固王朝之羽儀也，維君子使，而有不媚于天子乎？蓋吉士具馮翼孝德之蘊，而上不負天子，固其素所期待也。誠感任使之重，則竭順愛之忱，而以亮天工，以熈帝載，必親見其道之行於上而後已矣。此固吉士所自效也，而王可無以使

Associate Examiner Instructor Cheng's comment: Refined, pure, neat, and clean; it may be recorded as a model.
Associate Examiner Instructor Zhang's comment: The loyalty of worthy talents in rendering service and the righteousness of Duke Kang of Shao (Shao Kanggong 召康公) in serving his ruler by recommending men of ability are developed almost exhaustively, while the diction is moreover handsome, elegant, and worthy of recitation.
Associate Examiner Vice Prefect Yu's comment: Tactful and full of feeling, its chanting and admonition capture the proper tone; this is someone who excels at explicating the Book of Odes (Shi 詩).
Examiner Librarian Zhou's comment: Elegant and pure.
Examiner Left Admonisher Chen's comment: Clear and lustrous.

The poet twice uses evocative imagery (xing 興) to speak of worthy talents rendering service: some act for the ruler above to cultivate his virtue, and some act for those below to benefit the common people. Now, bringing one's ruler to perfection and bestowing blessings upon the people are the longstanding aspirations of the worthy. If they are elevated and employed, how could there be any who do not exert themselves in service? Rightly did the Duke of Shao rely on evocative imagery to admonish the king! It is as if to say: That the fulfillment of the ruler's virtue rests upon worthy talents is certainly true; yet among the worthy talents of today, how could there be none fit for employment? Does the king know of the phoenixes? When those phoenixes take flight, their wings rustle in a crowd as they gather and come to rest where they abide—such is the way creatures come in stately bearing. How much more so the many fine gentlemen (jishi 吉士) crowding in harmony around the king, who are truly the plumed ornaments of the royal court! Only let the sovereign employ them, and could any fail to show loving devotion to the Son of Heaven? For fine gentlemen possess the inner substance to serve as supports, wings, and exemplars of filial virtue, and above, not failing the Son of Heaven is indeed what they have always expected of themselves. If they are truly moved by the weight of being entrusted and employed, they will exhaust their sincerity of compliant affection to aid the work of Heaven and make resplendent the undertakings of the sovereign, never stopping until they personally witness their Way carried out above. This is assuredly how the fine gentlemen exert themselves in service—and how could the king fail to employ…

「五月癸丑，公會晉侯、齊侯、宋公、蔡侯、鄭伯、衛子、莒子，盟于踐土。」〔僖公二十有八年〕

translation_en:
… employ them? When the male and female phoenixes fly, their wings rustle and they soar up to heaven—such is the way creatures act as auspicious omens. How much more so the many admirable men of the king, so thriving and numerous, who are truly the supreme auspicious omens of a rare age! Once commanded by the sovereign, could they fail to show loving care toward the common people? For these admirable men cherish plans grounded in supportive and filial virtue, and not failing the living people below is what they have always ardently aspired to. If they truly receive the high favor of animperial charge, they will broaden the transforming influence of harmonious affection, enriching the people's livelihood and rectifying the people's virtue, and they will not stop until they personally see their Way put into practice among those below. This is indeed how admirable men devote themselves—so how could the king fail to give them his command?

Ah! Subtle indeed was Duke Kang's intent in admonishing the king. I have examined the antiphonal songs of the court of Yu, which sang, "How excellent are the legs and arms [the ministers]!" And when the ode "Curving Slope" (Juan'e) voiced its tones, it showed unceasing earnestness toward admirable gentlemen and admirable men. For the state's need for the worthy is deeply urgent, and veteran statesmen acting on behalf of the state are especially intent upon employing the worthy. As the saying goes, "The highest minister serves his ruler by means of men." This describes the Duke! Those who recite the verses on the "rustling wings" may well be inspired by them!

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

"In the fifth month, on the guichou day, the Duke met with the Marquis of Jin, the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Cai, the Earl of Zheng, the Viscount of Wei, and the Viscount of Ju, and made a covenant at Jiantu." [Twenty-eighth year of Duke Xi]

"In the sixth month, on the guiyou day, Jisun Xingfu, Zangsun Xu, Shusun Qiaoru, and Gongsun Yingqi led a force to join Xi Ke of Jin, Sun Liangfu of Wei, and Prince Shou of Cao, and fought with the Marquis of Qi at An; the army of Qi suffered a潰rout." [Duke Cheng, …]

One who repels external foes and presents his achievements may be praised; one who oppresses internal states and presents his achievements deserves criticism. Now, presenting spoils of victory is one and the same act, yet whether they are won from the barbarian tribes or from the Central States determines whether the affair is admirable or reprehensible. Moreover, from the time the King descended to comfort the troops at Jiantu and the captives of Chu were arrayed, to the time the army returned from the battle of An [written 鞏 in text] and Gong Shuo 鞏朔 was dispatched—both of these campaigns alike involved presenting spoils to the King, yet their merits and faults differed. Why is this?

I have heard that when the Man, Yi, Rong, and Di barbarians indulge in excess and destroy normal order, and the King commands a punitive expedition against them, one thereupon presents the achievements of war. Who was the ruler of Chu? He was a barbarian who usurped the title of King, and the disaster of his hostility shook the Central Lands. Duke Wen [of Jin] joined the armies of four states and crushed him at a single stroke—this achievement of his may indeed be called magnificent! Then he gathered the captives of a hundred chariots, went to Hengyong, and personally presented them. Internally, this manifested the majesty of shared righteous anger against the King's enemies; externally, it displayed a warning by striking and punishing them. This was truly worthy of being a celebrated tale! At that time, the King of Zhou feasted him with sweet wine and sent the head of the Yin 尹 clan to bestow a charge upon him, saying: "The King says to his uncle: 'Inspect and banish those who are evil toward the King.'" When Wen received the brevet and went forth, how could it not have been glorious?

之於是乎告事齊何人也是太師之後也夾輔
之勳載在盟府晉也憤起一戰遂摟而伐之即
有功奚足多者顧乃誇三周之捷望鞏洛而有
獻焉上昧乎尊獎之誼下乖乎親睦之情不過
逞其侈心而已維時周王弗見而使單襄公致

之，於是乎告事。齊何人也？是太師之後也，夾輔之勳，載在盟府。晉也憤起一戰，遂摟而伐之，即有功，奚足多者？顧乃誇三周之捷，望鞏、洛而有獻焉，上昧乎尊獎之誼，下乖乎親睦之情，不過逞其侈心而已。維時周王弗見，而使單襄公致之辭曰：「敢廢舊典，以忝叔父？」士莊伯之不能對也，得無有慙也耶？吁！山戎之捷，其為不必獻均也，矧不獻于周而遺之魯乎？是故《春秋》譏之。抑尤有可慨者，踐土之盟，出入三覲，雖曰晉文譎而不正，然共主之分尚存也。迨其後嗣，先業弗修，而悖道以逞。定王雖拒其使，猶且委之于三吏，將之以厚賄，蓋上下之陵替乆矣，君子深為王道憂焉。

… them, and thereupon one merely reports the matter. Who was Qi? He was the descendant of the Grand Preceptor (Taishi), whose meritorious service in flanking and assisting the royal house was recorded in the repository of covenants. Yet Jin, roused by anger into a single battle, dragged the allies along to attack him. Even if there was military success, how was it worth praising? Instead, Jin boasted of the victory of chasing Qi thrice around Huabuzhu, and looking toward Gong and Luo, presented captives there. Above, this was blind to the duty of honoring and encouraging the royal house; below, it violated the feelings of kinship and harmony. It was nothing more than indulging an arrogant and extravagant heart. At that time, the King of Zhou refused to receive the envoy in audience, sending Duke Xiang of Shan (Shan Xianggong 單襄公) to deliver this message: "How would I dare abolish the old statutes and thereby disgrace my uncle?" When Shi Zhuangbo 士莊伯 was unable to reply, how could he not have felt ashamed? Alas! As for Qi's victory over the Mountain Rong (Shanrong 山戎), it was equally unnecessary to present captives—how much more so when they were not presented to Zhou, but sent to Lu instead! Therefore the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) criticizes it. Yet there is something even more lamentable: at the covenant of Jiantu, Duke Wen of Jin went in and out for three audiences with the King. Although it is said that Duke Wen of Jin was crafty and not upright, the distinction of the common sovereign still remained. By the time of his descendants, the ancestral enterprise was no longer cultivated, and they violated the proper way to indulge themselves. Although King Ding (Dingwang 定王) rejected Jin's envoy, he still entrusted him to the three officials and sent him off with generous gifts. Indeed, the subversion and decline of superior and inferior had gone on for a long time, and the gentleman was deeply worried for the Kingly Way.

"In spring, Gongsun Guifu met the Viscount of Chu at Song." Fifteenth year of Duke Xuan.
By Yang Quan 楊銓.

考試官左諭德陳批善發明傳意
春秋鄙望國之賄夷以示經世之畧也夫以中
國制夷狄此經世之畧也不競如魯者至于荐
賄以免焉不亦鄙乎楚方圍宋魯人懼焉是以
有歸父之會夫小國之免于大國此其常也春
秋何鄙乎爾蓋夷夏之勢互為盛衰者也然勢
之盛衰雖乘乎天運而實關于經畧楚夷也無
故而凌上公之宋天下勢可知矣魯為人望列
辟宗之力苟及焉則鼓行赴救以摧蠢爾之鋒
===
力不及焉則遥為聲援以存中國之體豈異人
任哉柰何君臣動色共軫剥牀之憂而上卿奉
使僅從賄免之策楚何人也馮陵之惡上通于
天非三恪賓王之類也媚楚而棄宋謂之不順
宋何地也攻圍之慘朝不及夕非玉帛綢繆之
地也即宋而賄楚謂之不祥向也楚雖横而猶
懼天下之擬其後也以周公之裔而荐賄之不
遑中國之無人也已知之矣向也宋雖困而猶

《春秋》鄙望國之賄夷，以示經世之畧也。夫以中國制夷狄，此經世之畧也。不競如魯者，至于荐賄以免焉，不亦鄙乎？楚方圍宋，魯人懼焉，是以有歸父之會。夫小國之免于大國，此其常也，《春秋》何鄙乎爾？蓋夷夏之勢，互為盛衰者也；然勢之盛衰，雖乘乎天運，而實關于經畧。楚，夷也，無故而凌上公之宋，天下勢可知矣。魯為人望，列辟宗之。力苟及焉，則鼓行赴救，以摧蠢爾之鋒；力不及焉，則遥為聲援，以存中國之體，豈異人任哉？柰何君臣動色，共軫剥牀之憂，而上卿奉使，僅從賄免之策！楚何人也？馮陵之惡，上通于天，非三恪賓王之類也，媚楚而棄宋，謂之不順；宋何地也？攻圍之慘，朝不及夕，非玉帛綢繆之地也，即宋而賄楚，謂之不祥。向也，楚雖横，而猶懼天下之擬其後也；以周公之裔，而荐賄之不遑，中國之無人也，已知之矣。向也，宋雖困，而猶冀天下之拯其窮也；以千乘之邦，而事楚如弗…

The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) disdains a prestigious state's bribing of barbarians, so as to demonstrate the strategy for ordering the world. Now, using the Central States to control the barbarians—this is the strategy for ordering the world. For a state as uncompetitive as Lu to go so far as offering repeated bribes in order to escape trouble—is that not despicable? Chu was just then besieging Song, and the people of Lu were afraid; therefore there was the meeting conducted by Guifu. Now, for a small state to seek exemption from a great state is the normal course of things; why then did the Spring and Autumn Annals disdain it? It is because the relative power of barbarians and the Chinese states rises and falls in turn; yet although the rise and fall of power rides upon the destiny of Heaven, in reality it hinges upon statecraft and strategy. Chu was a barbarian state; when without cause it bullied Song, the state of a Superior Duke, the trend of the world could readily be known. Lu was looked up to by others, and the various rulers honored it as a model. Had its strength been sufficient, it should have beaten its drums and marched to the rescue to crush the edge of those wriggling savages; had its strength been insufficient, it should have lent moral support from afar to preserve the dignity of the Central States—how could this be anyone else's responsibility? Why then did ruler and ministers change countenance, jointly grieving over the danger of calamity reaching their own bed, while a senior minister sent on a mission merely followed the policy of escaping through bribery! What sort of people was Chu? The evil of their arrogant aggression reached up to Heaven; they were not of the same kind as the Three Revered Lineages who were guests of the King. To flatter Chu and abandon Song is what is called being unprincipled. What sort of place was Song? The misery of its siege was such that morning could not guarantee evening; it was no place for exchanging jade and silk in cordial diplomacy. To go right to Song in order to bribe Chu is what is called being inauspicious. Previously, although Chu was domineering, it still feared that the world might move against its rear; when the descendants of the Duke of Zhou had no leisure for anything but offering repeated bribes, Chu already knew that there were no true men left in the Central States. Previously, although Song was hard-pressed, it still hoped that the world would rescue it from its distress; when a state of a thousand chariots served Chu as if fearing not to…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
及南風之日競也又奚怪矣是諸夏非自衰也
有賄楚之魯諸夏安得不衰夷狄非自盛也有
屈體之魯夷狄安得不盛故經世者不爲強怵
不爲弱沮要使制命之權常在內而效命之勢
常在外然後夷夏各止其所而天下定矣後之
人此事以觀而得經世之畧焉此聖人筆之于
經之意也雖然以弱爲強難言哉夫爲國不先
自治而徒以力與犬羊競者是自敗之道也即
強且不足恃況弱乎唯內治無闕則夷狄之逆
===
順皆不足較何者外之也夫知外夷狄之義者
可與語經世之畧矣
禮記
夫樂者先王之所以飾喜也軍旅鈇鉞者
先王之所以飾怒也故先王之喜怒皆
得其儕焉喜則天下和之怒則暴亂者
畏之先王之道禮樂可謂盛矣

及，南風之日競也，又奚怪矣！是諸夏非自衰也，有賄楚之魯，諸夏安得不衰？夷狄非自盛也，有屈體之魯，夷狄安得不盛？故經世者不爲強怵，不爲弱沮，要使制命之權常在內，而效命之勢常在外，然後夷夏各止其所，而天下定矣。後之人此事以觀，而得經世之畧焉，此聖人筆之于經之意也。雖然，以弱爲強，難言哉！夫爲國不先自治，而徒以力與犬羊競者，是自敗之道也，即強且不足恃，況弱乎？唯內治無闕，則夷狄之逆順皆不足較。何者？外之也。夫知外夷狄之義者，可與語經世之畧矣。
《禮記》
夫樂者，先王之所以飾喜也；軍旅鈇鉞者，先王之所以飾怒也。故先王之喜怒，皆得其儕焉。喜則天下和之，怒則暴亂者畏之。先王之道，禮樂可謂盛矣。
張主敬

translation_en:
… reach them in time, what wonder is it that the southern power of Chu grew stronger day by day! Thus, the Chinese states (Zhuxia) did not decline of their own accord; with a state like Lu bribing Chu, how could the Chinese states not decline? The barbarians (Yidi) did not flourish of their own accord; with a state like Lu abasing itself, how could the barbarians not flourish? Therefore, one who orders the world is neither cowed by strength nor discouraged by weakness; the essential point is to ensure that the authority to command always rests within, while the posture of rendering obedience always remains without. Only then will Chinese and barbarian each abide in their proper place, and the world be settled. When people of later times examine these events in conjunction and grasp the strategy for ordering the world therefrom, this is the very intent for which the Sage recorded them in the Classic. Even so, turning weakness into strength is difficult to speak of! In governing a state, if one does not first put oneself in order, and merely contends in strength with dogs and sheep, that is the way to self-defeat; even strength cannot be relied upon in that case, how much less weakness? Only when internal governance is without flaw are the defiance or submission of the barbarians not worth reckoning with. Why is this? Because one treats them as external. Indeed, one who understands the principle of treating the barbarians as external is worthy of discussing the strategy for ordering the world.

Therefore the joy and anger of the former kings both found their proper counterparts. When they were joyful, all under heaven harmonized with them; when they were angry, the violent and disorderly feared them. In the Way of the former kings, rites and music may be called flourishing indeed."

Zhang Zhujing 張主敬

Contemplating the transforming influence of the sage kings’ rites and music, one perceives the greatness of their Way. Indeed, when joy and anger are adorned and the world responds with harmony and awe, that is the completed transformation of rites and music—how great then is their Way! Moreover, the governance of the world is brought about by the Way of the world. Where the Way is rooted in the ruler’s person and its transforming influence is attested among the people, I have observed this in the rites and music of the former kings. Truly, with the rise of every dynasty, there must be rites and music; and being stirred by things into motion, who is without joy and anger? What is music for? It is that by which the former kings adorned their joy—an instrument of peace and harmony, born only after taking joy in the world’s joy. What are armies and battle-axes for? They are that by which the former kings adorned their anger—statutes of punitive expedition, instituted out of shame that the world should fall into disorder. Now, with joy and anger, the only fear is that they cannot be properly adorned. When adorned with rites and music, their expressions all hit the proper measure; not merely indulging one’s own private inclinations, the Way brings like together with like and can truly share in what others deem right—how could they fail to find their proper counterpart? Thus, the king only refrains from rejoicing; once he rejoices, the whole world is pleased and harmoniously responds in unison, because what he adorns with music is for the sake of the world and not for himself. And he only refrains from anger; once he is angry, the violent and disorderly are terrified and submissively stand in awe, because what he adorns with armies and battle-axes is on account of the violent and disorderly and not for himself.
