translation_en:
… the application of rites and music is flourishing. In establishing the supreme standard, there is no selfishness, so that rewards and punishments, penalties and awe all accord with the rule of equilibrium and harmony; in moving and inspiring trust, there is no gap, so that the sagely and divine achievements and transformations draw sufficiency from the constancy of joy and anger. That emperors and kings yielded in courtesy and brought about order, and that the noble man exerted himself in this to achieve great peace—all of it is this very thing, so how can it not be called flourishing? Thus, when the former kings governed, they carried out the Way of rites and music to the utmost and were cautious about that by which they moved people. Moreover, the harmony and order of rites and music are rooted in human feelings. Human feelings change in many ways; how could the sage kings merely indulge them? Yet how could they go against them either? Therefore, they did not cause people to rejoice or be angry out of caprice, but shared their joy and anger publicly with the people. Only when desires and aversions are balanced and each person's lot and wishes are satisfied does the teaching of harmony and order prevail and compliant order come about. Hence it is said: "When music reaches its culmination, there is no resentment; when rites reach their culmination, there is no contention." Could this be done through artifice? Indeed, by looking at the odes "Spirit Tower" (Lingtai) and "August Indeed" (Huangyi), one understands the transforming influence seen in "The Jiang and the Han" (Jiang Han) and "The Banks of the Ru" (Rufen). What the House of Zhou called rites and music was like this.

於心也以此自盡而有二乎哉祭統君子意曰
賢者之所謂備固言內盡於己而外順於道矣
抑何言乎己之盡耶誠以吾人一身君臣父子
之倫屬焉臣之事君孰不知之顧事之而或猶
夫臣也不有忠臣以事其君者乎真見義不可
逃而凡夙夜匪懈承弼一人者純乎忠而已矣
子之事親孰不知之顧事之而或猶夫子也不
有孝子以事其親者乎真見恩不可解而凡明
發不寐有懷二人者純乎孝而已矣夫其所以
===
事君親者若此是倫之秩諸天也雖殊心之盡
諸己也則一逺之事君情非親矣而惟忠臣之
於君未有不自盡者也故輸忠猶所以全孝也
邇之事親分非君矣而惟孝子之於親未有不
自盡者也故崇孝猶所以作忠也遇君而忠遇
親而孝所遇不同均竭吾職分之當然爲子思
孝爲臣思忠所思不同均畢吾性分之能事此
豈有二心哉故曰其本一也是之謂內盡而達
斯順矣體斯備矣惟賢者能之此其所以受福

translation_en:
…in the mind; in thus fulfilling one's utmost with them, how could there be any duality?

The meaning of the gentleman in the "Summary of Sacrifices" (Jitong) is this: What a worthy calls "completeness" certainly means inwardly fulfilling one's utmost in oneself and outwardly complying with the Way; yet what is meant by fulfilling one's utmost in oneself? Truly it is because in our single person, the human relations of ruler and minister, father and son, are bound together. That a minister serves his ruler—who does not know this? Yet in serving him, one might still be just an ordinary minister. Is there not the loyal minister who serves his ruler? Truly seeing that righteousness cannot be escaped, in all his not slackening day and night to assist and support the One Man, he is purely loyal and nothing more. That a son serves his parents—who does not know this? Yet in serving them, one might still be just an ordinary son. Is there not the filial son who serves his parents? Truly seeing that the debt of grace cannot be dissolved, in all his lying awake until dawn, cherishing thoughts of his two parents, he is purely filial and nothing more.

Now, that whereby one serves ruler and parents being such as this, although the ordering of these relations by Heaven is distinct, the fulfilling of the mind's utmost within oneself is one and the same. In serving one's ruler from afar, the affection is not that of kin; yet only with a loyal minister toward his ruler is there never a failure to fulfill his utmost—therefore, rendering loyalty is just how one perfects filial piety. In serving one's parents close at hand, the status is not that of a ruler; yet only with a filial son toward his parents is there never a failure to fulfill his utmost—therefore, exalting filial piety is just how one arouses loyalty.

Meeting with a ruler and being loyal, meeting with parents and being filial—what one meets with differs, yet both exhaust what is right and proper to our allotted duty. As a son, thinking of filial piety; as a minister, thinking of loyalty—what one thinks of differs, yet both complete the capabilities of our allotted nature. How could there be two minds in this? Therefore it says, "their root is one." This is what is called inwardly fulfilling one's utmost; and when extended, there is compliance; when embodied, there is completeness. Only a worthy is capable of this—is this not why he receives blessings…

歟！昔夫子自言「祭則受福」，而記者以為「得其道」。夫道曷有大於忠孝哉？吾觀夫子進曾、閔，退沮、溺，身任君父之大倫，而至為子為臣之節，即食息起居靡不周慎。彼其得道如此，則天且不違，而况鬼神乎？是百順而一本，通乎幽明之理也。《詩》曰：「豈弟君子，求福不回。」其夫子是謂矣。

第貳塲
論
人君所以端拱無為
王士昌〔同考試官教諭楊批：「塲中作者多牽涉浮詞，殊覺可厭。此作發『無為』本之君心無逸，意切而詞渾，宜錄以式。」考試官洗馬周批：「詞氣雄渾，至說君心處，尤極精實。謂探本之論，非耶？」考試官左諭德陳批：「就題立說，切近明實，而意亦周匝。錄之以變文之競騁浮詞者。」〕

…[that this is why he receives blessings]! In the past, the Master himself said, "When I sacrifice, I receive blessings," and the recorder of the *Record of Rites* considered this to mean that he "attained the Way." Now, what aspect of the Way is greater than loyalty and filial piety? When we observe how the Master commended Zeng Shen and Min Ziqian while rejecting Changju and Jieni, how he personally shouldered the great human relationships of ruler and father, and how, down to the finest points of conduct as a son and a subject, he was thoroughly circumspect even in his eating, resting, and daily movements—since he attained the Way to such a degree, even Heaven did not oppose him, how much less the ghosts and spirits! This is how the hundred compliances spring from a single root, penetrating the principles of both the unseen and the manifest realms. The *Book of Odes* says: "Easy and self-possessed was our prince, seeking for blessings not回 [crookedly]." Surely this speaks of the Master!

Discourse
"How the Ruler Rules in Composed Non-Action with Folded Hands"

Comment by Examiner Librarian Zhou: "Its style and spirit are vigorous and profound, and when it comes to discussing the ruler's mind, it is especially precise and substantial. title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
端拱致焉是何故哉天下之大豈能晏然待理
而爲之鮮要力不暇給聖王知心者宰治之樞
而恒以逸失之逸則從欲而滋亂非以爲天下
也兢兢焉憂勤以務之惟恐一違於道是非爲
過慮也將防其晏安之心不使爲吾治累也而
終之被其成功焉甚大蓋吾心日運於天下則
所圖皆得其要而君道可不勞舉矣聖王無爲
而治者其以是歟宋儒胡氏知要者也其言曰
憂勤如此所以端拱無爲夫無爲之治尚矣說
===
蓋昉于孔子曰無爲而治惟舜者歟舜之無爲
豈遺棄萬務一無作用之謂哉蓋際時獨盛而
順君道以爲故享治若斯之極也或者不察遂
貶勤勵而尚恭默薄事功而跂神化謂端冕垂
旒拱揖羣后無爲之體也而爲擊柝授環之規
過矣東封西禪勒頌名德無爲之事也而爲櫛
風沐雨之功勞矣韜甲枕戈受符獻瑞無爲之
業也而爲衣袽復隍之戒迂矣如此者可示神
明於下也嗟乎治天下甚哉其難之也日接萬

punctuated:
端拱致焉，是何故哉？天下之大，豈能晏然待理？而爲之鮮要，力不暇給。聖王知心者宰治之樞，而恒以逸失之。逸則從欲而滋亂，非以爲天下也。兢兢焉憂勤以務之，惟恐一違於道。是非爲過慮也，將防其晏安之心，不使爲吾治累也，而終之被其成功焉甚大。蓋吾心日運於天下，則所圖皆得其要，而君道可不勞舉矣。聖王無爲而治者，其以是歟！

宋儒胡氏，知要者也。其言曰：「憂勤如此，所以端拱無爲。」夫無爲之治尚矣，說蓋昉于孔子，曰：「無爲而治，惟舜者歟！」舜之無爲，豈遺棄萬務、一無作用之謂哉？蓋際時獨盛，而順君道以爲，故享治若斯之極也。或者不察，遂貶勤勵而尚恭默，薄事功而跂神化。謂端冕垂旒、拱揖羣后，無爲之體也，而爲擊柝授環之規過矣；東封西禪、勒頌名德，無爲之事也，而爲櫛風沐雨之功勞矣；韜甲枕戈、受符獻瑞，無爲之業也，而爲衣袽復隍之戒迂矣。如此者，可示神明於下也。嗟乎！治天下甚哉其難之也！日接萬…
translation_en:
… it is achieved by sitting upright with hands folded. What is the reason for this? Given the vastness of All-under-Heaven, how could it simply await ordering in quiet comfort? Yet if in governing it one lacks what is essential, one's strength will not suffice. The sage-kings knew that the mind is the pivot that presides over governance, and that it is constantly lost through ease. When at ease, one follows desires and breeds disorder; that is not the way to govern the world. Cautiously and anxiously, they applied themselves with diligence and care, fearing only that in a single instance they might depart from the Way. This was not excessive worry; it was to guard against a mind inclined toward indulgent ease, lest it become a burden to their governance—and in the end, the resulting achievements that spread over the realm were great indeed. For when our mind operates daily over the world, whatever we plan grasps the essential, and the Way of the ruler can be carried out without toil. That the sage-kings governed through non-action—was it not by means of this?

The Song Confucian Master Hu (Hu Yin 胡寅) understood the essential. His words state: "Being anxious and diligent like this is the means by which one sits upright with folded hands in non-action." Now, governance by non-action is of great antiquity; the doctrine originated with Confucius, who said: "May not Shun be instanced as having governed through non-action?" How could Shun's non-action mean abandoning the myriad affairs of state and exercising no activity whatsoever? Rather, he met with an uniquely flourishing age and acted in accordance with the Way of the ruler, and therefore enjoyed governance at such a pinnacle. Some, failing to examine this, consequently disparage diligence and exertion while exalting reverent silence, slight practical achievements while standing on tiptoe for miraculous transformation. They claim that wearing the ceremonial crown with hanging jade pendants and bowing with folded hands to the assembled lords is the substance of non-action, whereas taking precautions like beating the night-watch clapper or bestowing the jade ring of vigilance is excessive; that performing the feng sacrifice in the east and the shan sacrifice in the west and inscribing eulogies to celebrated virtue are the affairs of non-action, whereas achievements won by combing one's hair in the wind and bathing in the rain are mere drudgery; that sheathing armor and resting on spears while receiving auspicious tallies and presented omens are the enterprise of non-action, whereas heeding the warnings of rags for caulking leaks and a city wall collapsing back into its moat (from the Book of Changes) is pedantic. By acting in such a manner, they think they can display divine illumination to those below! Alas! How exceedingly difficult it is to govern All-under-Heaven! Daily attending to the myriad…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
幾宵衣旰食猶懼弗勝矣奈之何以此治哉藉
令此足以治即託優游之美號享垂裳之休際
胡不得哉而理固不可也嘗觀天立君之意矣
使一人臨制六合詎徒以崇高富貴之極娛樂
之已乎欲其御宇握中體元經世宰制羣動役
使萬物屬之者甚大也既大屬之則當副之矣
思副之則當為之矣然君承天以為也有要焉
豈必課文例之具執操切之術役形疲力而事
斷物料之哉則拘儒所云有司庶吏之為世出
===
於此未有不敝者而乃執以論聖王之治哉聖
王之治不求之天下而求之乎無逸之心也何
也古今之治大抵以勤而成以逸而敗然勤生
於不足逸恣於無制蓋人情盡然而兩者又交
相勝也況君者尊居九重奔走萬國而莫敢不
供其威何弗逞也事務變化紛至沓來自我管
攝其勢可厭也聲色玩好日陳於前為我酖毒
其情易溺也挾難犯之威乘可厭之勢攻以易
溺之欲而心始侈然以縱自非深制之有不耽

translation_en: … affairs, dressing before dawn and eating after dusk, one still fears being unequal to the task—how then could one govern by such means? Even supposing such means were sufficient for governance, how could one not adopt the fine title of leisurely ease and enjoy a blessed era of governing with robes hanging down? Yet in principle this is certainly impossible. I have observed Heaven's intention in establishing a ruler: when it causes one man to oversee and control the six directions of the universe, is it merely to amuse him with the utmost heights of exalted status, wealth, and honor? Rather, it desires that he command the realm and grasp the center, embody the primal origin to order the world, govern all movements, and employ the myriad things—what is entrusted to him is immense indeed. Since an immense charge is entrusted to him, he ought to fulfill it; wishing to fulfill it, he ought to act upon it. Yet when a ruler acts in accordance with Heaven, there is an essential point to it. Why must he assess the tools of written regulations, cling to the techniques of harsh urgency, exhaust his body and weary his strength, judging every affair and calculating every matter? That is what narrow-minded scholars call "the work of functionaries and minor officials"; whenever the world proceeds from this, it never fails to fall into ruin—how then can one cling to it in discussing the governance of the sage kings? The governance of the sage kings is sought not in the world at large, but in a mind free of idleness. Why is this? Governance past and present has generally succeeded through diligence and failed through idleness. Yet diligence arises from a sense of insufficiency, while idleness runs rampant from a lack of restraint; human nature is entirely thus, and the two constantly prevail over one another in turn. How much more so for the ruler, who dwells in exalted state within the ninefold palace enclosure, sending the myriad states scurrying in service with none daring not to provide for him—what display of his majesty could not be indulged? As affairs transform and arrive in a tumultuous throng, all under his personal supervision, the circumstances easily breed weariness; as pleasing sounds, beauties, and curiosities are arrayed before him daily to act as poison to him, his passions are easily drowned in them. Possessing an awe-inspiring majesty that is hard to offend, riding upon circumstances that easily breed weariness, and assailed by desires in which it is easy to drown, his mind begins to grow extravagant and unrestrained. title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
逸樂為美事詆憂勤為過計蓋無幾矣夫一念
勤若甚微也而兢惕而警戒而抑畏而嚴恭日
進於勤而莫知逸矣一念逸若無傷也而昏迷
而怠棄而狎侮而盤游日流於逸而莫知勤矣
茲治忽所關也豈細故哉聖王知其然臨至尊
之位不異虎尾履盈成之祚不異春冰馭兆民
之衆不異朽索明廷以及深宮何地非勤即幽
獨弗敢逸也居處以及服御何事非勤即觴几
弗敢逸也聽政以及燕閒何時非勤即終食弗
===
敢逸也常伯以及虎賁何人非勤即工瞽弗敢
逸也閔閔皇皇不使縱情娛志之事一投其隙
而歆然若有所制聖王為天下未嘗一時而少
暇矣豈過于拘攣委瑣不觧自崇重之為利哉
誠見勤于有為乃可以無為而制心制事之要
未有易此者如之何敢逸也無逸故心清心清
故嗜慾節無逸故心存心存故志氣奮無逸故
心虛心虛故義理明憂勤之事以心圖之則主
術運而無迹君道要而可舉由是則百職効能

punctuated: 逸樂為美事、詆憂勤為過計，蓋無幾矣。夫一念勤，若甚微也，而兢惕、而警戒、而抑畏、而嚴恭，日進於勤而莫知逸矣；一念逸，若無傷也，而昏迷、而怠棄、而狎侮、而盤游，日流於逸而莫知勤矣。茲治忽所關也，豈細故哉？聖王知其然，臨至尊之位不異虎尾，履盈成之祚不異春冰，馭兆民之衆不異朽索。明廷以及深宮，何地非勤？即幽獨弗敢逸也；居處以及服御，何事非勤？即觴几弗敢逸也；聽政以及燕閒，何時非勤？即終食弗敢逸也；常伯以及虎賁，何人非勤？即工瞽弗敢逸也。閔閔皇皇，不使縱情娛志之事一投其隙，而歆然若有所制。聖王為天下，未嘗一時而少暇矣。豈過于拘攣委瑣，不觧自崇重之為利哉？誠見勤于有為乃可以無為，而制心制事之要未有易此者，如之何敢逸也？無逸故心清，心清故嗜慾節；無逸故心存，心存故志氣奮；無逸故心虛，心虛故義理明。憂勤之事以心圖之，則主術運而無迹，君道要而可舉。由是，則百職効能，
translation_en: …in comfort and pleasure as a fine thing and disparaging anxious diligence as excessive calculation would be few indeed. Now, a single thought of diligence may seem extremely slight, yet through apprehension and vigilance, through caution and admonition, through humble awe, and through stern reverence, one advances daily in diligence and knows nothing of idleness. A single thought of idleness may seem harmless, yet through befuddlement, through negligent abandonment, through familiar insolence, and through excursion and revelry, one drifts daily into idleness and knows nothing of diligence. This is where order and disorder hinge; how could it be a trivial matter? The sage kings knew this to be so. Occupying the position of supreme honor was no different to them from treading on a tiger's tail; walking upon athrone of fullness and achievement was no different from treading on spring ice; driving the multitude of the millions of people was no different from holding rotten reins. From the bright court to the inner palace, what place is not for diligence? Even in secluded solitude they did not dare take their ease. From their dwelling to their robes and equipage, what affair is not for diligence? Even at the wine goblet and armrest they did not dare take their ease. From hearing governance to moments of leisure, what time is not for diligence? Even for the space of a single meal they did not dare take their ease. From the Permanent Senior Advisors (changbo) to the Imperial Guardsmen (huben), what person is not for diligence? Even among the blind musicians they did not dare take their ease. Anxiously and urgently, they did not allow anything that indulges the passions or amuses the will to find a single opening to enter, remaining ever circumspect as though held in check. In governing the world, the sage kings never had a single moment of slight leisure. Was it that they were overly bound and petty, not understanding the advantage of exalting and dignifying themselves? Truly they saw that only by being diligent in active exertion can one achieve non-action, and that the essential way of mastering the mind and mastering affairs cannot be exchanged for anything else—how then could they dare take their ease? Because they are without idleness, their minds are clear; because their minds are clear, their desires are moderated. Because they are without idleness, their minds are preserved; because their minds are preserved, their will and spirit are roused. Because they are without idleness, their minds are receptive; because their minds are receptive, moral principles are illuminated. When the affairs of anxious diligence are planned within the mind, the ruler's art operates without leaving a trace, and the way of the sovereign is grasped in its essentials and can be carried out. From this, the hundred offices devote their abilities…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
□庶績咸熈也由是則巍然穆清以登上理而
恭巳受成也皆曰聖王之治如此乎振越千代
矣孰知爲之爲者自有在也猶於穆不已天以
神運而生成不測勤勵不息聖王以心運而治
功不顯故曰爲天下者不踰皇序而神通四海
此之謂矣彼云不輕有爲者無亦未察其所以
治哉聖王之所以治則順時通變因人盡能用
心於天下而不以私智擾之侈心弛之也無爲
而無不爲者也務玄寂失事幾因循頹廢而以
===
无心棄天下非聖王無爲也世俗之兀然無爲
也無爲果若此耳人君一目眄色授焉而天下
平矣何用孜孜商確爲哉嗟乎三家之市一日
不理牧其家計矣千金之子一日不籌隳其故
業矣況天下乎欲安坐而委置之此逸心也此
庸主欣豔爲得志也而豈聖王所恃爲理者邪
抑胡不引舜文之事觀之也舜自攝位以至登
庸命官咨牧封山濬川察器觀象之事皆身爲
之一歲周巡于五岳之間車轍馬迹且近萬里

translation_en: … [and] all achievements are resplendent. Through this, he stands lofty in serene purity to ascend to supreme governance, holding himself in reverence and receiving the completed work. Everyone says: "How the governance of the sage-king transcends a thousand generations like this!" Yet who knows that the exertion behind his action has its own source? Just as the profound solemnity of Heaven never ceases, Heaven operates through spirit and its generation and completion are unfathomable; untiring in diligence and exertion, the sage-king operates through his mind and the merits of his governance are gloriously manifest. Therefore it is said: "He who governs the world does not step beyond the imperial hall, yet his spirit reaches throughout the four seas"—this is what is meant. As for those who say one should not lightly take action, have they not failed to examine the means by which he achieves governance? The means by which the sage-king achieves governance is to accord with the times and adapt to changes, rely on others to exhaust their abilities, and apply his mind to the world without disturbing it with private cleverness or slackening it with an extravagant heart; he does nothing, yet nothing is left undone. To pursue abstruse quiescence, miss the critical moments of affairs, follow conventions in decadent neglect, and abandon the world with an unconcerned mind—this is not the non-action of a sage-king, but the stolidity and non-action of the vulgar world. If non-action were truly like this, a ruler could bring peace to the world with a single glance or a hint of his countenance—what need would there be for tireless deliberation? Alas! In a market of three households, if it is not managed for a single day, its family livelihood is ruined [?]; for the son of a family worth a thousand pieces of gold, if he does not plan for a single day, he destroys his ancestral estate—how much more so the empire! To wish to sit idly and cast it aside—this is an indolent mind, this is what a mediocre ruler admires and delights in as having attained his ambitions, yet how could it be what a sage-king relies upon to achieve order? Moreover, why not cite the deeds of Shun and King Wen to observe this? From the time Shun acted as regent until he ascended the throne, in matters of appointing officials and consulting the regional pastors, raising altars on mountains and dredging rivers, and examining the astronomical instruments to observe the celestial phenomena, he did them all in person. Within a single year he made a circuit of inspection among the Five Marchmounts, his chariot ruts and horse tracks covering nearly ten thousand li; …

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
即度量權衡至微析矣率為之同而無逸一書
敘文王卑服康功惠鮮勤政雖日昃不遑暇食
舜與文王世並以無為稱焉者也肯自處于逸
而忘天下哉不以心忘天下在聖人猶然矣况
餘主哉而世顧援是禁一切之為繆亦甚矣或
又曰聖人之心雖在憂勞未嘗不安豈勞逸互
相為用抑無不可歟吁是不然聖王憂而未嘗
不安者乃順理則裕寔憂勤所致非一於宴安
而能之也繇斯以談無逸非人君要術哉後言
===
無逸者吾惑焉有衡石程書衛士傳食若秦隋
之君非不勞且苦也逸於心而以身殉之卒罹
滅亡亦無怪矣故曰善治者逸而有成不善治
者勞而無功則心得與不得之說也雖然無逸
要矣用人急焉天下大器任一人則匱任眾人
則裕選賢使能助其不逮而委任責成之故臣
集於能君總其功而天下之治皆人主之為矣
疇咨岳牧慎獄罔兼又舜文所不廢故曰明主
勞於求賢逸於任人斯無為之義始備云

punctuated: 即度量權衡，至微析矣，率為之同。而《無逸》一書，敘文王卑服康功，惠鮮勤政，雖日昃不遑暇食。舜與文王，世並以無為稱焉者也，肯自處于逸而忘天下哉？不以心忘天下，在聖人猶然矣，况餘主哉？而世顧援是禁一切之為，繆亦甚矣！或又曰：「聖人之心，雖在憂勞，未嘗不安。豈勞逸互相為用，抑無不可歟？」吁，是不然。聖王憂而未嘗不安者，乃順理則裕，寔憂勤所致，非一於宴安而能之也。繇斯以談，無逸非人君要術哉？後言無逸者，吾惑焉。有衡石程書、衛士傳食，若秦、隋之君，非不勞且苦也，逸於心而以身殉之，卒罹滅亡，亦無怪矣。故曰：「善治者逸而有成，不善治者勞而無功。」則心得與不得之說也。雖然，無逸要矣，用人急焉。天下大器，任一人則匱，任眾人則裕。選賢使能，助其不逮，而委任責成之。故臣集於能，君總其功，而天下之治皆人主之為矣。疇咨岳牧，慎獄罔兼，又舜、文所不廢。故曰：「明主勞於求賢，逸於任人。」斯無為之義始備云。
translation_en: … Even down to measures of length, capacity, and weight—matters of the finest detail—he standardized them all. Meanwhile, the document Against Luxurious Ease (Wuyi) recounts how King Wen wore humble attire and devoted himself to the work of pacifying the people, showing kindness to the destitute and diligence in governance, so much so that even when the sun inclined past noon he had no leisure to eat. Shun and King Wen are both praised by the world as exemplars of non-action (wuwei); would they have been willing to place themselves in ease and forget the empire? Even for sages, their minds never forgot the empire—how much more so for other rulers! Yet the world instead cites this ideal to forbid all active endeavor; how utterly absurd! Someone might further say: "Although the mind of the sage is amid anxiety and toil, it is never without peace. Could it be that toil and ease serve each other in turn, and that this too is permissible?" Alas, that is not so. The reason a sage-king can be anxious and yet never lack peace of mind is that by following principle, all becomes abundant; it is truly brought about by anxious diligence, not something achieved by giving oneself wholly over to comfort and ease. Judged in this light, is not "avoiding luxurious ease" the essential art of a ruler? Yet when people of later ages speak of avoiding ease, I am perplexed by them. There were those who weighed documents by the stone-weight to set their daily quota, or had guardsmen pass them their meals—like the rulers of Qin and Sui. It is not that they failed to toil and suffer; rather, they were indulgent in mind while sacrificing their bodies to routine, and so it is no wonder that in the end they met with destruction. Thus it is said: "He who governs well is at ease and yet achieves success; he who governs poorly toils and yet achieves no merit." This is a matter of whether one has grasped it in the mind or not. Even so, while avoiding ease is essential, employing men is urgent. The empire is a vast vessel: entrust it to one man and resources fall short; entrust it to many and there is abundance. By selecting the worthy and employing the capable to assist where one falls short, and delegating authority to hold them accountable for results, the ministers gather their abilities while the ruler sums up the accomplishments—and thus the governance of the empire is entirely the doing of the sovereign. Consulting the pastors of the Four Peaks and exercising caution in punishments without encroaching on offices were practices that neither Shun nor King Wen abandoned. Therefore it is said: "The enlightened ruler toils in seeking the worthy and rests in employing men." Only with this is the meaning of non-action complete.

translation_en:
… Imperial screen, and were further bestowed silver and silk; we, your servants, respectfully receive them and express our gratitude.

The gates of heaven open wide, and your sacred learning is renewed through constant contemplation of Heaven's bright mandate; the palace screens shine beneath the sun, and in our foolishness we offer a modest contribution of admonitory counsel. Fortunate that even humble greens are not cast aside, we pour forth our loyalty before the throne; favored with gifts from the imperial treasury, your grace adorns the Hanlin Academy and Grand Secretariat. Wiping our eyes, we recognize the honor; engraving it upon our hearts, we are moved with gratitude.

We humbly reflect that the ruler of men orders the myriad transformations, all beginning from a single mind—just as the celestial bodies array the stars in warp and woof, pivoting upon the Purple Culmen. Only by maintaining strict and vigilant reverence can one perpetuate abundance and prosperity. Thus the Yellow Emperor engraved his carriage and armrest to correct his faults, and the Xia sovereign inscribed his bell-stands to invite remonstrance; brightly manifesting Tang's virtue, daily renewal was admonished upon his washbasin; matchless in King Wu's merit, the triumph of reverence was inscribed upon his doors and windows. The Way abides in what meets the eye; governance is rooted in the mind.

When the former sages had passed away, alas, the admirable models of antiquity grew ever more distant. Spider-silk and tortoise-shell screens competed merely in carved ornamentation; mica and rainbow-hued screens exhausted all skill in decoration. … failing to take warning from fullness and overflow; and the one who copied out ten sections from the Classic of Documents (Shu), the Classic of Changes (Yi), and the Mencius (Mengzi) ultimately proved of no benefit to the restoration of the dynasty. For if one's thoughts do not abide in admonition and caution, what is the use of mere formalities in affairs? How can the Way be practiced in vain? Only when a Sage arises is there true creation.

Now we humbly encounter Your Majesty the Emperor: your sagely wisdom is bestowed by Heaven, and your reverence ascends daily. At the morning bell of the Changle Palace, you always respectfully inquire after the well-being of the Two Empresses Dowager; by the daytime water-clock of the Jinhua Hall, you constantly attend with diligence to consulting the Three Ducal Ministers. You surpass the ancient learning of Gaozong of Shang, being ever humble and ever diligent; you match the devotion to the people of the sovereigns of Zhou, indulging in neither idle excursions nor sightseeing. Having already spread the august ultimate of royal perfection until all is vast and level, you nonetheless remain cautious toward the Mandate of Heaven in fear and trembling. You consider that since the imperial residence is deep and secluded, its newly established name was drawn from the Odes (Shi) of Zhou; yet when the axe-screen is brightly displayed, how could admonition and warning be forgotten from the cautions of Wei? There ought to be a discourse and exposition to serve in place of the leather strap and bowstring. Therefore, …

朴忠顧
punctuated: 詔承明，俾新著作。臣等仰模德意，俯罄悃誠，念王道爰周郅隆，而周德于文爲至，以古爲鑑，亶文可師。乃繹《思齊》之章，庸申箴砭之義。曰不和則戾起，必樂以平情，而雝雝其在宮；曰不敬則慢生，必禮以飭志，而肅肅如在廟。述《箕疇》而戒作好作惡，援《夏訓》以懲荒色荒禽。始之欽止慎幾，終于覆車朽索。治心育德之道，炳若具陳；智臨保泰之猷，昭乎斯在。詞尚體要，意則朴忠。顧睿旨淵微，方虞管蠡之難竟；而聖懷虛受，猥蒙渤澥之兼收。遂命司存，屬之登寫，被諸緗素，謝舜采於丹青；置之座隅，純文心於保翼。萬幾清燕，時陟降而不違；千古淵源，每羹墻之有見。儼乎若冠鑑、几杖、帶履、弓劔之誡，常在
translation_en: … issued a decree to the Court of the Bright Presence, commanding the composition of a new work. Your servants, looking up to model ourselves on Your virtuous intent and bending down to exhaust our utmost sincerity, reflected that the Kingly Way reached its highest flourishing in the Zhou, and that the virtue of Zhou found its pinnacle in King Wen; taking antiquity as a mirror, truly King Wen is the model to follow. We therefore expounded the stanzas of the ode "Siqi" (Loving and Reverent) to set forth the meaning of admonition and remonstrance. It says that without harmony, perversity arises, so one must use music to calm the passions, being harmonious and congenial in the palace; it says that without reverence, negligence grows, so one must use ritual to rectify the will, being solemn and reverent as if in the ancestral temple. We recounted the "Plan of Jizi" to warn against playing favorites and indulging dislikes, and cited the "Instructions of Xia" to caution against addiction to sensual pleasure and the hunt. Beginning with reverent composure and attentiveness to the subtle springs of action, it concludes with the warnings of the overturned chariot and rotten reins. The way of cultivating the mind and nurturing virtue is brilliantly set forth in full; the counsel for ruling with wisdom and preserving great peace is clearly present herein. The diction values substance and conciseness, while the intent is simple and loyal. Yet considering how profound and subtle is Your Imperial purport, we were just fearing that our narrow vision—like peering through a tube or measuring the sea with a calabash—could hardly fathom it; whereas Your Sacred Mind receives with humility, and we have undeservedly been favored with an all-embracing acceptance like that of the vast sea. Thereupon You commanded the officials in charge to have it transcribed, spread upon fine light-yellow silk, eschewing the flashy brilliance of painted colors; and placed it beside Your throne, making pure the mind of King Wen through protective guidance. In the quiet leisure amid ten thousand affairs of state, You constantly ascend and descend without departing from it; tracing the fountainhead of a thousand ages, You ever behold the ancients as if seeing them in Your soup and on Your walls. Dignified, it is as though the admonitions inscribed on caps, mirrors, armrests, staffs, sashes, shoes, bows, and swords were ever present before…

translation_en:
… the imperial crown; and how pleasing it is, as though ministers likened to boats and oars, seasonal rain, yeast and malt, and salt and plum were constantly participating in instruction and recitation! Thus Your learning yields rich rewards, and Your governance is truly without fault. Previously, at the Classics Mat lectures, when the pages of the Mirror for Emperors (Dijian) were opened, the distinction between sagehood and folly was brightly illuminated; and now, in the side palace halls, as the records of Your ministerial assistants are arrayed, civil and military merits are clearly known. Such grand perfection is magnificently displayed, a rarity seldom heard of in the past.

To have our loyal counsel accepted is already a great fortune; to be bestowed with Your favor is an even greater honor. Fine gold is apportioned from the treasures of the Inner Treasury, wondrously bearing the mark of the unicorn's hoof; colorful robes are awarded from the manufactures of the Directorate for Imperial Manufactories, their craftsmanship rivaling that of the Heavenly Weaver. Your grace is weightier than metal-severing unity, yet our shame runs deeper than the pelican's unmerited wetting of its beak. How could Your servants dare not swear diligence in assisting Your rule, hoping to live up to Your reliance and trust? Setting forth "Against Luxurious Ease" (Wuyi) to pray for everlasting years, we secretly aspire to Duke Dan of Zhou; submitting memorials on seeing things through to the end to remonstrate on governance, how dare we lag behind Wei Zheng? We shall all the more strengthen our sincerity in serving as a whetstone, forever assisting the transformative rule of Your robes-hanging-down non-action. We humbly pray that You will be devoted to learning from beginning to end, establish the Supreme Ultimate in centrality and harmony, …

蓋聞君臣之際，《易》備之矣。〈泰〉之《象》曰：「天地交，泰。」《彖》曰：「天地交而萬物通也，上下交而其志同也。」夫泰，天地之象也，而君臣則之。故天道下濟，地道上行，絪縕訢合，陰陽相得，而萬物生焉，是天地交而泰也；君親乎臣，臣比乎君，聚精會神，相得益章，而萬化行焉，是君臣交而泰也。顧天地之交，造物之恒運也；而君臣之間，則未易矣。尊卑闊絕，其情未易聯；禮節森嚴，其勢未易合。自非君人者降志以接之，虛懷以聽之，披衷愫以見情，忘忌諱以盡物，則為之臣者，何…
translation_en:
…and thorough. The end of the piece fully displays his loyal sincerity; it is worthy of being presented to the throne.

Examiner and Librarian of the Left Spring坊 (Xima) Zhou comments: The exposition is clear and substantive, praising while not forgetting to remonstrate. It should be recorded for publication as an aid to preserving peace and harmony (Tai).

Examiner and Left Mentor (Zuo Yude) Chen comments: He extols the flourishing virtues of the dynasty and at the end offers remonstrance; all of these are earnest and pertinent arguments. He must be a scholar who harbors loyal sincerity. Selected.

I have heard that the relationship between ruler and minister is fully set forth in the Book of Changes (Yi). The Image (Xiang) of the hexagram Tai (Peace) says: "Heaven and earth in communion: Peace." The Commentary on the Decision (Tuan) says: "Heaven and earth are in communion, and the myriad things communicate freely; superiors and inferiors are in communion, and their wills are the same." Now Tai is the image of heaven and earth, and ruler and minister model themselves upon it. Therefore, when the Way of heaven descends to bring relief and the Way of earth ascends, interweaving in harmonious union so that yin and yang complement one another, the myriad things are generated thereby—this is heaven and earth in communion, resulting in Peace (Tai). When the ruler is close to his ministers and the ministers are devoted to their ruler, concentrating their energies and uniting their spirits so that they bring out the best in one another, the myriad transformations operate thereby—this is ruler and minister in communion, resulting in Peace (Tai). Yet the communion of heaven and earth is the constant cycle of nature, whereas between ruler and minister it is not so easy. Exalted and humble are widely separated, so their feelings are not easily connected; ritual protocols are stern and strict, so their positions are not easily joined. Unless the one who rules over men humbles his will to receive them, empties his mind to listen to them, lays bare his innermost sincerity to show his true feelings, and sets aside taboos to allow everyone to speak fully, then how could those who serve as his ministers…

臣相悅泰交之盛猶可想焉由漢而下若
文帝問相職而善陳平之對詢署郎而動
===
摶髀之思可謂明矣而擴國士於長沙則
失賢光武日昃罷朝數引公卿郎將講論
經理可謂勤矣而責三公以吏事則失體
唐太宗令學士更日宿直引入内殿講論
商榷似急賢矣而與者或匪其人宋仁宗
溫顔訪問開閣求言似虛受矣而賢者弗
究于用之四君者以稱賢於當代則可爾
比跡虞周不旣遠邈矣哉洪惟我
太祖高皇帝以神武開基延攬英傑于時才儁
punctuated:
由自結于主，以攄其所蘊積也哉？故《泰》之九二，以剛中之臣任治泰之責，而六五惟柔中虛已以聽之，故能受元吉之祉，而成治泰之功。蓋明主藎臣相須以成泰者，其道若此。愚請繹是說以尚論古人，敷揚昭代，可乎？

粤昔唐虞之朝，都俞吁咈，喜起賡載，此泰交最盛時也。成周之隆，《鳧鷖》、《假樂》，君臣相悅，泰交之盛猶可想焉。由漢而下，若文帝問相職而善陳平之對，詢署郎而動拊髀之思，可謂明矣；而擯國士於長沙，則失賢。光武日昃罷朝，數引公卿郎將講論經理，可謂勤矣；而責三公以吏事，則失體。唐太宗令學士更日宿直，引入內殿講論商搉，似急賢矣；而與者或匪其人。宋仁宗溫顏訪問，開閤求言，似虛受矣；而賢者弗究于用。之四君者，以稱賢於當代則可爾，比跡虞、周，不旣遠遜矣哉！

洪惟我太祖高皇帝以神武開基，延攬英傑。于時才雋
translation_en:
…means could he bind himself to his sovereign so as to pour forth what he has accumulated within? Therefore, in the hexagram Tai (Peace), the Nine in the Second place, as a minister of firm centrality, takes on the responsibility of governing in a time of peace, while the Six in the Fifth place, through gentle centrality, humbles himself to listen to him; thus he is able to receive the blessing of supreme auspiciousness and accomplish the merit of governing in peace. Indeed, the way in which an enlightened sovereign and a loyal minister depend on one another to achieve peace is like this. May I, in my humble way, unpack this explanation to critically evaluate the ancients and extol our glorious dynasty?

In antiquity, at the courts of Tang (Yao) and Yu (Shun), there were expressions of approval and agreement as well as warnings and dissent, and joyful exchanges of songs to carry on great undertakings—this was the most flourishing era of harmonious communion (taijiao). At the height of the Accomplished Zhou, as seen in the odes Wild Ducks (Fuyi) and Felicitous and Joyful (Jiale), sovereign and minister delighted in one another, and the flourishing of their harmonious communion can still be imagined. From the Han dynasty onward, someone like Emperor Wen inquired into the duties of the Counselor-in-Chief and approved of Chen Ping’s陳平 reply, and questioned a Court Gentleman in his office, which stirred him to slap his thigh in longing for great generals—he may be called enlightened; yet by banishing a scholar of national stature (Jia Yi 賈誼) to Changsha, he lost a worthy. Emperor Guangwu did not adjourn court until the sun inclined to the west, and frequently summoned Dukes, Ministers, and Gentlemen-of-the-Palace as Generals to expound on the classics and principles of governance—he may be called diligent; yet by holding the Three Dukes accountable for routine clerical matters, he lost proper institutional form. Emperor Taizong of Tang ordered Academicians to take turns on night duty and brought them into the inner palace to discuss and deliberate—he seemed eager for worthies; yet those who participated were sometimes not the right men. Emperor Renzong of Song inquired with a gentle countenance and opened the palace cabinets to seek remonstrance—he seemed open-minded and receptive; yet the worthies were not utilized to their full capacity. As for these four rulers, to praise them as worthy in their own ages is permissible, but compared to the footsteps of Yu and Zhou, do they not fall far short indeed!

Greatly reflecting upon our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu), he founded the dynasty with divine martial prowess and broadly recruited heroes and outstanding talents. At that time, men of talent and distinction…

text:
仰流雲合鱗卒征伐則徐常李鄧輩獻其
功運籌則劉宋陶章輩與其議披心造膝
畫聽績效武允戡亂文克經邦蓋
君臣之交不啻心體之喻矣所以
創天下之大業而垂休萬世者非以此邪
列聖紹休繼繩罔替迨于弘治尤赫厥聲粵惟
我
孝宗敬皇帝以睿文纘緒寤寐英賢于時群哲
嚮臻協恭勵翼政府則有若宜興洛陽長
===
沙餘姚九列則有若禹州華容浮梁洪洞

暖閣咨謀疏擬則裁定必詳論奏或掖扶乃
起蓋
君臣之交不啻家庭之密矣所以
保天下之大業而克熈
昌運者非以此邪是故頌創始者蹤堯禹歌

punctuated: 仰流，雲合鱗卒。征伐，則徐、常、李、鄧輩獻其功；運籌，則劉、宋、陶、章輩與其議。披心造膝，畫聽績效，武允戡亂，文克經邦，蓋君臣之交，不啻心體之喻矣。所以創天下之大業，而垂休萬世者，非以此邪？列聖紹休，繼繩罔替，迨于弘治，尤赫厥聲。粵惟我孝宗敬皇帝以睿文纘緒，寤寐英賢，于時群哲嚮臻，協恭勵翼。政府，則有若宜興、洛陽、長沙、餘姚；九列，則有若禹州、華容、浮梁、洪洞。文華議政，暖閣咨謀，疏擬則裁定必詳，論奏或掖扶乃起，蓋君臣之交，不啻家庭之密矣。所以保天下之大業，而克熈昌運者，非以此邪？是故頌創始者蹤堯、禹，歌太平者媲殷、周，而一時鴻碩，亦獲以附景光、垂休聲焉。於哉，盛矣！今

…looked up to his current, gathering like clouds and assembling like fish scales. In military campaigns, men such as Xu [Da 徐達], Chang [Yuchun 常遇春], Li [Wenzhong 李文忠], and Deng [Yu 鄧愈] presented their achievements; in strategic planning, men such as Liu [Ji 劉基], Song [Lian 宋濂], Tao [An 陶安], and Zhang [Yi 章溢] participated in his deliberations. Baring their hearts and drawing close knee-to-knee, their plans were heeded and their achievements proved effective; military might truly quelled rebellion, and civil administration succeeded in ordering the state. Indeed, the communion between ruler and minister was nothing less than the metaphor of heart and body! Was it not by this means that he founded the great enterprise of the realm and handed down blessings for ten thousand generations?

Successive sacred emperors continued these blessings, carrying on the line without fail, and down to the Hongzhi 弘治 reign (1488–1505) the dynasty's renown shone with particular brilliance. When our Emperor Xiaozong Jinghuangdi 孝宗敬皇帝 (r. 1487–1505) succeeded to the line with sagely civil virtue, longing waking and sleeping for outstanding worthies, at that time the assembled wise men eagerly gathered, assisting with harmonious reverence and dedicated support. In the Grand Secretariat there were men such as those from Yixing 宜興 [Xu Pu 徐溥], Luoyang 洛陽 [Liu Jian 劉健], Changsha 長沙 [Li Dongyang 李東陽], and Yuyao 餘姚 [Xie Qian 謝遷]; among the Nine Ministers there were men such as those from Yuzhou 禹州 [Ma Wensheng 馬文升], Huarong 華容 [Liu Daxia 劉大夏], Fuliang 浮梁 [Dai Shan 戴珊], and Hongdong 洪洞 [Han Wen 韓文]. Deliberating on governance in the Hall of Literary Brilliance (Wenhua dian 文華殿) and consulting on counsels in the Warm Pavilion (Nuange 暖閣), when memorials and draft rescripts were submitted, his decisions were invariably thorough; when officials presented oral memorials, at times he even had them supported by the arm to help them rise. Indeed, the communion between ruler and minister was nothing less than the intimacy of a family household! Was it not by this means that he preserved the great enterprise of the realm and succeeded in making the prosperous destiny shine brightly?

Therefore, those who extol the dynasty's founding trace its steps to Yao 堯 and Yu 禹, and those who sing of its great peace match it with the Yin 殷 and Zhou 周; and the great scholars and eminent worthies of the age were likewise able to attach themselves to its resplendent light and hand down their fine reputations. Oh, how magnificent! Now, the present…

At the very beginning of His accession to the throne, He immediately summoned the Grand Secretaries for an audience at the Ping Platform (Pingtai); in the spring of His second year, He summoned the officials gathered for the Triennial Evaluation (jili), generously bestowing praise and edicts of encouragement upon those who had demonstrated effective governance; for the selection and appointment of officials, He restored the regulation of personal imperial oversight; and among the historiographical offices, He established the compilation of the Imperial Diaries (Qijuzhu): the magnificence of His gracious condescension toward His subjects has already become brilliantly manifest. As the Grand Secretariat is the root of governance, He relies upon it for assistance all the more earnestly, and amidst the multitude of state affairs, He constantly takes care to receive and consult its ministers. In recent years, because His Majesty's sacred age was growing daily more mature and He was becoming increasingly versed in affairs of state, the Grand Secretaries deliberated and petitioned to suspend the calligraphy exercises in favor of expounding upon and discussing memorials. His Majesty gladly approved and accepted this. At the beginning of the new year, this was carried out for the first time in the Hall of Fasting. The Imperial Preceptors opened the documents to set forth their explanations, while His Majesty viewed, listened, and made His selections and decisions. What was first deliberated upon were the weighty state institutions concerning the marriages, enfeoffments, and annual stipends of the imperial clansmen. At first His Majesty said, "Deliberate with the competent authorities and put it into effect," and subsequently He said, "This should be deliberated upon and handled with unhurried care." The sacred countenance was pure and solemn, and the heavenly words were earnest and gentle. At that moment, there was none among the officials who did not stand in awe with a brightened expression, joyfully telling one another that from this point onward, the footsteps of the Imperial Ancestors could be followed and the fundamental policies of the state could be settled; from this point onward, the imperial discernment would grow daily brighter and sacred governance would be renewed; from this point onward, He would personally decide the myriad affairs of state, and from this point onward, He would independently exercise His imperial judgment—taking these up and putting them into practice, the order of Great Peace could be hoped for! punctuated: 亦罔不拭目傾心，喁喁然思見德化之成焉。而執事猶詢所以仰裨萬一者，愚則何辭以對？無已，則以法祖博延之說，區析言之，為芹曝獻乎？竊聞之：聖祖昧爽臨朝，日晏忘食，公卿郎吏，俱備咨訪，無擇於人也；法宮便殿，時加延接，無擇於地也。今密勿陳議，裁畫講求，允惟厥中矣。顧機務至繁，而不時之召希聞，得無晉接之尚疎者乎？列卿當職，而殿陛僅聞一唯，得無詳延之未廣者乎？則勤宣召之命，復午朝之規，俾公卿執事時獲畢誠者，或弗可已也。聖祖初設中書，後分九列，而文學侍從日在左右，耆儒宿德咸待質難。今虎觀諸臣橫經講論，啓沃日新矣。而講畢即出，
translation_en:
… there is none who does not wipe his eyes and incline his heart, eagerly longing to see the perfection of virtuous transformation. Yet the Examiner still inquires after ways to offer even the slightest assistance on high—with what words, then, shall this foolish student reply? If I must speak, may I present, as a humble offering of wild celery and warm sunlight, a detailed analysis of the doctrine of emulating the Ancestor and broadly receiving officials?

I have humbly heard that the Sacred Ancestor (Emperor Taizu) attended court at the crack of dawn and forgot to eat until late in the day; high ministers, Chief Ministers, and Bureau Officials were all kept ready for consultation and inquiry, making no distinction as to persons. In the main ceremonial palace and in the side halls, he frequently granted audiences, making no distinction as to place. Today, in the privy chambers, counsel is presented, plans are decided upon and investigated, and the due mean is truly attained. Yet state affairs are exceedingly numerous, while unscheduled summonses are rarely heard of—could it be that audiences with the throne are still too infrequent? The assembled Chief Ministers hold their offices, yet at the steps of the throne one hears from them only a single word of assent—could it be that thorough and broad consultation has not yet been wide enough? Therefore, to issue frequent commands of summons and to restore the institution of the midday court, so that high ministers and functional officials may regularly have the opportunity to pour out their utmost sincerity, is perhaps something that cannot be dispensed with.

When the Sacred Ancestor first established the Secretariat and later divided authority among the Nine Chief Ministers, literary attendants were at his side day by day, and aged Confucian scholars and men of long-standing virtue all waited upon him to resolve difficult questions. Today, the ministers of the White Tiger Hall hold forth on the Classics in lectures and discussions, enlightening and enriching the imperial mind anew each day. Then restoring the regulation of rotating night-duty, so that upright and erudite men may regularly join the close attendants, is perhaps something that ought to be discussed. In the time of the Sacred Ancestor (Emperor Taizu), when the various officials of the outer provinces took their leave after an audience, they were invariably questioned about the advantages and ills of the four quarters and the means by which they governed the people, thereby assessing their worthiness or incompetence. In former times, the Song official Su Shi 蘇軾 once set forth five matters. title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
垂情問察則不遺微小者亦豈非保泰之
一助哉抑愚猶有說焉戒平陂危復隍易
於泰爻蓋兩致儆云故罔游干佚伯益以
之警虞所其無逸公旦以之規周蓋不以
已治已安自足而惟以憂治危明為心者
此盛世君臣所以共維熙昌之運而保有
道之長者也苟逸豫一萌則流漸莫挽而
陂隍之虞且至矣
聖主誠鏡理道之原崇儆戒之實敬止就將無
===

虞周宇宙間哉

垂情問察，則不遺微小者，亦豈非保泰之一助哉？抑愚猶有說焉。戒平陂、危復隍，《易》於〈泰〉爻蓋兩致儆云。故「罔游干佚」，伯益以之警虞；「所其無逸」，公旦以之規周。蓋不以已治已安自足，而惟以憂治危明為心者，此盛世君臣所以共維熙昌之運，而保有道之長者也。苟逸豫一萌，則流漸莫挽，而陂隍之虞且至矣。聖主誠鏡理道之原，崇儆戒之實，敬止就將，無少間息；而又弘延攬之門，大用中之量，則所謂通天下為一身者，而泰交之盛，真與治古並隆矣！雍熙泰和，亦豈獨在虞、周宇宙間哉？

第二問
游應龍

translation_en:
… deigns to show concern by inquiring and investigating, then not overlooking the minute and trivial—would this not also be an aid to preserving great peace (Tai)?

Yet I have still more to say. Warning that level ground may become a slope and that the city wall may crumble back into the moat—the Book of Changes (Yi) in the lines of the Tai hexagram twice delivers this admonition. Thus, "Do not wander in idleness" was how Boyi 伯益 admonished Shun of Yu; and "Make ease-avoidance his abiding place" was how Duke Dan 公旦 (the Duke of Zhou) counseled Zhou. Indeed, not being self-satisfied with governance already achieved and peace already secured, but taking anxiety in times of order and vigilance in times of enlightenment as one's mind—this is whereby sovereign and ministers in a flourishing age jointly sustain a prosperous destiny and preserve the longevity of a state guided by the Way. Should idleness and indulgence once sprout, the gradual slide cannot be reversed, and the peril of the slope and the crumbling wall will soon arrive.

If the Sacred Sovereign truly mirrors the source of principle and the Way, exalts the substance of vigilance and admonition, abides in reverence and advances daily without the slightest pause or rest; and furthermore widens the gate of recruiting talent and enlarges the capacity of employing the Mean—then this will be what is called uniting All-under-Heaven into a single body, and the flourishing of the harmonious communion of Tai will truly rival well-governed antiquity in splendor! Why should harmonious prosperity and supreme peace exist solely within the cosmos of Yu and Zhou?

Second Question
You Yinglong 游應龍

At the end, it places primary weight on governing through capable men, deeply grasping the root of reforming the administration and rescuing the times. When he goes forth to take up office, we may reckon there will surely be much worth beholding in him.

同考試官教諭吳批議論宏博攷究詳明
敘述法所由弊處切中事情必通達國體之士
考試官洗馬周批論事纚纚洞悉原本而
文復古雅可以覘所蘊矣
考試官左諭德陳批說飭法濟時意有卓見
而辭足以發之可取
蓋聞議法者甚不可執一為也必因積漸
之勢而審變通之宜然後可以長治夫法
之始立皆權於利害是非以為之計何有
===
於弊哉而行之旣久人心易玩不能盡如
其故於是法紀怠而釁孽萌遂有頹靡不
振之患使因仍旦暮不亟為之議弊所滋
蔓長此安窮於是更化善治苟以便國不
襲其安苟以利民不徇其俗雖迹有沿革
損益而要當乎立法之意自昔計臣達士
感激於辨朝憂危於令主者用此道也歟
執事以議法為問愚竊聞焉詩曰不愆不
忘率由舊章易又曰通其變使民不倦言

Where it describes how the laws came to suffer abuses, it hits squarely upon the realities of the situation; this must be a scholar who thoroughly understands the fundamentals of statecraft."

Examiner and Librarian Zhou comments: "He discusses affairs in an orderly and continuous flow, thoroughly grasping their origins and foundations, while his prose is moreover classical and elegant; from this one can observe the depth of his learning."

I have heard that those who deliberate on laws must by no means cling stubbornly to a single course. Only when one takes into account the momentum of gradual accumulation and examines what is appropriate for adaptation and change can long-lasting order be achieved. When laws are first established, they are all devised by weighing benefit and harm, right and wrong—how could there be any abuses in them? Yet once they have been in effect for a long time, human minds easily grow lax and take them lightly, so that things cannot remain entirely as they were of old. Thereupon law and discipline slacken and the seeds of trouble sprout, leading to the malady of decline and stagnation. If one merely drifts along from day to day without urgently deliberating upon them, as abuses multiply and spread, where will it ever end if it continues like this? Therefore, in reforming governance and perfecting rule, so long as a measure benefits the state, one does not cling to comfortable routine; so long as it profits the people, one does not pander to existing customs. Even though in outward trace there is continuity and change, subtraction and addition, the essential point is that it should accord with the original intent of establishing the laws. Since antiquity, statesmen of sound planning and men of far-reaching vision who were moved to earnest zeal in a discerning court and expressed anxious concern before a worthy ruler have made use of this very principle, have they not!

text:
議法者亂以聰明起紛更之害狃以積習
貽裕蠱之虞惟追俗而易化觀變而預圖
審時所宜而不膠於久安一定之迹非明
達治體者不能也試觀往牒漢自武帝好
大喜功海內虛耗矣宣帝繼之魏相乃條
陳便宜請其施行言方今之務在修復故
事帝雖勵精爲治而德教未純寧以漢制
可守耳宋自神宗任用非人變壞舊政矣
哲宗繼之司馬光復起爲相言安石惠卿
===
所建宜一切報罷若先法之善百世不可
改蓋亟除新法以安民心獨以恢復自任
耳若文帝以德化民幾于成康矣賈誼疏
陳治安勸其更制帝繼高惠之後制度闊
疏侯王僭儗雖寬大之規不可失然稽古
改制以光先業非其時邪惜說未及用使
禮樂不興秦俗尚熾亦謙讓之過也仁宗
恭儉忠厚可以有爲矣范仲淹奉答手詔
條陳十事帝紹三世之業吏治不振紀綱

…those who deliberate on the laws either disrupt them with their own cleverness, giving rise to the harm of disorderly alterations, or grow accustomed to accumulated habits, leaving behind the danger of indulgent decay. Only one who thoroughly understands the essentials of governance can examine customs to transform them, observe changes to plan ahead, judge what is appropriate for the times, and not cling stubbornly to the fixed traces of long-standing peace.

Let us examine the records of the past. In the Han dynasty, after Emperor Wu delighted in grandiose achievements, the realm within the seas was exhausted. When Emperor Xuan succeeded him, Wei Xiang 魏相 submitted itemized proposals on what was expedient and requested their implementation, stating that the urgent task of the moment lay in restoring the established precedents. Although the Emperor exerted himself vigorously in governing, his moral instruction was not yet pure, and he simply considered the Han institutions worth preserving. In the Song dynasty, after Emperor Shenzong employed the wrong men, the old administration was altered and ruined. When Emperor Zhezong succeeded him, Sima Guang 司馬光 was recalled to serve as Grand Councilor and argued that everything established by [Wang] Anshi 王安石 and [Lü] Huiqing 呂惠卿 should be completely abolished, whereas the excellence of the former laws should not be changed for a hundred generations. Indeed, in urgently removing the New Laws to calm the hearts of the people, he took restoration solely upon himself.

As for Emperor Wen of Han, he transformed the people through virtue and nearly equaled Kings Cheng and Kang of Zhou. Jia Yi 賈誼 submitted a memorial setting forth his "Policy for Peace and Order" (Zhi'an ce), urging him to reform the institutions. When the Emperor succeeded Emperors Gao and Hui, the institutional framework was loose and sketchy, and the marquises and kings usurped prerogatives. Although the principle of magnanimity was not to be lost, was that not the time to examine antiquity and reform institutions so as to glorify the enterprise of his predecessors? Alas, his advice was not adopted in time, with the result that rites and music did not flourish and Qin customs remained rampant—this too was a fault of excessive modesty and deference. Emperor Renzong of Song was reverent, frugal, loyal, and generous, and could have accomplished great things. In response to an imperial edict written in the Emperor's own hand, Fan Zhongyan 范仲淹 submitted a memorial itemizing ten matters. The Emperor had inherited the enterprise of three reigns, yet official administration was uninspired and regulatory discipline…

漸隳，雖仁厚之法不可易，若光復一統以保成功，非其時邪？惜言不獲施，使大險失據，國勢益弱，亦姑息之咎也。可見論治者貴識體，濟時者當通變。法所宜守，則相條便宜之事，光革熙、豐之弊，修復舊章而不妨於因；法所當飭，則誼陳治安之策，仲淹答天章之問，恢張先業而不嫌於變。時不同而道非相悖也已。

方今熙平之日久矣，法之所立，皆列聖睿思踔識，誠哉淵乎其深遠也！著在令甲，守之有司，又非不赫然具也，踰漢、宋遠甚，夫復何議？顧寧謐久而沿襲滋，玩愒生而法守眩，行之不能盡如其舊，稍亦有焉。以故上之督責雖勤，而實効蓋尠；下之簿書徒具，而美意未宣。昔爲良法，後乃云敝政矣，亦窮則變、變則通之時也。曩者，深計遠慮之士，石畫而籌當世；殫忠畢智之臣，
translation_en:
… was gradually decaying. Although the benevolent and generous laws could not be changed, as for recovering unified rule in order to preserve past achievements, was this not the right time for it? Alas, his words were not put into effect, causing the great strategic passes to be lost and the state's power to grow ever weaker; this too was the fault of overly indulgent tolerance. From this it can be seen that those who discuss governance value understanding the fundamental principles, and those who rescue the age must adapt to change. Where the laws ought to be preserved, [Wei] Xiang submitted his itemized matters of convenience, and [Sima] Guang abolished the abuses of the Xining (1068–1077) and Yuanfeng (1078–1085) eras, restoring the old statutes without shrunk from following precedent. Where the laws ought to be rectified, [Jia] Yi presented his strategies for peace and order, and [Fan] Zhongyan answered the questions in the Tianzhang Pavilion, expanding upon the achievements of their predecessors without shying away from reform. The times were different, yet their Way was not mutually contradictory.

At present, the days of peaceful prosperity have lasted long. The laws that have been established all stem from the imperial wisdom and lofty foresight of the successive sacred emperors—truly, how profound and far-reaching they are! Recorded in the foremost statutes and guarded by the authorities, they are by no means not brilliantly complete; they surpass those of the Han and Song dynasties by far, so what more is there to debate? Yet when tranquility lasts long, routine adherence proliferates; when laxity arises, the observance of the laws becomes confused, and to some slight extent they cannot be carried out entirely as they were of old. For this reason, although supervision and reproof from above are diligent, actual results are few; below, official documents are merely prepared as a formality, while the fine intentions behind the laws are not made manifest. What were formerly good laws are later called decayed governance; this too is a time when, reaching an impasse, one must change, and by changing, achieve smooth passage. In recent years, men of deep planning and far-reaching foresight have devised rock-solid plans to manage the present age, and ministers who exhaust their loyalty and wisdom …

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
矢心而謀
朝政酌考成以覈名實祛姑息以振紀綱務
精詳以勵怠弛破拘攣以審經制六七年
之間庶務畢舉人心益惕斯亦極治之盛
際焉蓋非振飭胡以臻此執事謂保泰持
盈之體愚生竊韙之矣夫法之在天下也
使皆如其立法之初則曷以飭為哉柰之
何久而漸趨於敝者無異故云大抵先世
創制而繼統之後席故業而享盈成于是
===
文物盛於聲容物力衰於侈汰矣守成易
玩而積漸之後惡檢束而樂安逸於是士
便文以自營民玩弊以巧法矣蓋其勢固
爾哉勢之所在圖於先事易返於亟重難
此非極亂大壞之形而有其漸矣漸則胡
可長也即立法者身值其時不有乘其漸
而預飭之乎夫琴瑟不調更張之乃可鼓
也車轍或敝更新之乃可御也法漸敝矣
僅僅守持重之虛名而不思捄時狃怠玩

===

僅僅守持重之虛名而不思捄時狃怠玩
punctuated:
矢心而謀朝政，酌考成以覈名實，祛姑息以振紀綱，務精詳以勵怠弛，破拘攣以審經制。六七年之間，庶務畢舉，人心益惕，斯亦極治之盛際焉。蓋非振飭，胡以臻此？執事謂保泰持盈之體，愚生竊韙之矣。
夫法之在天下也，使皆如其立法之初，則曷以飭為哉？柰之何久而漸趨於敝者，無異故云。大抵先世創制，而繼統之後，席故業而享盈成，于是文物盛於聲容，物力衰於侈汰矣；守成易玩，而積漸之後，惡檢束而樂安逸，於是士便文以自營，民玩弊以巧法矣。蓋其勢固爾哉！勢之所在，圖於先事易，返於亟重難。此非極亂大壞之形，而有其漸矣；漸則胡可長也？即立法者身值其時，不有乘其漸而預飭之乎？夫琴瑟不調，更張之乃可鼓也；車轍或敝，更新之乃可御也。法漸敝矣，僅僅守持重之虛名而不思捄時，狃怠玩
translation_en:
…pledged their hearts to take counsel on court administration: weighing the evaluation of official performance to verify title against reality, dispelling lax indulgence to rouse discipline and order, striving for precision and thoroughness to spur on the indolent and slack, and breaking through rigid constraints to scrutinize the fundamental institutions. Within six or seven years, all administrative affairs have been fully attended to and the minds of the people have grown ever more vigilant—this too is a flourishing era of supreme governance. Indeed, without rousing and rectifying, how could this have been achieved? What Your Excellency calls the essential principle of preserving peace and maintaining abundance, I, a foolish student, venture to approve of.

Now, as for laws in the empire, if they always remained as they were when first established, what need would there be for rectification? Why is it that over time they gradually tend toward decay? There is no other reason than this: generally speaking, earlier generations create the institutions, and after successors inherit the throne, they rest upon the established patrimony and enjoy full abundance; thereupon ritual and cultural forms flourish in outward display, while material resources decline through extravagance and excess. Maintaining an existing order easily leads to complacency, and after gradual accumulation, people resent restraint and delight in ease and comfort; thereupon officials manipulate written rules for their own advantage, and the common people trifle with abuses to artfully evade the law. Such is the natural tendency of things! Where a tendency lies, to plan for it beforehand is easy, while to reverse it once it has grown acute and entrenched is difficult. This is not yet a state of extreme disorder and total ruin, but its gradual beginnings are present; and once such a gradual trend exists, how can it be allowed to grow? Even if the original lawgivers themselves had lived to see such a time, would they not have seized upon that gradual trend and rectified things in advance? When the qin and se zithers are out of tune, only by restringing them can they be played; when carriage wheels or tracks become worn out, only by renewing them can the carriage be driven. When laws have gradually fallen into decay, if one merely clings to the empty name of prudent caution without thinking of rescuing the times, or remains habituated to indolence and laxity…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之往習而不知達變將瑕纇叢生蠹壞日
起名為循法法且盡亡則迂儒之說而滋
亂之途矣望以底績不亦難哉或者曰遵
道而行上逸而下順緣法而治吏習而民
安茲不幾為拂衆乎夫古謂從衆者非從
口之所言從其心所不言而同然者乃真
從也輿人之頌公孫不以民譽墮工惟其公不惟其
之黜司城不以民謠毀政邑中
私耳茲察人情同欲者以飭之乃與民同
===
其好惡是矣非所以拂之也或又曰積習
之弊一旦易之久曠之典一旦舉之重懲
既往而亟圖所難如成法何愚曰立法之
意與時宜之耳誠得其意即事不相沿皆
良法也失其意則拘守繩墨皆虛文也周
公兼三王而仰思不合孟子論井田而終
於潤澤古聖賢議治類如此矣寧有意於
為異哉今之弊豈皆置法初意乎蓋後所
踵襲之過正患振刷未盡耳與時消息因

translation_en:
… the past habits of indolence and neglect, and fails to understand how to adapt to change, then flaws and defects will spring up in profusion and rot and ruin will arise daily. Though called following the laws, the laws will in fact utterly perish. This is the talk of pedantic scholars and a path that breeds disorder; to hope thereby to achieve results—is it not difficult indeed!

Someone may say: "When one proceeds by following the established way, superiors are at ease and inferiors are compliant; when one governs by adhering to existing laws, officials are accustomed to them and the people are at peace. Does this present course not come close to opposing the multitude?" Now, what the ancients meant by following the multitude was not following what their mouths utter; rather, following what their hearts do not utter yet all agree upon is true following. In the chants of the commoners, Gongsun (Zichan 子產) did not abandon his work on account of popular praise or blame [?]; and in the complaints within the city, the Minister of Works (Sicheng 司城, Zihan 子罕) did not ruin his administration on account of folk rhymes, simply because he cared only for the public good and not for private interests [?]. Now, examining what human sentiment commonly desires in order to rectify the laws is indeed sharing the likes and dislikes of the people; it is not opposing them.

Someone else may say: "If the abuses of accumulated custom are changed in a single morning, if long-neglected statutes are revived in a single morning, and if past offenses are severely punished while difficult reforms are urgently pursued, what becomes of the established laws?" I reply: "The intent in establishing laws is simply to make them suit the times. If one truly grasps their intent, even if the specific measures do not follow precedent, they are all good laws; if one loses their intent, then clinging rigidly to the marking-line produces nothing but empty words. The Duke of Zhou (Zhougong 周公) combined the ways of the Three Kings, looking up in thought when anything did not suit the time; Mencius (Mengzi 孟子) discussed the well-field system and concluded with adapting and refining it. When the sages and worthies of antiquity discussed governance, they generally spoke like this—did they have any intention of merely being different? Are the abuses of today all part of the original intent when the laws were established? Rather, they are the faults of later blind adherence, and the real worry is precisely that the invigoration and cleansing have not been thorough enough. Growing and diminishing with the times, and…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
變焉守法所甚賴也嗟乎古今迭運皇王
代興方冊所載規制畧盡如岐黃内經百
方畢具有行之久而變者有變之久而復
者有復而變變而又復者民俗無恒國是
靡定在相時善用耳如病者寒以寒治熱
以熱治或寒熱變以變治察標本緩急之
勢而投之此倉公扁鵲所以計日而奏功
也而議法者獨務於因陋蹈常之為不亦
計左而失當哉况今所整飭者亦修其已
===
試去其泰甚非特有驚世駭俗之舉而不
得議以更張也易言通變詩述舊章與今
飭法之意奚悖哉夫今之法固犁然舉矣
執事猶求以議之無亦慮其終而思維其
漸歟愚又聞之天下之法作于上常格于
下人之情謹于初常弛於終今之議者要
察法所由弊而其咎則在人耳是故補葺
偏漏以支目前而迂視萬全之計猶扺安
流而止維楫非以濟遠也建立方新責効

計左而失當哉况今所整飭者亦修其已
===

得議以更張也易言通變詩述舊章與今

流而上維檝非以濟遠也建立方新責効
punctuated: 變焉，守法所甚賴也。嗟乎！古今迭運，皇王代興，方冊所載，規制畧盡，如岐、黃《内經》，百方畢具。有行之久而變者，有變之久而復者，有復而變、變而又復者。民俗無恒，國是靡定，在相時善用耳。如病者寒以寒治，熱以熱治，或寒熱變以變治，察標本緩急之勢而投之，此倉公、扁鵲所以計日而奏功也。而議法者獨務於因陋蹈常之為，不亦計左而失當哉？况今所整飭者，亦修其已試，去其泰甚，非特有驚世駭俗之舉，而不得議以更張也。《易》言「通變」，《詩》述「舊章」，與今飭法之意奚悖哉！夫今之法固犁然舉矣，執事猶求以議之，無亦慮其終而思維其漸歟？愚又聞之：天下之法，作于上，常格于下；人之情，謹于初，常弛於終。今之議者，要察法所由弊，而其咎則在人耳。是故補葺偏漏以支目前，而迂視萬全之計，猶扺安流而止維楫，非以濟遠也；建立方新，責効…
translation_en: …adapt to change—this is what those who uphold the laws heavily rely upon. Alas! Antiquity and the present succeed one another in turn, and sovereigns and kings arise generation after generation; what is recorded in the historical documents encompasses almost all regulations and institutions, just as the Inner Canon (Neijing) of Qibo and the Yellow Emperor contains every sort of medical prescription in full. There are measures that change after being practiced for a long time, those that are restored after having been changed for a long time, and those that change after being restored and are restored again after changing. Popular customs are not constant, and state policies are not fixed; it lies only in observing the times and making good use of them. It is just like treating a sick person: coldness is treated as coldness, heat is treated as heat, or when cold and heat fluctuate, the treatment is adapted to those fluctuations. Examining the urgency or Mildness of the symptoms and root causes before administering the medicine—this was how Master Cang (Canggong) and Bian Que were able to achieve results within a matter of days. Yet those who deliberate on the laws devote themselves solely to following crude precedents and treading in routine; is their calculation not misguided and inappropriate? Moreover, what is being rectified and put in order today merely repairs what has already been tested and removes what is excessive; it is not as though there are extraordinary measures meant to startle the world and shock common customs, so they cannot be criticized as radical overhauls. The Book of Changes (Yi) speaks of "comprehending change," and the Book of Odes (Shi) recounts "ancient statutes"—how is the intent of rectifying the laws today in any way contrary to these? Now, today's laws have indeed been clearly and thoroughly instituted, yet Your Excellency still seeks deliberations upon them; is it not because you are concerned about their ultimate outcome and wish to guard against gradual decay? I have also heard it said: the laws of the realm are initiated from above, yet are often obstructed from below; it is human nature to be diligent at the beginning, yet often grow lax at the end. Those who deliberate today must examine how the laws fall into abuse, and the fault lies simply with people. Therefore, patching up partial omissions merely to sustain the present moment while regarding a thoroughly sound plan as impractical is like reaching a calm current and stopping the oars and rigging—it is no way to cross to a distant shore; when an institution is newly established, demanding results…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
甚速猶朝揉輪而夕欲乘車非以需化也
當事者未及展半而輒執揣摩之見以求
詆勝猶左書而右息之非以示信也權宜
可行反株守顧忌而坐失事幾猶夏虫井
蛙非通方之識也下有煩言而欲敺之使
從猶倍招而必拘之非以順民也利一害
百以利冒害害一利百以害揜利猶立朝
夕於運均之上擔竿而欲定其末非以樹
功也數者其咎在人儻一有之國是必淆
===
人心不定而大妨於法非賈范諸賢惄然
而深憂者乎今之議議諸此而已此之不
務而曰吾以更化吾以捄時將一法立復
一弊興一法罷復一議起非識治體者也

translation_en:
… too quickly is like bending wood for a wheel in the morning and wanting to ride the carriage by evening—it is no way to await gradual transformation. When those in charge have not even carried out half of their plans and others immediately cling to speculative opinions to attack and prevail over them, it is like writing with the left hand while erasing with the right—it is no way to demonstrate trustworthiness. When expedient measures are feasible, yet one instead clings stubbornly to scruples and sits by as opportunities are lost, it is like being a summer insect or a frog in a well—it is not a comprehensive understanding. When there are clamorous complaints among the people below and one seeks to drive them into compliance by force, it is like pulling an animal away while trying to catch it [?]—it is no way to accord with the people. When there is one benefit and a hundred harms, letting the benefit obscure the harms, or when there is one harm and a hundred benefits, letting the harm eclipse the benefits, it is like trying to determine east and west on top of a spinning potter's wheel, or carrying a pole on one's shoulder while trying to keep its tip steady—it is no way to establish achievement. In all these cases, the fault lies with men. Should even one of them occur, state policy will inevitably be confused, people's minds will be unsettled, and great harm will be done to the laws. Is this not what worthy men such as Jia Yi 賈誼 and Fan Zhongyan 范仲淹 grieved over with such deep anxiety? Today's deliberations should simply deliberate upon these matters and nothing more. If one does not attend to this, yet claims, "I am reforming the administration; I am rescuing the times," then as soon as one law is established, another abuse will arise, and as soon as one law is abolished, another dispute will spring up. This is not someone who understands the essentials of governance.

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
是有關於世道者
同考試官教諭章批聖人作經之意晦於
傳疏久矣子能剖析羣言獨見聖心左胡諸儒當爲
斂衽矣
同考試官同知俞批經生類多勦說是作
剖析四傳而斷案了然是有得於心學者錄之
考試官洗馬周批評隲四傳論甚明確知
子非拘儒矣
考試官左諭德陳批辨析諸儒異同而歸於明
===
聖人之意必窮經而有心得者
甚哉說經之難也非說之難能明聖人之
意則難矣非明聖人之意之難也能不牽
於先儒之說則難矣彼以爲聖人之意有
以異於人乎哉是是而非非善善而惡惡
雖堯舜與塗人同而儒者之談經則曰此
非聖人莫能修之自游夏所不能贊一詞
者也於是乎平也而詭求之易也而艱尋
之其尊聖人彌甚其說彌長而作者之志

甚哉，說經之難也！非說之難，能明聖人之意則難矣；非明聖人之意之難也，能不牽於先儒之說則難矣。彼以爲聖人之意，有以異於人乎哉？是是而非非，善善而惡惡，雖堯、舜與塗人同。而儒者之談經則曰：「此非聖人莫能修之，自游、夏所不能贊一詞者也。」於是乎平也而詭求之，易也而艱尋之。其尊聖人彌甚，其說彌長，而作者之志
translation_en:
… it is something of real consequence for the moral order of the world.

Associate Examiner and Instructor Zhang 章 comments: The intent of the Sage in composing the Classic has long been obscured by commentaries and subcommentaries. You are able to analyze the multitude of views and perceive the mind of the Sage on your own; scholars like Zuo 左 and Hu 胡 would surely adjust their robes in respect before you.

Associate Examiner and Vice Prefect Yu 俞 comments: Students of the Classics mostly just repeat clichés, yet this essay analyzes the Four Commentaries and reaches clear-cut conclusions. It is the work of one who has attained insight into the learning of the mind; let it be recorded for publication.

Examiner and Librarian Zhou 周 comments: In evaluating the Four Commentaries, your arguments are exceedingly clear and accurate; one knows from this that you are no hidebound pedant.

Examiner and Left Admonisher Chen 陳 comments: Differentiating and analyzing the similarities and differences among the various scholars, while returning in the end to clarifying the intent of the Sage—this must be someone who has thoroughly mastered the Classic and gained personal insight from it.

How difficult it is to explicate the Classics! Yet the difficulty lies not in explicating them, but in being able to clarify the intent of the Sage; and the difficulty lies not even in clarifying the intent of the Sage, but in being able to avoid being bound by the interpretations of earlier scholars. Do they really suppose that the intent of the Sage is somehow different from that of other men? Affirming what is right and condemning what is wrong, praising the good and hating the evil—in this, even Yao 堯 and Shun 舜 are the same as the common man on the street. Yet when scholars discuss the Classic, they say: "None but the Sage could have compiled this; it is something to which even Ziyou 子游 and Zixia 子夏 could not add a single word." Consequently, where the meaning is plain, they seek it through tortuous ways; where it is easy, they search for it with strained difficulty. The more intensely they revere the Sage, the more prolix their explanations become, and the original purpose of the author…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
益以漓矣嗟夫獨抱遺經之歎豈非千古
之所同哉執事以春秋疑義策諸生夫說
春秋者類古所稱大儒也愚何敢以末議
干之雖然執事固曰六經將與天地無終
極而存非一人一世之私論也敢效其一
得而執事試擇焉夫自秦人滅學六經缺
如漢律既除孔壁始出諸儒掇拾煨燼各
名其家源遠而流益分其間悖理亂真者
固不少矣然易詩書之屬皆以理勝理悖
===
矣吾以理絀之其誣可立而辨也春秋以
事詞勝事往矣吾從千載之下隃度之孰
徵之而孰信之乎是故說經者宜莫難於
春秋也自漢而下說春秋者亡慮數百家
而獨公羊穀梁左氏最著胡氏最晚出亦
最著至我
昭代胡氏始得顓立于學官而諸家之說幾盡
廢矣夫左丘明與孔子共觀史記者也公
羊穀梁皆受業子夏者也洙泗之淵源非

punctuated: 益以漓矣。嗟夫！獨抱遺經之歎，豈非千古之所同哉！執事以《春秋》疑義策諸生，夫說《春秋》者，類古所稱大儒也，愚何敢以末議干之？雖然，執事固曰：「六經將與天地無終極而存，非一人一世之私論也。」敢效其一得，而執事試擇焉。夫自秦人滅學，六經缺如。漢律既除，孔壁始出，諸儒掇拾煨燼，各名其家。源遠而流益分，其間悖理亂真者固不少矣。然《易》、《詩》、《書》之屬，皆以理勝。理悖矣，吾以理絀之，其誣可立而辨也。《春秋》以事詞勝。事往矣，吾從千載之下隃度之，孰徵之而孰信之乎？是故說經者，宜莫難於《春秋》也。自漢而下，說《春秋》者亡慮數百家，而獨公羊、穀梁、左氏最著，胡氏最晚出，亦最著。至我昭代，胡氏始得顓立于學官，而諸家之說幾盡廢矣。夫左丘明與孔子共觀史記者也，公羊、穀梁皆受業子夏者也，洙泗之淵源非
translation_en: … becomes ever more diluted. Alas! Is not the lament of clinging alone to the surviving Classics shared across all ages? Your Honor has posed a policy question to us students regarding doubtful points in the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu). Now, those who have expounded the Spring and Autumn Annals are generally those whom antiquity called great Confucians; how could this ignorant student dare to intrude upon them with his humble opinions? Even so, Your Honor has indeed said that the Six Classics will endure without end alongside heaven and earth, and are not the private discourse of a single person or a single age. I venture to offer my modest insight, and may Your Honor test and select from it. Ever since the people of Qin destroyed learning, the Six Classics were left incomplete. Once the Han prohibitions were repealed and the texts from Confucius's wall first emerged, the various scholars gathered up the remnants from the ashes, each establishing his own school. As the source grew distant, the streams divided ever further, and among them there were certainly not a few that went against principle and confounded the truth. Yet works such as the Classic of Changes (Yi), the Classic of Odes (Shi), and the Classic of Documents (Shu) all prevail through principle. When a principle is violated, we can refute it by means of principle, and its falsity can be immediately discerned. The Spring and Autumn Annals, however, prevails through events and phrasing. Once the events have passed, if we conjecture about them from afar a thousand years later, who can verify them and who can confirm their credibility? For this reason, in expounding the Classics, nothing is more difficult than the Spring and Autumn Annals. From the Han dynasty onward, those who have expounded the Spring and Autumn Annals number roughly several hundred schools, yet only Gongyang, Guliang, and Zuo [Qiuming] are the most renowned; Hu [Anguo] appeared last, and is also most renowned. Down to our Illustrious Dynasty, Mr. Hu's commentary alone was established in the state schools, while the doctrines of the other schools were almost entirely discarded. Now, Zuo Qiuming觀察 examined the historical records together with Confucius, and Gongyang and Guliang both received instruction from Zixia. The fountainhead of the Zhu and Si rivers was not…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
遠筆削之微旨尚存然而口說流行事多
失實如一盟也而或以為蔑或以為眛一
工築也而或以為郿或以為微一會也而
或以為屈銀或以為厥憖一卒也而或以
為君氏或以為尹氏盖自名氏土壤已瞀
亂不能盡原况乃雌黃出其唇吻去取憑
諸胸臆如馬端臨以意增損之疑者又烏
能玄覽精詣劵合聖人之志乎至安國之
作傳也總三家紛紜之說而錄其似彙諸
===
家後出之論而采其長義例炳然衮鉞斯
備可謂素王之忠臣麟經之鼓吹矣雖然
以為不詭於聖人之教則可以為盡得聖
人之意則未也夫經之為言常也聖人之
作經也簡易明白不以微曖難明之詞眩
天下也不以操切繳繞之文誤後世也要
以是是而非非善善而惡惡以仍人道以
達王事如斯而已矣廼胡氏一時進御之
言意存納約是故不免激焉而偏索聖人

…distant, and the subtle import of Confucius's writing and editing still survived; yet as oral traditions circulated, the facts were often lost. For example, in recording a single covenant, one version has it at "Mie" while another has "Mei"; in recording a single construction project, one has it at "Mei" (郿) while another has "Wei" (微); in recording a single meeting, one has it at "Quyin" while another has "Jueyin"; in recording a single death, one has "Lady Jun" (Junshi) while another has "the Yin clan" (Yinshi). Indeed, even in names, clans, and places, they are already so confused and disordered that their origins cannot be fully traced; how much more so when alterations and criticisms issue from their own lips, and what is accepted or rejected rests solely on their own subjective notions—just as Ma Duanlin 馬端臨 suspected them of "adding and subtracting at will"—how then could they attain profound insight and exact comprehension so as to tally with the intent of the Sage?

When it came to Hu Anguo 胡安國 composing his Commentary (Zhuan), he brought together the tangled explanations of the three traditions and recorded what seemed plausible, and gathered the later discussions of various scholars and adopted their strengths. Its principles and precedents are luminous, and its praise and blame—like ceremonial robes and battle-axes—are complete; he may truly be called a loyal minister to the Uncrowned King and a trumpeter for the Unicorn Classic (the Spring and Autumn Annals)! Even so, if one considers it not contrary to the Sage's teachings, that is permissible; if one considers it to have fully grasped the Sage's intent, it has not yet done so. For the word "classic" (jing) means what is constant. When the Sage composed the Classic, he made it simple, easy, and clear; he did not dazzle the world with obscure and inscrutable words, nor did he mislead later generations with harsh, hair-splitting, and convoluted writing. In essence, he sought only to affirm what is right and condemn what is wrong, to praise the good and despise the evil, thereby adhering to the way of humanity and carrying forward the business of the true king—nothing more than this. Yet Master Hu's commentary consisted of words presented to the throne for the moment, with his intention set on offering admonition through the window of opportunity; therefore, he could not avoid being vehement and one-sided. In seeking the Sage's…

而深名其可通者曰常例而強名其不可
通者曰變例是故不免窮焉而鑿如以春
王正月爲行夏之時是以周人而改周朔
於義則不順以夏時而紀魯事於史則不
倫非夫子之志也以王不稱天爲貶夫事
干宗國往往諱稱其過舉而尊爲共主輕
以小故削奪之非夫子之志也以子滕侯
爲懲亂賊之黨夫躬爲篡逆者無誅焉而
===

其慘礉而亡謂也非夫子之志也以止不
嘗藥而被之以大惡之名是以微文而致
重辟於人申商之所不爲也非夫子之志

也曷不重貶子圍之會而姑諱其弑是登

translation_en: …essential meaning of [the Sage] in the wording of single-character additions and deletions, and for this reason he could not avoid being forced and overly abstruse; he named what could be made sense of "regular principles" (changli), and forcibly named what could not be made sense of "variant principles" (bianli), and for this reason he could not avoid being driven into a corner and becoming contrived. For example, taking "Spring, the King's first month" as practicing the calendar of the Xia dynasty means that as a man of Zhou, [Confucius] altered the calendar of Zhou, which in principle is improper; and using the Xia calendar to record the affairs of the state of Lu is in terms of historiography incoherent—this was not the intent of the Master. Taking the reference to "the King" without the epithet "Heavenly" as censure: now, in matters touching upon his ancestral state [of Lu], he often concealed and avoided mentioning its transgressions; yet toward the one revered as the common sovereign [the Zhou king], to lightly strip and deprive him [of his title] over a minor matter—this was not the intent of the Master. Taking the downgrading of the Marquis of Teng to Viscount ("Viscount-ing the Marquis of Teng") as punishing the partisans of rebels and traitors: now, those who personally committed usurpation and treason went unpunished, yet to demote a marquis appointed by the Son of Heaven, and moreover to strip his descendants along with him—how harsh, unforgiving, and senseless that would be! This was not the intent of the Master. On account of [Crown Prince] Zhi not tasting the medicine, to saddle him with the name of a great crime [regicide/patricide] is to use subtle wording to inflict the heaviest penalty upon a man—something even Shen Buhai 申不害 and Shang Yang 商鞅 would not do; this was not the intent of the Master. Regarding the recording of the "death" (zu) of Jun of Chu, [Hu Anguo] says it was to "uphold the Central States." Even if he truly wished to uphold the Central States, why did [Confucius] not severely censure the meeting of Ziwei, instead of temporarily concealing his regicide? That would be to promote rebellion; this was not the intent of the Master. Regarding the recording of the restitution of the lands [by Qi to Lu], he says that [Confucius] "assumed for himself the position of Heaven." Now, the wording contains no praise—where in it is there any recording of merit? [Confucius] simply wrote it down straightforwardly according to the facts, yet [Hu] insists on saying that he "assumed for himself the position of Heaven." This is to exalt the Sage…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
過而誣其實也非夫子之志也絶筆于獲
麟也而曰以天道終是以瑞應神其書也
且麟之出經曷故焉蓋所謂感麟而作者
近之而必曰文成麟至非聖人之志也又
有甚焉者以爲夫子託二百四十二年南
面之權以誅賞人也夫孔子雖聖周人也
賤而自專灾且及之苟無其位不作禮樂
斯非孔氏之烱戒乎夫子作春秋以尊周
室而攔然攬天子之權以誅賞天下奪人
===
之國貶人之爵去人之氏没人之族操縱
自我而無少顧忌焉則是干紀犯義已爲
戎首而顧以履忠效順責僭王之吳楚專
魯之三家也豈不鑿哉然則孟氏所謂天
子之事者何曰天子之事者猶云周天子
之法耳當是時姬轍雖東典刑猶在春秋
而有所刺譏夫子曰非吾奪之也是文武
之法之所誅也春秋而有所褒進夫子曰
非吾予之也是文武之法之所賞也知我
