punctuated: 過，而誣其實也，非夫子之志也。絶筆于獲麟也，而曰「以天道終」，是以瑞應神其書也。且麟之出，經曷故焉？蓋所謂「感麟而作」者近之，而必曰「文成麟至」，非聖人之志也。又有甚焉者，以爲夫子託二百四十二年南面之權以誅賞人也。夫孔子雖聖，周人也。「賤而自專，灾且及之」，「苟無其位，不作禮樂」，斯非孔氏之烱戒乎？夫子作《春秋》以尊周室，而攔然攬天子之權以誅賞天下，奪人之國，貶人之爵，去人之氏，没人之族，操縱自我，而無少顧忌焉，則是干紀犯義，已爲戎首，而顧以履忠效順責僭王之吳、楚，專魯之三家也，豈不鑿哉！然則孟氏所謂「天子之事」者何？曰：「天子之事」者，猶云周天子之法耳。當是時，姬轍雖東，典刑猶在。《春秋》而有所刺譏，夫子曰：「非吾奪之也，是文、武之法之所誅也。」《春秋》而有所褒進，夫子曰：「非吾予之也，是文、武之法之所賞也。」知我
translation_en: … excess and falsifying the facts; this was not the Master's intent. As for his laying down his brush at the capture of the unicorn (lin), to say that "it ends with the Way of Heaven" is to mystify his book by means of auspicious omens. Moreover, what bearing did the appearance of the unicorn have on the Classic? Indeed, the saying that "he was moved by the unicorn to compose it" comes close to the truth, whereas to insist that "when the text was completed, the unicorn arrived" is not the intent of the Sage. There is an even more extreme view, which holds that the Master entrusted himself with the authority of a ruler facing south over two hundred and forty-two years in order to punish and reward men. Now, although Confucius was a sage, he was a man of Zhou. "If one who is of low station acts on his own authority, disaster is sure to befall him," and "if one does not occupy the position, one does not create rites and music"—were these not the clear warnings of Confucius himself? The Master composed the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) in order to honor the House of Zhou; if he had brazenly usurped the authority of the Son of Heaven to punish and reward the realm—stripping men of their states, demoting them in rank, removing their clan names, erasing their lineages, holding sole power to grant and take away without the slightest scruple—then in violating institutional order and offending against righteousness, he himself would have been the chief offender! Yet for him to turn around and demand loyalty and obedience from Wu and Chu, which usurped the title of king, and from the Three Families, which monopolized power in Lu—how preposterous would that be! If so, then what did Mencius mean by "the business of the Son of Heaven"? I say: "the business of the Son of Heaven" simply means the laws of the Zhou Son of Heaven. At that time, although the carriage tracks of the Ji ruling house had moved east, the old statutes and penalties still remained. Where the Spring and Autumn Annals criticized and censured, the Master said: "It is not I who strip them; it is what the laws of Kings Wen and Wu punish." Where the Spring and Autumn Annals praised and promoted, the Master said: "It is not I who grant it to them; it is what the laws of Kings Wen and Wu reward." Those who understand me…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
者文武之法明謂我能尊周也罪我者僭
亂之罪著則諸侯惡其害己也此亂賊所
爲懼也第令夫子以匹夫自爲天子天下
不軌之夫羣起而議其後之不暇而又誰
能懼之是故學春秋者明於天子之事之
一言則孔氏筆削之大義昭昭乎若揭日
月而行而彼紛紛者之說可不辨而息矣
繇斯以談漢儒之說經也專門名師保殘
守缺不相合而相存其失也固宋儒之說
===
經也師心背古揣摩傅會有所合而不必
盡合也其失也鑿彼固焉者信滯而不通
矣然而是非錯陳若蒼素然不可殽而雜
也鑿焉者雖辨而可喜矣然而憑私臆决
若射覆然不可倖而中也是故三傳立而
聖人之教分聖人之志則未失也胡氏之
傳出而聖人之教尊其得者固多而失者
亦不少矣愚竊考春秋之作寔孔子口授
弟子退而異言流傳失真其有無疑似之

者文武之法明謂我能尊周也罪我者僭
亂之罪著則諸侯惡其害已也此亂賊所
爲懼也夢令夫子以匹夫自爲天子天下
不執之夫羣起而議其後之不暇而又誰
能懼之是故學春秋者明於天子之事之

月而行而彼紛紛者之說可不辨而息矣
繇斯以談漢儒之說經也專門名師保殘
守缺不相合而相存其失也固宋儒之說
===
經也師心背古揣摩傳會有所合而不必
盡合也其失也鑿彼固焉者信滯而不通
矣然而是非錯陳若蒼素然不可淆而雜
也鑿焉者雖辨而可喜矣然而憑私臆决
若射覆然不可倖而中也是故三傳立而
聖人之教分聖人之志則未失也胡氏之
傳出而聖人之教尊其得者固多而失者
亦不少矣愚竊考春秋之作寔孔子口授
弟子退而異言流傳失真其有無疑似之
punctuated:
者，文武之法明，謂我能尊周也；罪我者，僭亂之罪著，則諸侯惡其害己也。此亂賊所爲懼也。第令夫子以匹夫自爲天子，天下不軌之夫羣起而議其後之不暇，而又誰能懼之？是故學《春秋》者，明於「天子之事」之一言，則孔氏筆削之大義，昭昭乎若揭日月而行，而彼紛紛者之說可不辨而息矣。

繇斯以談，漢儒之說經也，專門名師，保殘守缺，不相合而相存，其失也固；宋儒之說經也，師心背古，揣摩傅會，有所合而不必盡合也，其失也鑿。彼固焉者，信滯而不通矣，然而是非錯陳，若蒼素然，不可殽而雜也；鑿焉者，雖辨而可喜矣，然而憑私臆决，若射覆然，不可倖而中也。是故三傳立而聖人之教分，聖人之志則未失也；胡氏之傳出而聖人之教尊，其得者固多，而失者亦不少矣。愚竊考《春秋》之作，寔孔子口授，弟子退而異言，流傳失真，其有無疑似之
translation_en:
… me, the laws of King Wen and King Wu will be made clear, and they will say that I was able to honor the Zhou. As for those who condemn me, the crimes of usurpation and rebellion will be made manifest, and the feudal lords will hate it for harming their own interests.” This is why rebellious ministers and villainous sons were afraid. If the Master, as a commoner, had merely arrogated to himself the role of the Son of Heaven, lawless men throughout the realm would have risen up in droves and been all too quick to criticize him from behind—whom, then, could he have made afraid? Therefore, if students of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) clearly understand this single phrase, “the prerogative of the Son of Heaven,” then the great principles by which Confucius wrote and expunged will be as radiantly clear as holding aloft the sun and moon as one walks, and the theories of those multitudinous disputants will subside without even needing to be refuted.

Speaking from this perspective, when the Han scholars explained the Classic, they were specialists and renowned masters who guarded殘fragments and preserved incomplete texts; they did not agree with one another, yet they coexisted, and their flaw was obstinacy. When the Song scholars explained the Classic, they took their own minds as their master and turned their backs on antiquity, speculating and forcing interpretations; they hit the mark in some respects but did not necessarily do so in all, and their flaw was forced subtlety. Those who are obstinate are indeed bogged down and lack comprehension; yet right and wrong are laid out side by side like black and white, and cannot be confused or mixed together. Those who indulge in forced subtlety, though eloquent and pleasing, rely on private conjecture to make judgments, as if playing the guessing game of “shooting at covered objects,” and cannot hit the mark by mere luck. Therefore, when the Three Commentaries were established, the teachings of the Sage were divided, yet the intent of the Sage was not lost; when the commentary of Master Hu [Hu Anguo 胡安國] appeared, the teachings of the Sage were revered, and while what it got right was certainly much, what it got wrong was also not inconsiderable. I have privately examined the composition of the Spring and Autumn Annals: in truth, Confucius transmitted it orally, and when his disciples withdrew, they gave differing accounts; as it was handed down, the truth was lost, and its doubtful passages, whether present or absent…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
文蓋不特魯魚亥豕而已惟左丘明論本
事而作傳於經文為近自餘百家之說未
可定以為不刊之訓也學者誠超然遠覽
本之以經翼之以左氏折衷之以諸家之
論要以會夫子仍人道達王事之意而不
牽于一曲之議此亦所以恢弘聖緒而俟
萬世於無窮矣若必強經以從已狗傳以
蔑經即使左氏授簡公穀操牘愚猶未敢
盡信也况其它乎噫此難與拘儒道也
===
第四問
王士昌
同考試官教諭楊 批 知人之哲自古稱難
子能綜覈往昔不欲狥法術而歸重辨心端本之論尤有卓見
考試官洗馬周 批 答問詳核至名實之辨
深究物情是必有知人之鑑者
考試官左諭德陳 批 知人先在辨心自是確
論而此作敷對明悉錄之
夫天下非乏才之患所貴得論才之要論

夫天下非乏才之患所貴得論才之要論
punctuated:
文，蓋不特魯魚亥豕而已。惟左丘明論本事而作傳，於經文為近；自餘百家之說，未可定以為不刊之訓也。學者誠超然遠覽，本之以經，翼之以左氏，折衷之以諸家之論，要以會夫子仍人道、達王事之意，而不牽于一曲之議，此亦所以恢弘聖緒，而俟萬世於無窮矣。若必強經以從已，狗傳以蔑經，即使左氏授簡、公穀操牘，愚猶未敢盡信也，况其它乎！噫！此難與拘儒道也。

第四問
王士昌
同考試官教諭楊，批：〔知人之哲，自古稱難。子能綜覈往昔，不欲狥法術而歸重辨心，端本之論，尤有卓見。〕
考試官洗馬周，批：〔答問詳核，至名實之辨，深究物情，是必有知人之鑑者。〕
考試官左諭德陳，批：〔知人先在辨心，自是確論，而此作敷對明悉，錄之。〕

夫天下非乏才之患，所貴得論才之要。論
translation_en:
… text are probably not merely cases of copyist errors like confusing "Lu" with "yu" or "hai" with "shi." Only Zuo Qiuming (左丘明) composed his commentary by discussing the original events, coming closest to the Classic's text; as for the theories of the hundred other schools, they cannot be established as immutable precepts. If scholars truly take a transcendent and far-reaching view—grounding themselves in the Classic, flanking it with the Zuo Commentary (Zuoshi 左氏), and striking a balance among the discussions of the various schools—seeking in essence to grasp the Master's intent in following the human way and conveying kingly affairs without being bound by one-sided arguments, this too is the way to expand the sage's legacy and await ten thousand generations without end. If one insists on forcing the Classic to conform to oneself, or blindly following the commentaries [reading 徇 for 狗] to the detriment of the Classic, then even if Zuo Qiuming himself handed down the bamboo slips and Gongyang (公羊) and Guliang (穀梁) wielded the writing tablets, I still would not dare to believe them completely—how much less the others! Alas, this is difficult to discuss with narrow-minded scholars!

Fourth Question
Wang Shichang (王士昌)
Associate Examiner and Instructor Yang comments: "The wisdom to know men has been called difficult since antiquity. You are able to synthesize and verify the past, declining to merely follow legalist methods and administrative techniques while placing ultimate weight on discerning the mind; your discussion of rectifying the fundamental shows particularly outstanding insight."
Examiner and Librarian Zhou comments: "The response to the question is detailed and well-verified. When it comes to distinguishing between name and reality, it probes deeply into the nature of things; this is surely someone who possesses the mirror for knowing men."
Examiner and Left Admonisher Chen comments: "That knowing men first lies in discerning the mind is naturally an indisputable argument, and this piece sets forth its reply with clarity and thoroughness; it is selected for inclusion."

Now, the empire does not suffer from a lack of talent; what is valued is grasping the essentials of evaluating talent. Evaluating…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
才之要豈易言哉蓋人主羅海內之才而
陶冶驅策之論辨一失其要則堂陛懸殊
而眾情易壅衡鑑靡定而士品逾淆有之
未必知知之未必盡才難自古嘆之矣官
人者察其然以為品藻宜精固詳以法法
術難徧尤論以心由是較量審而眩巧飾
詐無所容名實覈而真賢實能有所見羣
才各適於用而天下之治輻輳於前矣若
心之弗辨而汎然求之乎法術之間欲以
===
盡知而任使之詎足為定論哉愚考覽典
謨稱引堯舜者焯哉盛矣而道莫大於知
人夫堯諸臣中豈復賢于舜哉而又豈待
更相推譽始可用哉乃疇咨之命周於四
岳諸艱之試歷於三載當是時野稱無遺
賢矣而君曰明揚臣曰俞受其所動色相
戒陳謨致儆者不徐徐焉是求知人於朞
隆之世聖哲之主猶然難之矣彼下代又
何論哉嗣是之君若有易焉者漢時呂姬

何論哉嗣是之君若有易焉者漢時呂娅
punctuated:
才之要，豈易言哉？蓋人主羅海內之才，而陶冶驅策之，論辨一失其要，則堂陛懸殊而眾情易壅，衡鑑靡定而士品逾淆。有之未必知，知之未必盡，「才難」自古嘆之矣。官人者察其然，以為品藻宜精，固詳以法；法術難徧，尤論以心。由是較量審而眩巧飾詐無所容，名實覈而真賢實能有所見，羣才各適於用，而天下之治輻輳於前矣。若心之弗辨，而汎然求之乎法術之間，欲以盡知而任使之，詎足為定論哉？

愚考覽《典》、《謨》，稱引堯、舜者，焯哉盛矣，而道莫大於知人。夫堯諸臣中，豈復賢于舜哉？而又豈待更相推譽始可用哉？乃疇咨之命周於四岳，諸艱之試歷於三載。當是時，野稱無遺賢矣，而君曰「明揚」，臣曰「俞受」，其所動色相戒、陳謨致儆者，不徐徐焉。是求知人於朞隆之世、聖哲之主，猶然難之矣，彼下代又何論哉？嗣是之君，若有易焉者。漢時，呂姬
translation_en:
… essential principle of evaluating talent—how could it be easy to speak of? Indeed, when the ruler gathers the talents within the seas to mold and employ them, if his evaluation and discernment once lose hold of the essential principle, then because the distance between the throne hall and the steps below is vast, the sentiments of the multitude are easily obstructed; and when the balance and mirror of judgment are unsettled, the grades of scholars become ever more confused. One may possess talent without its necessarily being known, and it may be known without necessarily being fully utilized; "the scarcity of talent" has been lamented since antiquity. Those who appoint men to office observe that this is so, and consider that while grading and appraisal ought to be precise—which is assuredly detailed through regulations—methods and techniques cannot cover everything, so one must especially evaluate them through the mind. Consequently, comparisons are thorough, leaving dazzling artifice and disguised deceit nowhere to hide; reputation and reality are verified, allowing true worthies and genuine abilities to become manifest; the myriad talents are each suited to their use, and the governance of the empire converges before the throne like spokes at a hub. If one fails to discern the mind and instead seeks talent vaguely among regulations and techniques, wishing thereby to know men completely and employ them in office, how could that suffice as a definitive principle?

I have examined and perused the "Canons" and "Counsels" [of the Book of Documents]: their praise and citations of Yao 堯 and Shun 舜 are辉煌 and glorious indeed, yet no way in them is greater than knowing men. Now among all the ministers of Yao, how could anyone have been worthier than Shun? And how could it have required their mutual recommendation and praise before he could be employed? Yet the charge asking "Who will search out someone?" went all around to the Four Mountains (Siyue 四岳), and the trials through various hardships extended over three years. At that time, it was said that no worthy was left overlooked in the wilderness; yet the sovereign said, "Promote plainly," and the minister said, "Accept with approval," and in changing countenance to admonish one another and setting forth counsels to urge caution, they were by no means leisurely about it. Thus, even when seeking to know men in an age of consummate flourishing and under sage and wise rulers, they still found it this difficult—what, then, is there to say of later ages? Among rulers who succeeded them, there were some for whom it seemed easy. In the Han dynasty, before Empress Lü's (Lü Ji 呂姬) …

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
專制未著也高帝知周勃重厚少文必成
安劉之功七國之變未兆也文帝知周亞
夫爲將可任緩急之用則幾於識鑒素定
矣霍光輔政昭帝以冲年覺上書之詐而
稱爲忠臣皇甫無逸守蜀唐高祖知其爲
人誣構而勞以清正則幾於讒言不惑矣
房琯初爲將也明皇聞之而評其才非破
賊卒以僨師李藩被杜兼之誣德宗一見
儀度安雅信其状非爲惡則幾於料人屢
===
中矣之數君於其臣預决後来立辨倉卒
若符券然不爽要以性資明達故一時評
隲偶合也然酈食其之佞疎賈生之才劉
文靜以譖沮宋璟以直疑陸贄以猜忌廢
得此失彼僅優於庸闇之主則可耳未足
與聖人較難易也若堯難於得舜非其明
不足也憂天下之心爲之耳憂之深故求
之慎求之慎故得之難而天下後世卒不
以爲聖智累何者智周天下而不自用也

punctuated: 專制未著也，高帝知周勃重厚少文，必成安劉之功；七國之變未兆也，文帝知周亞夫爲將，可任緩急之用，則幾於識鑒素定矣。霍光輔政，昭帝以冲年覺上書之詐，而稱爲忠臣；皇甫無逸守蜀，唐高祖知其爲人誣構，而勞以清正，則幾於讒言不惑矣。房琯初爲將也，明皇聞之，而評其才非破賊，卒以僨師；李藩被杜兼之誣，德宗一見，儀度安雅，信其状非爲惡，則幾於料人屢中矣。之數君於其臣，預决後来，立辨倉卒，若符券然不爽，要以性資明達，故一時評隲偶合也。然酈食其之佞，疎賈生之才，劉文靜以譖沮，宋璟以直疑，陸贄以猜忌廢。得此失彼，僅優於庸闇之主則可耳，未足與聖人較難易也。若堯難於得舜，非其明不足也，憂天下之心爲之耳。憂之深故求之慎，求之慎故得之難，而天下後世卒不以爲聖智累。何者？智周天下而不自用也。
translation_en: … autocratic rule had not yet become manifest, yet Emperor Gaozu knew that Zhou Bo 周勃, though grave and lacking in refinement, would surely accomplish the feat of securing the Liu 劉 clan. Before the Rebellion of the Seven States had shown any sign, Emperor Wen knew that Zhou Yafu 周亞夫 as a general could be entrusted with service in an emergency. Thus they came close to having a settled discernment of character beforehand. When Huo Guang 霍光 was assisting in government, Emperor Zhao, though young in years, detected the deceit of the memorial presented against him and praised him as a loyal minister; when Huangfu Wuyi 皇甫無逸 was guarding Shu, Emperor Gaozu of the Tang knew that he had been falsely framed by others and consoled him for his purity and rectitude. Thus they came close to being unswayed by slander. When Fang Guan 房琯 first became a general, Emperor Minghuang [Xuanzong] heard of it and judged that his talent was not suited to defeating rebels, and in the end he ruined his army; when Li Fan 李藩 was falsely accused by Du Jian 杜兼, Emperor Dezong, upon seeing his calm and refined demeanor at first glance, trusted that his bearing was not that of an evildoer. Thus they came close to repeatedly hitting the mark in judging men. That these several rulers, in regard to their ministers, could foresee the future and make immediate distinctions in a moment of haste, unerring as matching tallies, was essentially because their natural endowments were bright and perceptive, so their momentary evaluations happened to hit the mark. Yet there was the flattery of Li Yiji 酈食其, the estrangement of the talent of Master Jia [Jia Yi 賈誼], Liu Wenjing 劉文靜 thwarted by slander, Song Jing 宋璟 suspected for his uprightness, and Lu Zhi 陸贄 discarded out of jealous suspicion. Gaining one while losing another, they may simply be deemed superior to mediocre and benighted rulers, yet they are not worthy of being compared with the sages as to the difficulty or ease of knowing men. As for Yao's difficulty in obtaining Shun, it was not that his discernment was insufficient; it was simply caused by a heart anxious for the empire. Because his anxiety was deep, his search was cautious; because his search was cautious, obtaining him was difficult. Yet the empire and later generations ultimately did not consider this a blemish upon his sagely wisdom. Why is this? Because his wisdom encompassed the whole empire, yet he did not rely solely upon himself.

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
嗟乎世之需才無古今一才所見知於世
有難易豈上天生才為後世增多而全盛
之世更減算哉亦豈古之人殊形異狀而
不可肖似哉其論而知之者殊矣蓋人才
有似有真以真論之真者出以似論之似
者出真似之間則才之難易世之汚隆胥
係焉甚哉論才不可無要也愚考執事所
問視之有五者李克告文侯卜相是矣說
非不詳也如言居視所親與管寧同處者
===
從逆矣富視所與以大斗貸民者篡國矣
貧視所不取避居於陵者大倫亂矣以此
例克之說其他未信皆當也又考徵之有
九者莊生之論是矣說非不詳也如言卒
然問之以觀智而帝丘之對佞矣急與之
期以觀信而柱下之期固矣告之危以觀
節而不死崔難者稱賢矣以此例莊之說
其他未信無遺也至若劉劭人物志述十
二流之業陸贄言八計以稽吏司馬光言

punctuated: 嗟乎！世之需才，無古今一；才所見知於世，有難易。豈上天生才，為後世增多，而全盛之世更減算哉？亦豈古之人殊形異狀，而不可肖似哉？其論而知之者殊矣。蓋人才有似有真。以真論之，真者出；以似論之，似者出。真似之間，則才之難易、世之汚隆胥係焉。甚哉，論才不可無要也！愚考執事所問：視之有五者，李克告文侯卜相是矣，說非不詳也。如言居視所親，與管寧同處者從逆矣；富視所與，以大斗貸民者篡國矣；貧視所不取，避居於陵者大倫亂矣。以此例克之說，其他未信皆當也。又考徵之有九者，莊生之論是矣，說非不詳也。如言卒然問之以觀智，而帝丘之對佞矣；急與之期以觀信，而柱下之期固矣；告之危以觀節，而不死崔難者稱賢矣。以此例莊之說，其他未信無遺也。至若劉劭《人物志》述十二流之業，陸贄言八計以稽吏，司馬光言
translation_en:
Alas! The world's need for talent is the same whether in antiquity or the present, yet whether talent comes to be recognized by the world varies in difficulty. Could it be that Heaven on high produces more talent for later ages while curtailing its tally in eras of supreme flourishing? Or could it be that the people of antiquity were of such extraordinary forms and strange appearances that they cannot be resembled? Rather, it is how people evaluate and come to know them that differs. Indeed, among human talents there is the specious and there is the genuine. When evaluated by what is genuine, genuine talents emerge; when evaluated by what is specious, specious ones emerge. On the distinction between the genuine and the specious hang both the difficulty or ease of finding talent and the decline or flourishing of the age. How vital it is that the evaluation of talent not lack an essential principle!

I have examined what Your Excellency has asked. As for the "five observations," this refers to Li Ke 李克 advising Marquis Wen of Wei 魏文侯 on selecting a chief minister. That theory is by no means lacking in detail. Yet if one says, "In private life, observe whom he is close to," the one who shared quarters with Guan Ning 管寧 (Hua Xin 華歆) went on to follow a usurper! If one says, "When wealthy, observe to whom he gives," the one who loaned grain to the people using a large peck-measure (Tian Chang 田常) usurped a state! If one says, "When poor, observe what he refuses to take," the one who withdrew to live at Wuling 於陵 (Chen Zhongzi 陳仲子) threw the great human relationships into disorder! Judging Li Ke's theory by these cases, one cannot trust that the rest of it is entirely fitting either.

I have also examined the "nine tests," which refers to the discourse of Master Zhuang (Zhuangzi 莊子). That theory, too, is by no means lacking in detail. Yet if one says, "Question him suddenly to observe his wisdom," the reply given at Diqiu 帝丘 was mere glib flattery! If one says, "Press him with an appointment to observe his trustworthiness," the one who kept his appointment beneath the pillar (Wei Sheng 尾生) was merely obstinate! If one says, "Inform him of crisis to observe his integrity," the one who did not die in the disaster of Cui Zhu 崔杼 (Yan Ying 晏嬰) was nonetheless acclaimed as a worthy! Judging Zhuangzi's theory by these cases, one cannot trust that the rest of it is free of omissions either.

As for Liu Shao's 劉劭 Treatise on Personalities (Renwu zhi 人物志) describing the vocations of the twelve types, Lu Zhi 陸贄 speaking of the eight criteria for auditing officials, and Sima Guang 司馬光 speaking of…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
十科以舉士采其說而行之品流甄别亦
能得其大較似未可以槩少要之猶求於
術也人才至衆多矣而以術盡之是舉有
限之智慮勝無窮之奸欺據一時之踪跡
槩平生之淑慝力既不足而日亦不給矣
惟宋儒朱子推易書陰陽之理爲君子小
人之辨其言曰凡正大光明疎暢通達無
纖芥可疑者知必爲君子依阿淟涊回互
隱伏不可方物者知必爲小人夫易以陽
===
爲君子故于陽之進則有欣幸扶植之意
而其義爲剛爲明爲義爲公也易以陰爲
小人故於陰之進有防懼戒抑之意而其
義爲柔爲暗爲利爲私也此則不拘於術
獨究以心酌而考之以論天下之士不必
深求隱索而君子小人之情狀可坐籌之
矣以視諸說蓋尤要哉執事又感
今日需才之切慮名實之眩而究論辨之道
愚生復何說以進竊亦聞焉迪知忱恂則

punctuated: 十科以舉士，采其說而行之，品流甄别，亦能得其大較，似未可以槩少，要之猶求於術也。人才至衆多矣，而以術盡之，是舉有限之智慮，勝無窮之奸欺；據一時之踪跡，槩平生之淑慝，力既不足，而日亦不給矣。惟宋儒朱子推《易》書陰陽之理，爲君子小人之辨。其言曰：「凡正大光明、疎暢通達、無纖芥可疑者，知必爲君子；依阿淟涊、回互隱伏、不可方物者，知必爲小人。」夫《易》以陽爲君子，故于陽之進，則有欣幸扶植之意，而其義爲剛、爲明、爲義、爲公也；《易》以陰爲小人，故於陰之進，有防懼戒抑之意，而其義爲柔、爲暗、爲利、爲私也。此則不拘於術，獨究以心，酌而考之，以論天下之士，不必深求隱索，而君子小人之情狀可坐籌之矣。以視諸說，蓋尤要哉！執事又感今日需才之切，慮名實之眩，而究論辨之道，愚生復何說以進？竊亦聞焉：迪知忱恂，則
translation_en:
… ten categories for recommending scholars—if one adopts their theories and puts them into practice, in grading and distinguishing men of different ranks one can indeed grasp the general outline. It seems they should not be dismissed altogether; yet in essence, they still seek to do so through techniques. Men of talent are exceedingly numerous, and to try to exhaust them all by means of techniques is to pit limited calculation against boundless deceit and fraud, and to judge a lifetime of virtue or vice on the basis of a single moment's conduct—one's strength will not suffice, nor will there be enough days.

Only the Song Confucian Master Zhu [Zhu Xi 朱熹] extended the principle of yin and yang in the Book of Changes (Yi) to distinguish between the noble man (junzi) and the petty man (xiaoren). His words were: "Whenever someone is upright, great, bright, and open, clear and unobstructed, without the slightest ground for suspicion, one knows he must be a noble man; whenever someone is compliant and obsequious, filthy and muddled, devious, evasive, and lurking in secret so that he cannot be pinned down, one knows he must be a petty man." Now, the Book of Changes takes yang to represent the noble man; therefore, when yang advances, there is an intent to rejoice in and foster it, and its meaning is firmness, brightness, righteousness, and public-spiritedness. The Book of Changes takes yin to represent the petty man; therefore, when yin advances, there is an intent to guard against, fear, warn, and suppress it, and its meaning is softness, darkness, profit, and selfishness. This approach is not bound by techniques, but investigates solely through the mind. If one weighs and examines by this means to evaluate the scholars of the world, there is no need to probe deeply or search into hidden things, and the true nature and circumstances of noble men and petty men can be reckoned while sitting at ease. Compared with all those other theories, is this not even more essential!

Your Excellency, moreover, feels keenly today's urgent need for talent, worries about the confusion between reputation and reality, and seeks to thoroughly investigate the way of evaluating and distinguishing men. What further words could this foolish student offer? Yet I have humbly heard it said: when one truly knows those who are sincere and trustworthy, then…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
夏以籲俊克知灼見則周以興賢古帝王
辨才而官器能而使豈沾沾然藉法術已
哉毋亦以心論之已耳愚生反覆古今士
之能建鴻業而垂休光者雖才智之全而
實心術之正才智以致用心術以立本兩
者交相濟而正心其要也夫豫章栟櫚雖
有寸朽匠石不棄若膚完而腹蠹即合抱
不一操引顧焉馬有逸足而調馴者此良
馬也或詭銜竊轡失故步而倍周行即伯
===
樂造父不願有焉士累於心術者猶是矣
然而未易知也伺以獨見耳目易窮求之
衆情參驗無據惟在上者深辨之耳今之
時豈常患乏才哉而往往病品之不定論
之不一者無異故也患在人之飾其心以
售上之知而或不盡辨是以名溢於實業
負於望遂有薦墨未乾旋以無竒黜矣謗
篋方騰尋以善狀聞矣論之逾詳失之彌
遠需之甚切遘之甚難執事謂名實相貿

punctuated: 夏以籲俊；克知灼見，則周以興賢。古帝王辨才而官，器能而使，豈沾沾然藉法術已哉？毋亦以心論之已耳。愚生反覆古今，士之能建鴻業而垂休光者，雖才智之全，而實心術之正。才智以致用，心術以立本，兩者交相濟，而正心其要也。夫豫章、栟櫚，雖有寸朽，匠石不棄；若膚完而腹蠹，即合抱不一操引顧焉。馬有逸足而調馴者，此良馬也；或詭銜竊轡，失故步而倍周行，即伯樂、造父不願有焉。士累於心術者猶是矣，然而未易知也。伺以獨見，耳目易窮；求之衆情，參驗無據。惟在上者深辨之耳。今之時豈常患乏才哉？而往往病品之不定、論之不一者，無異故也。患在人之飾其心以售上之知，而或不盡辨，是以名溢於實，業負於望。遂有薦墨未乾，旋以無竒黜矣；謗篋方騰，尋以善狀聞矣。論之逾詳，失之彌遠；需之甚切，遘之甚難。執事謂名實相貿…
translation_en: …it was how the Xia dynasty summoned men of outstanding talent; truly knowing and clearly perceiving them was how the Zhou dynasty promoted the worthy. When the emperors and kings of antiquity discerned talent to bestow office and measured ability to assign tasks, how could they have relied smugly on mere methods and techniques alone? Surely they evaluated men simply by their minds and hearts! Looking repeatedly over past and present, I, your humble student, find that scholars who were able to establish great enterprises and hand down glorious reputations, though complete in talent and wisdom, in reality possessed uprightness of mind and intent. Talent and wisdom serve practical application, while mind and intent establish the foundation; the two complement each other, yet rectifying the mind is the essential point. Now, even if camphor or coir-palm timber has an inch of rot, Artisan Shi (Jiang Shi 匠石) will not discard it; yet if its bark is intact while its core is worm-eaten, even if it is a tree of an arm's span in circumference, he would not once take up his marking line or give it a second glance. A horse that has fleet feet and is well-broken and docile is a fine steed; yet if it spits out the bit and slips the reins, losing its proper pace and turning away from the highway, even Bo Le 伯樂 and Zao Fu 造父 would not wish to own it. A scholar compromised in his mind and intent is just like this. And yet, this is not easy to know. If one watches with one's own solitary view, one's eyes and ears are easily exhausted; if one seeks it in the opinions of the multitude, cross-examination lacks a solid basis. It rests solely with those above to discern it deeply. In the present age, how could we constantly suffer from a lack of talent? That we so often suffer from assessments of character being unsettled and evaluations being inconsistent has no other cause than this: the trouble lies in men disguising their minds in order to win recognition from superiors, while superiors sometimes fail to discern them fully. Thus reputation exceeds reality, and actual achievement falls short of expectations. Consequently, before the ink on a letter of recommendation has even dried, the man is soon dismissed for having nothing extraordinary to offer; or just as chests full of slander are rising up against someone, his fine conduct is shortly reported to the throne. The more detailed the evaluations, the further they miss the mark; the more urgent the need for talent, the harder it is to encounter it. When Your Excellency says that reputation and reality are confounded with one another…

託之乎多聞如此者非實小廉曲謹激節

肯先事見便則赴見難則避者心在私圖

觀高自標榜藉口恬退寔希榮進者心在

translation_en: …surely lies right in this! I venture to say that if one wishes to distinguish between reputation and reality, then the doctrine of judging men by their minds cannot but be urgently examined. Therefore, those who indulge in grandiose and sweeping discourses, plagiarize stale clichés, and are merely skillful in glib debate without fitting the actual circumstances—their minds are set on extravagant disputation, yet they hide behind the pretext of broad learning; such men are not genuine. Those who practice petty integrity and punctilious caution, display extreme austerity and affected conduct, show outward simplicity and sincerity yet betray their feelings over a mere bowl of soup—their minds are set on fishing for fame, yet they hide behind the pretext of being free of desires; such men are not genuine. Those who are clever at advancing their own interests, refuse to take the lead in affairs, rush toward whatever is advantageous, and shy away from whatever is difficult—their minds are set on selfish schemes, yet they hide behind the pretext of understanding expediency; such men are not genuine. Those who presume upon their talents and delight in bravado, act rashly with little foresight, inflate an empty reputation, and fail to shoulder great and far-reaching responsibilities—their minds are set on sensationalizing the multitude, yet they hide behind the pretext of taking charge of affairs; such men are not genuine. Those who affectedly adorn their demeanor and appearance, loftily advertise themselves, use quiet retirement as an excuse while in reality hoping for glorious advancement—their minds are set on angling for praise, yet they hide behind the pretext of cultivating lofty detachment; such men are not genuine. Those who resent the world and criticize the times, form cliques with the like-minded and attack those who differ, and employ a hundred schemes to obstruct any achievement that does not originate with themselves—their minds are set on jealousy of the capable, yet they hide behind the pretext of following the straight Way; such men are not genuine. As for all other cases of outwardly complying while inwardly rebelling, or borrowing the name of the public good to serve private ends, these are all habits that pervert governance and currents that confound the true, wherein the disposition of the mind becomes the root of the trouble. One must discern them early and see through them thoroughly, clearly showing the empire that it is the mind that is valued. When a man's mind is upright, to say nothing of one with great talent, even if his talent is less than superior, his mind still allows him to devote himself to service, and we should not discard…

text:

足以害心弗錄之矣宋儒易書之旨虞廷
官人之治要無外於此者舉以知人人何
難知哉若夫為伺察為智術非帝王明哲

在上焉愚聞之漢武好英風其時富瓌詭
立名之士漢宣精吏治其時萃循良核實

持之至公燭之至明先以其心振作之而

之矣；其心不正，無論非才，即才能過人，適足以害心，弗錄之矣。宋儒易書之旨，虞廷官人之治，要無外於此者。舉以知人，人何難知哉？若夫為伺察、為智術，非帝王明哲之事，不足為執事道也。雖然，轉移化導，機在上焉。愚聞之，漢武好英風，其時富瓌詭立名之士；漢宣精吏治，其時萃循良核實之能。此言人之材性，與時升降耳。自非上持之至公，燭之至明，先以其心振作之，而欲天下皆以心應，難矣。故曰：辨心而覈實者，任官之定論也；端本而率下者，致理之美業也。有進退人才之責者，加之意焉耳。

translation_en:
… will not discard them; if a man's mind is not upright, to say nothing of those without talent, even if his talent and ability surpass others, it is just enough to harm his mind, and one will not select him. The import of the Song Confucians' writings on the Classic of Changes and the Classic of History, and the governance of appointing men to office in the court of Yu, in essence go no further than this. If one uses this to know men, how could men be difficult to know? As for engaging in spying and surveillance or using clever stratagems, these are not the affairs of the sagely wisdom of emperors and kings, and are not worth speaking of to Your Reverences. Even so, the pivot for transforming and guiding lies with those above. I, in my simplicity, have heard it said that Emperor Wu of Han loved heroic spirit, and in his time there was an abundance of extraordinary and eccentric scholars who sought to establish a name; Emperor Xuan of Han was meticulous about administrative governance, and in his time there gathered capable men who were virtuous, upright, and attentive to reality. This means only that men's talents and natures rise and fall with the times. Unless those above uphold utmost impartiality and illuminate with utmost clarity, first rousing them with their own minds, to wish that the whole world should respond with their minds will be difficult indeed. Therefore it is said: discerning the mind and verifying the reality is the settled principle for appointing officials; rectifying the foundation and leading those below is the admirable achievement that brings about order. May those who bear the responsibility for advancing and dismissing men of talent simply pay heed to this.

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
蓋究心時務者
考試官左諭德陳批理財時政之大子指陳利
弊皆切要之論取之
執事以財計策〔𢠢〕生咨所以便
國家者顧書生委瑣拘墨未明於天下之大
計也雖然竊抱杞憂久矣敢不攄睹聽抒
衷臆以對蓋聞詩書所述王者之盛要在
安民富而教之故制地域民畫為井田正
其疆界灑為溝渠時其蓄洩百畝而徹賦
===

業曰登餘三年食再登曰平餘六年食三
登曰太平餘九年食然後王德流洽禮樂
成焉故盛王所以致太平之理者以其經
國理民有此具也自井田廢而王迹熄矣
王迹熄而一切權宜之術用矣管仲官山
海則籠百姓之利而收之官是富國之術
也猶可言也計然論積著則觀萬貨之情
而制其權是市賈之智也非國體也漢桑

成焉故盛王所以致太平之理者以其經
國理民有此具也自井田廢而王迹熄矣
王迹熄而一切權宜之術用矣管仲官山
海則籠百姓之利而收之官是富國之術
也猶可言也計然論積著則觀萬貨之情
而制其權是市賈之智也非國體也漢桑
punctuated:
蓋究心時務者。
考試官左諭德陳批：理財，時政之大。子指陳利弊，皆切要之論。取之。
執事以財計策〔𢠢〕生，咨所以便國家者。顧書生委瑣拘墨，未明於天下之大計也。雖然，竊抱杞憂久矣，敢不攄睹聽、抒衷臆以對？蓋聞《詩》《書》所述王者之盛，要在安民，富而教之。故制地域民，畫為井田，正其疆界，灑為溝渠，時其蓄洩，百畝而徹，賦稅有經。民三年耕，則餘一年之食；九年進業曰「登」，餘三年食；再登曰「平」，餘六年食；三登曰「太平」，餘九年食。然後王德流洽，禮樂成焉。故盛王所以致太平之理者，以其經國理民有此具也。自井田廢而王迹熄矣，王迹熄而一切權宜之術用矣。管仲官山海，則籠百姓之利而收之官，是富國之術也，猶可言也；計然論積著，則觀萬貨之情而制其權，是市賈之智也，非國體也。漢桑
translation_en:
…indeed one who has devoted his mind to current affairs.

Comment by Examiner Chen, Left Mentor in the Secretariat of the Heir Apparent (Zuo yude): Fiscal management is a paramount matter in current governance. You point out its advantages and abuses in terms that are all incisive and essential arguments. Selected.

You, the Examiner, have posed a policy question to this foolish student concerning fiscal administration, inquiring into what is advantageous for the state. Yet a bookish scholar is petty and bound to ink and rules, not comprehending the grand plans of the realm. Even so, I have privately harbored the anxieties of the man of Qi for a long time; how dare I not set forth what I have seen and heard and pour out my innermost thoughts in reply?

I have heard that the flourishing of the true kings described in the Book of Odes (Shi) and the Book of Documents (Shu) lay essentially in bringing peace to the people—enriching them and then instructing them. Therefore, in apportioning land and settling the people, they laid it out as well-fields (jingtian), rectified its boundaries, channeled it into ditches and canals, timed its retention and drainage of water, and levied the one-tenth tax (che) on each hundred mu, so that land taxes and imposts followed a regular norm. When the people farmed for three years, they had a surplus of one year's food; advancing in their work for nine years was called an "ascent" (deng), yielding a surplus of three years' food; two ascents was called "equilibrium" (ping), yielding a surplus of six years' food; three ascents was called "Great Peace" (taiping), yielding a surplus of nine years' food. Only after this did kingly virtue flow and pervade, and rites and music reach completion. Thus, the reason flourishing kings were able to achieve the governance of Great Peace was that they possessed this instrument for ordering the state and governing the people.

Once the well-field system was abolished, the traces of the true kings died out; and once the traces of the true kings died out, all manner of expedient techniques came into use. When Guan Zhong 管仲 placed the mountains and seas under official control, he monopolized the profits of the common people and gathered them into the hands of the officials; this was a technique for enriching the state, and could still be spoken of with some justification. When Jiran 計然 discoursed on accumulation and hoarding, he observed the conditions of the myriad goods and manipulated their balance of value; this was the cleverness of market merchants, not befitting the dignity of the state. In the Han dynasty, Sang…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
弘羊領大農置部丞分筦郡國鹽鐵則修
管氏之餘法置平準於京師盡籠天下貨
物官貿易之則師計然之遺意然彼用之
一國而此則用之天下取利愈博則陰奪
之途逾廣言利愈析則剥膚之慘彌深故
雖以佐國家一時之急而實以滋海内虚
耗萑苻羣起之患向使漢武無改文景之
恭儉則家給人足自若也貫朽粟腐自若
也雖捐租減賦可矣又安用是爲哉然則
===
盈縮之原可逆覩已我
國家以仁儉造邦其取民也不盡其財其制
用也必有其式
成憲舊章藏諸計府者犂然具在也廼頃歳度
支費鉅率歳出踰歳入以數十百萬計司
計所恃以補苴者直先歳羡餘耳積貯有
限殫竭可虞計臣謀士蓋日憂焉而未有
信必然之畫建長久之策者竊嘗計之財
用之在天下其生出有原其制用有節而

之途逾廣言利愈祈則剝膚之慘彌深故

耗萑苻羣起之患向使漢武繇改文景之
恭儉則家給人足自若也貫朽粟腐自若
也雖捐租減賦可矣又安用是爲哉然則
===

用也必有其式
成憲舊章藏諸計府者犂然具在也迺頃歲度

計所恃以補苴者直先歲羨餘耳積貯有
限殫竭可虞計臣謀士蓋日憂焉而未有
信必然之畫建長久之策者竊嘗計之財
用之在天下其生出有原其制用有節而
punctuated:
弘羊領大農，置部丞，分筦郡國鹽鐵，則修管氏之餘法；置平準於京師，盡籠天下貨物，官貿易之，則師計然之遺意。然彼用之一國，而此則用之天下。取利愈博，則陰奪之途逾廣；言利愈析，則剥膚之慘彌深。故雖以佐國家一時之急，而實以滋海内虚耗、萑苻羣起之患。向使漢武無改文、景之恭儉，則家給人足自若也，貫朽粟腐自若也，雖捐租減賦可矣，又安用是爲哉！然則盈縮之原，可逆覩已。
我國家以仁儉造邦，其取民也不盡其財，其制用也必有其式，成憲舊章藏諸計府者，犂然具在也。廼頃歳度支費鉅，率歳出踰歳入以數十百萬計，司計所恃以補苴者，直先歳羡餘耳。積貯有限，殫竭可虞，計臣謀士蓋日憂焉，而未有信必然之畫、建長久之策者。竊嘗計之，財用之在天下，其生出有原，其制用有節，而
translation_en:
… [Sang] Hongyang 桑弘羊 took charge of the Ministry of Agriculture, appointing Regional Assistant Ministers to separately manage the salt and iron monopolies across the commanderies and principalities, thereby reviving the leftover methods of Master Guan [Guan Zhong 管仲]; and when he established the Bureau of Equalization and Standards in the capital, monopolizing all the goods of the realm for the government to trade in them, he was imitating the lingering ideas of Jiran 計然. Yet those earlier men applied such measures to a single state, whereas he applied them to the entire empire. The more broadly profit was extracted, the wider the avenues of covert deprivation became; the more minutely profit was calculated, the deeper the misery of skinning the people to the flesh grew. Thus, although these measures aided the state in its momentary emergencies, in reality they bred the calamity of internal exhaustion throughout the realm and bandits rising in swarms in the marshes. Had Emperor Wu of Han 漢武 not altered the reverent frugality of Emperors Wen 文 and Jing 景, then every household would have remained well-supplied and every person content just as before, and strings of cash would have rotted and grain decayed in the granaries just as before; even remitting land rents and reducing taxes would have been possible—what need would there have been to resort to such practices! This being so, the origins of fiscal surplus and deficit can be foreseen with certainty.

Our Dynasty founded the state upon benevolence and frugality. In taking from the people, it does not exhaust their wealth; in regulating expenditures, it unfailingly adheres to established formulas. The accomplished statutes and old regulations preserved in the accounting bureaus are all clearly and completely in place. Yet in recent years, the expenditures of revenue and disbursements have been enormous, with annual outlays generally exceeding annual revenues by hundreds of thousands or millions. What the fiscal authorities rely upon to patch the deficits is merely the surpluses accumulated from previous years. Since stored reserves are finite, there is cause to fear their total depletion. Fiscal officials and counselors worry over this daily, yet none have been able to place faith in an unfailing plan or establish a permanent policy. I have ventured to calculate the matter: regarding the wealth and resources of the empire, their production has its source, their regulated expenditure has its measure, and…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
其補救有要今天下銀課自
上供外其領於度支之經費者歲二百九十萬
有竒耳而諸邊兵餉殆且稱是竊聞
祖宗開立各邊以陝西八府供延寧甘肅以山
西三府供宣大以山東永平供遼東而又
各以畿輔河南諸郡麥銀益之率歲入自
足一歲之用即如宣鎮歲九十萬兩而民
賦居十之七他鎮亦畧相埒發帑金以代
賦乃救急權宜非經制也今乃為額且歲
===
有加益矣夫宣大增於辛丑壬寅薊鎮增
於庚戌蓋一時懲虜侵軼故厚集廣募冀
一創折之今虜欵雖不足恃而土兵久練
計必服習諸鎮之入衛南兵之寄寓不可
議撤乎諸召募脩邊等費不可議覈乎而
又推之各邊稽民賦之由耗考經制之當
復則費必大省矣是議邊餉者其一也
國初親王歲祿五萬石數歲而裁為萬石或
千石蓋不以親故殫民力也

其補捄有要今天下銀課自
上供外其領於度支之經費者歲二百九十萬
有奇耳而諸邊兵餉殆且稱是竊聞

西三府供宣大以山東永平供遼東而又

賦居十之七他鎮亦畧相埒發帑金以代
賦乃捄急權宜非經制也今乃為額且歲
===
有加益矣夫宣大增於辛丑壬寅薊鎮增
於庚戌蓋一時懲虜侵軼故厚集廣募冀
一創折之今虜款雖不足恃而土兵久練
計必服習諸鎮之入衛南兵之寄寓不可
議撤乎諸召募脩邊等費不可議槩乎而
又推之各邊稽民賦之由耗考經制之當
復則費必大省矣是議邊餉者其一也
國初親王歲祿五萬石數歲而裁為萬石或
千石蓋不以親故殫民力也
punctuated:
其補救有要。今天下銀課，自上供外，其領於度支之經費者，歲二百九十萬有竒耳，而諸邊兵餉殆且稱是。竊聞祖宗開立各邊，以陝西八府供延、寧、甘肅，以山西三府供宣、大，以山東、永平供遼東，而又各以畿輔、河南諸郡麥銀益之，率歲入自足一歲之用。即如宣鎮歲九十萬兩，而民賦居十之七，他鎮亦畧相埒。發帑金以代賦，乃救急權宜，非經制也，今乃為額，且歲有加益矣。夫宣、大增於辛丑、壬寅，薊鎮增於庚戌，蓋一時懲虜侵軼，故厚集廣募，冀一創折之。今虜欵雖不足恃，而土兵久練，計必服習，諸鎮之入衛、南兵之寄寓，不可議撤乎？諸召募、脩邊等費，不可議覈乎？而又推之各邊，稽民賦之由耗，考經制之當復，則費必大省矣。是議邊餉者，其一也。
國初，親王歲祿五萬石，數歲而裁為萬石或千石，蓋不以親故殫民力也。
translation_en:
… and its remedies have essentials. Today, of the empire's silver revenues, aside from those supplied to the Imperial Household, the regular funds received by the Ministry of Revenue amount to only some two million nine hundred thousand taels a year, yet military rations and pay for the various frontier defenses nearly equal this sum. I have heard that when the Imperial Ancestors established the various frontier defenses, they used the eight prefectures of Shaanxi to supply Yansui, Ningxia, and Gansu; the three prefectures of Shanxi to supply Xuanfu and Datong; and Shandong and Yongping to supply Liaodong; and they further supplemented each of them with wheat commutation silver from the prefectures of the Capital Region and Henan, so that in general the annual revenue sufficed for a year's expenditure. Take Xuanfu Defense Command, for instance: its annual requirement is nine hundred thousand taels, of which taxes from the people accounted for seven-tenths, and the other defense commands were roughly comparable. Disbursing treasury silver in place of civilian taxes was an expedient to relieve emergencies, not the permanent system; yet now it has become the fixed quota, and is even increased year after year. Now, the increases in Xuanfu and Datong occurred in the xinchou and renyin years (1541–1542), and the increase in Jizhou Defense Command occurred in the gengxu year (1550). This was because, at the time, taking warning from the caitiffs' raids and incursions, forces were heavily massed and widely recruited in hopes of dealing them a decisive blow. Today, although the tribute pact with the caitiffs cannot be relied upon, the local troops have long been trained and can be counted on to be well-practiced; can we not deliberate on withdrawing the rotating guard troops from the various defense commands and the southern troops stationed there? Can we not deliberate on auditing and verifying the expenses for recruitment, frontier wall repairs, and the like? And if we extend this to every frontier, investigating why civilian tax revenues have dwindled and examining which permanent systems ought to be restored, then expenditures will surely be greatly reduced. This—deliberating on frontier military supplies—is the first point.

At the beginning of the dynasty, the annual stipend of an Imperial Prince of the First Degree was fifty thousand piculs of grain, which after a few years was reduced to ten thousand piculs or one thousand piculs, because the strength of the people was not to be exhausted on account of imperial kinship. …

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
祖訓言將軍以下有才能者得改官陞轉如銓
法又不以親故妨其仕也今嫡長世及支
庶遞降而麗屬籍者萬五千餘歲禄之數
即竭天下之賦不能贍也誠宜斟酌變通
稍為限制遞降之法視親疎為等殺絶封
之後令為業以自資而弛禁階仕一如齊
民法則禄必漸省而法可經久是議
藩禄者其一也軍職世及報功也
聖祖垂永世無窮之諭而復嚴犯罪謫配之律
===
蓋仁義並行之道也今前澤不斬而後勳
復繼故繫籍日繁而制禄日廣至錦衣之
冗濫則又其甚者也夫箕裘不世則豢養
不足以勸功干紀不懲則詐諼益恃以無
恐誠宜禁其旁襲而嚴其比試諸不中式
與試不如期者奪其禄編為士伍無少貸
有犯法者即案劾謫遣之如律諸冗濫非
功次者檢籍而褫革焉武胄其少清乎是
議軍職者其一也他如職以事列則内外

即竭天下之賦不能贍也誠宜斟酌變通

punctuated: 《祖訓》言將軍以下有才能者，得改官陞轉如銓法，又不以親故妨其仕也。今嫡長世及、支庶遞降，而麗屬籍者萬五千餘，歲禄之數，即竭天下之賦不能贍也。誠宜斟酌變通，稍為限制：遞降之法，視親疎為等殺；絶封之後，令為業以自資，而弛禁階仕，一如齊民法。則禄必漸省，而法可經久，是議藩禄者其一也。軍職世及，報功也。聖祖垂永世無窮之諭，而復嚴犯罪謫配之律，蓋仁義並行之道也。今前澤不斬，而後勳復繼，故繫籍日繁，而制禄日廣，至錦衣之冗濫，則又其甚者也。夫箕裘不世，則豢養不足以勸功；干紀不懲，則詐諼益恃以無恐。誠宜禁其旁襲，而嚴其比試。諸不中式與試不如期者，奪其禄，編為士伍，無少貸；有犯法者，即案劾謫遣之如律；諸冗濫非功次者，檢籍而褫革焉，武胄其少清乎！是議軍職者其一也。他如職以事列，則内外
translation_en:
The Ancestral Injunctions (Zuxun) state that those of the rank of Imperial Clansman General (jiangjun) and below who possess talent and ability may have their offices changed and be promoted or transferred according to the regulations of personnel selection—thus again not letting kinship hinder their official careers. Nowadays, legitimate eldest sons succeed in perpetuity while collateral and secondary sons descend in rank generation by generation, yet those registered on the imperial clan rolls number more than fifteen thousand, and the amount of their annual stipends could not be supplied even if the revenues of the entire empire were exhausted. Truly we ought to deliberate and adapt, establishing moderate limits: the rule for descending in rank should be graded according to closeness or distance of kinship; after enfeoffment ceases, they should be allowed to pursue livelihoods to support themselves, while the prohibition against their advancing into officialdom should be relaxed, treating them entirely under the same laws as commoners. Then the stipends will surely diminish gradually and the system can endure for a long time. This is one point: deliberating on the stipends of the princely establishments.

That military offices are hereditary is a way of rewarding merit. The Sacred Ancestor handed down edicts promising endless hereditary succession for all generations, yet at the same time strictly enforced the statutes on banishment and penal servitude for committing crimes; this was indeed the way of practicing benevolence and righteousness side by side. Nowadays, earlier favors are not cut off while later merits continue to be added; consequently, those entered on the registers grow more numerous by the day and the stipends allotted grow ever broader, and when it comes to the superfluity and abuse in the Embroidered-Uniform Guard (Jinyiwei), it is even more extreme. Now, if descendants fail to carry on their ancestors' profession, supporting them at state expense is insufficient to encourage merit; if violations of discipline go unpunished, deceit and fraud will all the more rely on impunity and know no fear. Truly we ought to prohibit collateral succession among them and strictly enforce their martial-skills tests. For all those who fail to meet the standard or who fail to take the test on schedule, strip them of their stipends and enroll them in the common ranks without the slightest leniency; if any violate the law, promptly investigate, impeach, and banish them according to the statutes; and for all superfluous and abusive appointments not based on grades of merit, inspect the registers and strip and dismiss them—then might the military hereditary lineages be somewhat purified! This is another point: deliberating on military offices.

As for other matters: if offices are established according to actual duties, then inside and outside the capital…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
剩員之無關事守者可汰也廩以稱事則
匠藝力男之詭名篡籍者可革也費必有
經則不時之
宣索無名之
賞賚可停也斷而行之於財計豈少補乎夫
是數者皆節約之說也若生出之原則賦
法備矣即計桑持籌亦何以加者無已則
愚謂屯政之當修也鹽法之當復也夫
國家實邊之策斯二者實賴焉議者蓋屢及
===
矣而卒柅不行者患在行之不果而撓於
沮事之議也往諸邊武備廢弛虜騎充斥
耕稼之地灌莽彌望今北虜業講欵而環
慶以西亦稍革面塞上之腴可墾必多誠
宜以時相度利便為封畛堡砦使足居守
募軍民耕墾其中期以三年方徵之稅仍
薄其額則願耕者必衆矣其內地之侵于
官豪者量時久近以漸清之要在當事者
虛心任怨勿縱勿擾事必有濟也或乃謂
alt_text:
剰員之無關事守者可汰也廩以稱事則
匠藝力男之詭名纂籍者可革也費必有
經則不時之
宣索無名之
賞賚可停也斷而行之於財計豈少補乎夫
是數者皆節約之說也若生財之原則賦
法備矣即計桑持籌亦何以加者無已則
愚謂屯政之當修也鹽法之當復也夫
國家實邊之策斯二者實賴焉議者蓋屢及
===
矣而卒梗不行者患在行之不果而撓於
沮事之議也往諸邊武備廢弛虜騎充斥
耕稼之地灌莽彌望今北虜業講款而環
慶以西亦稍革面塞上之腴可墾必多誠
宜以時相度利便為封畛堡砦使足居守
募軍民耕墾其中期以三年方徵之稅仍
薄其額則願耕者必衆矣其內地之侵于
官豪者量時久近以漸清之要在當事者
虛心任怨勿縱勿擾事必有濟也或乃謂
punctuated: 剩員之無關事守者可汰也；廩以稱事，則匠藝、力男之詭名篡籍者可革也；費必有經，則不時之宣索、無名之賞賚可停也。斷而行之，於財計豈少補乎？夫是數者，皆節約之說也。若生出之原，則賦法備矣，即計、桑持籌，亦何以加者？無已，則愚謂屯政之當修也，鹽法之當復也。夫國家實邊之策，斯二者實賴焉。議者蓋屢及矣，而卒柅不行者，患在行之不果，而撓於沮事之議也。往諸邊武備廢弛，虜騎充斥，耕稼之地，灌莽彌望。今北虜業講欵，而環慶以西亦稍革面，塞上之腴可墾必多。誠宜以時相度利便，為封畛、堡砦，使足居守；募軍民耕墾其中，期以三年方徵之稅，仍薄其額，則願耕者必衆矣。其內地之侵于官豪者，量時久近，以漸清之。要在當事者虛心任怨，勿縱勿擾，事必有濟也。或乃謂
translation_en:
…superfluous personnel who have no connection to actual duties and responsibilities may be eliminated; if rations are made commensurate with the work performed, then artisans and laborers who falsify their names and tamper with the registers may be dismissed; and if expenditures must follow regular norms, then irregular palace requisitions and unmerited rewards and bestowals may be halted. If we carry these measures out decisively, will this be of small benefit to our fiscal administration?

Now, these several points are all arguments for economizing. As for the sources of generating revenue, our taxation system is already complete; even if Ji Ran and Sang Hongyang were to hold the counting rods, what more could they add? If I must speak further, then in my humble view it is the military farming administration (tunzheng) that ought to be restored, and the salt laws (yanfa) that ought to be revived. Indeed, the dynasty's policy for provisioning the frontiers relies truly upon these two measures. Those who deliberate on state affairs have touched upon them repeatedly, yet in the end they are blocked and not carried out; the trouble lies in a lack of decisiveness in execution and in being thwarted by the arguments of obstructionists.

In the past, military preparedness along the various frontiers fell into neglect, enemy horsemen overran the region, and arable lands were overgrown with brush as far as the eye could see. Now the northern caitiffs have already negotiated tributary terms, and west of Huanzhou and Qingyang they have also somewhat changed their ways, so there must be much fertile land along the frontier that can be reclaimed. We truly ought to survey the terrain and assess conveniences in a timely manner, constructing boundary dikes and fortified stockades so that they are sufficient for habitation and defense. If we recruit soldiers and civilians to plow and reclaim the land within them, stipulating that taxes will only be levied after three years while still keeping the quota light, then those willing to till the soil will surely be numerous. As for lands in the interior that have been encroached upon by official and powerful families, we should weigh how long they have been held and clear them up gradually. The key is for those in charge to be open-minded and willing to bear resentment, neither indulging abuses nor causing disturbance; then the undertaking will surely succeed. Yet some say that…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
計其羨僅足以供軍豈未計養軍之重費
邪鹽政一壞於輸粟之易銀再壞於餘鹽
之榷制故商人木樂趨塞而競逐餘鹽之
利坐是飛輓利失而諸邊愈窘一有災警
帑金雖出乃至無從得粟始懲穀賤之利
商不計穀貴之弊反移之
國也屯田既復芻粟且易得宜處給工本盡
收餘鹽而并正課悉開之邊仍輕估以召
之約非由報中者則無從得引而私販轄
===
害等弊則厲其禁勿使犯商人必趨塞下
矣商通則塞地益墾邊庾可滿而帑金可
以漸革减也或乃計開中之入無當於原
估其殆者易銀之淺見邪愚又謂河以北
水利稼政宜修也夫京輔諸郡古燕趙用
以內支諸雄外禦胡狢者唐之三鎮亦以
其力抗天下未聞借資於他境也今瀕海
千里萑葦極目而瀛深諸郊一遇霖潦溟
渤為區豈地利之不如古邪誠宜倣元人
alt_text:
計其羨僅足以供軍豈未計養軍之重費
邪鹽政一壞於輸粟之易銀再壞於餘鹽
之權制故商人不樂趨塞而競逐餘鹽之
利豈是飛輓利失而諸邊倉庫一有災警
帑金雖出乃至無從得粟始悠穀賤之利
商不計穀貴之弊反移之
國也屯田既復芻粟且易得宜廢給工本盡
收餘鹽而并正課悉開之邊仍輕估以召
之約非由報中者則無從得引而私販轄
===
害等弊則厲其禁勿使犯商人必趨塞下
矣商通則塞地益墾邊庾可滿而帑金可
以漸革減也或乃計開中之入無當於原
估其始者易銀之淺見邪愚又謂河以北
水利稼政宜修也夫京輔諸郡古燕趙用
以內支諸雄外禦胡貉者唐之三鎮亦以
其力抗天下未聞借資於他境也今瀕海
千里萑葦極目而瀛深諸郊一遇霖潦濱
渤為區豈地利之不如古邪誠宜倣元人
punctuated:
計其羨僅足以供軍，豈未計養軍之重費邪？鹽政一壞於輸粟之易銀，再壞於餘鹽之榷制，故商人木樂趨塞，而競逐餘鹽之利。坐是飛輓利失，而諸邊愈窘。一有災警，帑金雖出，乃至無從得粟。始懲穀賤之利商，不計穀貴之弊反移之國也。屯田既復，芻粟且易得，宜處給工本，盡收餘鹽，而并正課悉開之邊，仍輕估以召之。約非由報中者則無從得引，而私販、轄害等弊，則厲其禁，勿使犯，商人必趨塞下矣。商通則塞地益墾，邊庾可滿，而帑金可以漸革减也。或乃計開中之入無當於原估，其殆者易銀之淺見邪？

愚又謂河以北水利、稼政宜修也。夫京輔諸郡，古燕、趙用以內支諸雄、外禦胡狢者。唐之三鎮亦以其力抗天下，未聞借資於他境也。今瀕海千里，萑葦極目，而瀛、深諸郊，一遇霖潦，溟渤為區，豈地利之不如古邪？誠宜倣元人
translation_en:
…calculating that their surplus is barely enough to supply the troops—have they not calculated the heavy expense of maintaining the army? The salt administration was first ruined by commuting grain deliveries into silver, and ruined a second time by the monopoly regulations on surplus salt. Consequently, merchants do not [木, OCR for 不] gladly hasten to the frontiers, but instead compete to pursue the profits of surplus salt. Because of this, the benefits of rapid grain transport are lost, and the various frontiers grow ever more hard-pressed. Whenever there is a disaster or border alarm, even though treasury silver is disbursed, there is nowhere to obtain grain. At first, authorities sought to curb the advantage merchants gained when grain was cheap, without reckoning that the harm of expensive grain would instead be shifted onto the Dynasty! Once military farms are restored, fodder and grain will become easy to obtain. We should arrange to provide production capital, buy up all the surplus salt, and allocate it together with the regular quota entirely to the frontiers under the salt-barter system, while still setting a light valuation to attract merchants. If we stipulate that unless they go through registering for frontier grain delivery (baozhong) they have no way to obtain salt vouchers, and if we strictly enforce prohibitions against abuses such as illicit trafficking and extortionate obstruction [轄害, ?] so that no one violates them, merchants will surely flock to the frontier regions. When merchants circulate, frontier lands will be increasingly brought under cultivation, frontier granaries can be filled, and the annual subsidies of treasury silver can be gradually abolished or reduced. Yet some calculate that the receipts from the salt-barter system do not match the original valuation—is that not the shallow view of those who favor commuting to silver [殆者, OCR for 殆嗜]?

I further maintain that water conservancy and agricultural administration north of the Yellow River ought to be rehabilitated. The prefectures around the capital region are what ancient Yan and Zhao used to hold off rival powers within and repel the northern barbarians without. The Three Defense Commands of the Tang dynasty likewise relied on their own resources to stand against the entire empire; one never heard of them borrowing supplies from other regions. Today, along the coast for a thousand li, reeds and rushes stretch as far as the eye can see, and in the countryside of Ying and Shen, as soon as heavy rains and flooding occur, the land turns into a vast sea. Is it really that the productivity of the land is inferior to that of antiquity? Truly, we ought to imitate the Yuan dynasty men in…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
疏渾灅障滹沱遺跡於濱河之地或築隄
灑渠或瀦為陂澤或去其壅塞使水有所
歸則不為患矣而又修虞集之議於京東
瀕海地用南人水耕法募民田之亦以三
年起輕科仍禁貴戚毋請奪諸他郡濱水
者悉準是則地利必興畿輔殷阜亦可漸
減漕粟以紓東南之困此永世利也他如
長淮以北河濟左右諸封域類多蕪棄倘
營田之使悉心講畫勤行勞徠而以闢土
===
勸農計其吏治於財計亦豈無裨乎至補
捄之要宜莫如社倉積穀法夫井田不可
復則所謂三年耕餘一年食者靡可冀矣
金矢之入於古有之故罪穀備賑荒政遺
意也乃有司者易粟以鏹囊橐其間經
國者懲其冒也因而收之以濟邊夫世之有
饑穰天之行也今東南被之矣枵腹之民
嗷嗷待哺而郡邑曾無儲峙之備弱者溝
洫彊者聚而衡擊耳安有阽危若是而不

救之要宜莫如社倉積穀法夫井田不可

金夫之入於古有之故罪穀備賑荒政遺

饑穰天之行也今東南被之矣枵腹之民
嗷嗷待哺而郡邑曾無儲峙之備弱者溝
洫彊者聚而衡擊耳安有阽危若是而不
punctuated: 疏渾灅、障滹沱遺跡，於濱河之地，或築隄灑渠，或瀦為陂澤，或去其壅塞，使水有所歸，則不為患矣。而又修虞集之議，於京東瀕海地，用南人水耕法，募民田之，亦以三年起輕科，仍禁貴戚毋請奪。諸他郡濱水者悉準是，則地利必興，畿輔殷阜，亦可漸減漕粟，以紓東南之困，此永世利也。他如長淮以北，河、濟左右諸封域，類多蕪棄。倘營田之使悉心講畫，勤行勞徠，而以闢土勸農計其吏治，於財計亦豈無裨乎？至補捄之要，宜莫如社倉積穀法。夫井田不可復，則所謂三年耕餘一年食者，靡可冀矣。金矢之入，於古有之，故罪穀備賑，荒政遺意也。乃有司者易粟以鏹，囊橐其間；經國者懲其冒也，因而收之以濟邊。夫世之有饑穰，天之行也，今東南被之矣。枵腹之民，嗷嗷待哺，而郡邑曾無儲峙之備，弱者溝洫，彊者聚而衡擊耳。安有阽危若是而不
translation_en:
… traces of dredging the Hun and Lei rivers and dyking the Hutuo River. Along the riverbanks, one should either build dykes and branch out canals, impound the water into ponds and marshes, or clear away blockages so that the water has a place to return to, and then it will no longer be a disaster. Furthermore, we should revive the proposal of Yu Ji 虞集: in the coastal lands east of the capital, employ the wet-rice farming methods of southerners, recruit people to cultivate them, and likewise begin levying a light tax after three years, while strictly forbidding noble relatives from petitioning to seize the land. If all other prefectures bordering on water follow this standard, the productivity of the land will surely flourish and the metropolitan area will become prosperous and abundant. One may then gradually reduce the tribute grain transported by canal in order to relieve the distress of the Southeast—this would be an eternal benefit. As for other regions, such as the territories north of the Huai River and around the Yellow and Ji rivers, they are mostly left overgrown and abandoned. If Commissioners for State Farms were to devote their whole hearts to planning and designing, diligently encouraging and attracting settlers, and if local officials' governance were evaluated on the basis of opening up land and encouraging agriculture, how could this fail to benefit our fiscal administration as well?

As for the essentials of remedial relief, nothing is more fitting than the method of storing grain in community granaries (shecang). Since the well-field system cannot be restored, the ancient ideal of three years of farming leaving a surplus of one year's food can no longer be hoped for. Revenue from metal and arrows [paid by litigants to redeem offenses] existed in antiquity; thus, using grain paid in redemption of crimes to prepare for famine relief preserves the surviving intent of ancient famine administration. Yet local authorities replaced grain with strings of cash, pocketing profits in the process; those managing the state, seeking to curb their embezzlement, consequently confiscated those funds to supply the frontiers. Now, the alternation of famine and abundance in the world is the course of Heaven, and today the Southeast has suffered from it. Famished people cry out waiting to be fed, yet the prefectures and counties have no stockpiled reserves whatsoever; the weak end up in ditches and gullies, while the strong band together to pillage and attack. How can the people be in such perilous extremity and yet not be…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
收卹者誠宜歸贖爰于有司以備積貯仍
飭自今凡罪贖一切輸穀毋聽折納而嚴
侵漁之禁積久而裕則倣李悝平糴法行
之斯藏富郡國之策而亦可以收豪民貴
出賤取之權即有饑饉民無捐瘠矣補捄
孰要於此者昔蘇轍曰天下之患生於太
怯而成於牽俗太怯則見利而不敢爲牽
俗則自顧而愛其身是以天下之事舉無
可爲者蓋興事之難自昔歎之矣雖然亦
===
在乎加之意焉爾
明天子以四海爲家賢公卿以
國爲家監司守令以所治爲家視天下之利
病若休戚之關於一身也將所爲而無不
成矣庸詎財計一端而已哉
alt_text:
收䘏者誠宜歸贖𠀌于有司以備積貯仍
飭自今凡罪贖一切輸穀毋聽折納而嚴
侵漁之禁積久而裕則倣李悝平糴法行
之斯藏富鄰國之策而亦可以收豪民貴
出賤取之權即有饑饉民無捐瘠矣補救
孰要於此者昔蘇轍曰天下之患生於太
怯而成於牽俗太怯則見利而不敢爲牽
俗則自顧而愛其身是以天下之事舉無
可爲者蓋興事之難自昔歎之矣雖然亦
===
在乎加之意焉爾
明天子以四海爲家賢公卿以
國爲家監司守令以所治爲家視天下之利
病若休戚之關於一身也將所爲而無不
成矣庸詎財計一端而已哉
punctuated: 收卹者？誠宜歸贖爰于有司，以備積貯。仍飭自今凡罪贖一切輸穀，毋聽折納，而嚴侵漁之禁。積久而裕，則倣李悝平糴法行之。斯藏富郡國之策，而亦可以收豪民貴出賤取之權，即有饑饉，民無捐瘠矣。補捄孰要於此者？昔蘇轍曰：「天下之患，生於太怯，而成於牽俗。太怯則見利而不敢爲，牽俗則自顧而愛其身，是以天下之事，舉無可爲者。」蓋興事之難，自昔歎之矣。雖然，亦在乎加之意焉爾。明天子以四海爲家，賢公卿以國爲家，監司、守令以所治爲家，視天下之利病，若休戚之關於一身也，將所爲而無不成矣，庸詎財計一端而已哉！
translation_en:
… be taken in and relieved? It is truly appropriate to return the redemption payments to the local authorities so as to provide for grain reserves. Furthermore, an order should be issued that from now on all penal redemptions must be paid entirely in grain, without allowing commutation into silver, while strictly enforcing prohibitions against embezzlement. When reserves have accumulated over a long time and become abundant, the system should be operated in imitation of Li Kui's (李悝) equitable grain-purchase method (pingdi fa 平糴法). This is a policy for storing wealth in the prefectures and counties, and it can also reclaim from powerful families the power of selling dear and buying cheap; even if famine occurs, the people will not die of starvation or waste away. What remedial measure could be more essential than this?

In the past, Su Zhe (蘇轍) said: "The troubles of the Empire arise from excessive timidity and are brought to completion by being bound to custom. When one is overly timid, one sees a benefit yet dares not act upon it; when one is bound to custom, one looks out for oneself and cherishes one's own person. Consequently, among the affairs of the Empire, there is nothing at all that can be accomplished." Indeed, the difficulty of initiating great undertakings has been lamented since antiquity. Even so, it simply depends on applying one's mind to it. When the enlightened Son of Heaven takes all within the Four Seas as his household, worthy high ministers take the state as their household, and provincial surveillance officials, prefects, and magistrates take their jurisdictions as their households—viewing the advantages and ills of the Empire as if they were joys and sorrows affecting their own bodies—then whatever they undertake will never fail to succeed. How could this apply solely to the single matter of fiscal administration!

萬曆己卯秋天下例賓興士

斌斌經學由顯第專門世業
博存眾家而統一聖真則有

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefectural Provincial Examination

In the autumn of the jimao year of the Wanli era [1579], the empire, in accordance with precedent, presented worthy scholars for recommendation. Your servants Siyu and Ziyi received the imperial command to take charge of the examination affairs of Shuntian. Now that the affair is concluded and the record compiled, it is fitting that your servant Ziyi should offer a few words to append to the final pages.

Your servant reflects that among the tasks of a true king, none is more important than the moral instruction of the age and the customs of the literati. At the height of the Zhou dynasty, scholars were gathered in local schools and promoted on the basis of their virtuous conduct and mastery of the Way and the arts; the efficacy of this could readily be seen. When the Zhou declined and royal instruction fell into neglect, Confucius first critically harmonized the Six Classics so as to hand down teaching for future generations. When the Han arose, inheriting the aftermath of the Qin destruction of learning, classical scholarship and the Way had ceased to flourish. In the Jianyuan era [140–135 BCE], they were first honored and promoted; testing proficiency in the arts to fill official posts was inscribed into the statutory regulations, and with Confucian scholars flourishing in refined abundance, classical learning thereby became prominent. Yet because specialists transmitted their studies as hereditary professions, preserving a wide array of diverse schools, when it came to unifying them in the authentic truth of the sages, they still…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
未逮宋程朱氏出理奧始明
廼世顧莫之尚也我
高皇帝載闢函夏作民君師建學
貞教一準孔氏而翼以宋儒
傳訓盡罷黜諸說不用取士
以經義論策而剷詞賦諸科
蓋教明法一自成周而後未
===

業風教攸同非其效邪今
天子明聖
志大有為日與二三大臣討求故
實紹修
聖祖之章憲於崇正學成人材尤
孜孜焉嚮歲

translation_en: … yet failed to attain it. In the Song dynasty, the Cheng brothers and Master Zhu [Cheng Hao 程顥, Cheng Yi 程頤, and Zhu Xi 朱熹] emerged, and the profound depths of principle first became clear; yet the age nevertheless did not hold them in supreme esteem. Our Exalted Emperor [Gao Huangdi 高皇帝, i.e., the Hongwu Emperor], having newly opened up the Chinese realm, acted as ruler and teacher to the people. In establishing schools and rectifying instruction, he took Confucius as his sole standard, supported by the commentaries and explications of the Song Confucians, and completely dismissed all other doctrines from use. He selected scholars through expositions on the Classics, discourses, and policy essays, while abolishing the examination categories for lyric-meters and rhapsodies. Indeed, in the clarity of its teaching and the unity of its system, since the flourishing Zhou dynasty there had never been anything to match this. For two hundred years, scholars have pursued no divergent studies and customs and teachings have been uniform—is this not its efficacy? Today the Son of Heaven is brilliant and sage, his ambition set on great achievements. Daily, with two or three grand ministers, he investigates and seeks out historical precedents to continue and cultivate the statutes and constitutions of the Sacred Ancestor, devoting himself with especial diligence to exalting orthodox learning and bringing men of talent to completion. In recent years, …

translation_en: … issued detailed regulations for the curriculum and broadly encouraged the educational officials, making all manner of injunctions and admonitions most thorough. Those of the blue-collared student class, gazing upon the imperial wind and receiving its beneficence, even in remote, deep, and obscure places, ought to shine forth in the light of their own accord—how much more so in the Capital, the premier place of goodness and the first to receive the transformative teaching of the Court! The world says that the scholars of Yan and Zhao are spirited and upright in their sense of duty, profound, vigorous, and rich in grand strategy. People of ancient and modern times are not far apart. Now, moreover, as gentlemen of the imperial metropolis, basking in the reflected radiance of the sun and moon, their inspiration and rousing to action ought to be manifold what it was in former times; how, then, could there be any who fail to measure up to the Sovereign's intentions and directives? Yet recently, men of discernment still sigh repeatedly over literary style and scholarly ethos. Indeed, your servant has examined and surveyed past and present, and privately harbors doubts about this as well. In antiquity, scholars cultivated themselves at…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
家而效之天子之庭窮居以
之誦說遭遘用之措注無二
道也今士佔畢一經矻矻昕
夕斯以勤矣乃事口耳者資
談說而不概於身心攻帖括
者競剽掇而靡關於世務侈
藻績者或扶疏枝葉闊畧本
===
===

即學術且淺駁繆鑿又何建
樹之足云夫本所爲
設科羅士與
申飭廣厲者固期得經明行修
出入不悖所聞者爲

樹之足云夫本所爲
設科羅士與

punctuated: 家，而效之天子之庭；窮居以之誦說，遭遘用之措注，無二道也。今士佔畢一經，矻矻昕夕，斯以勤矣。乃事口耳者資談說而不概於身心；攻帖括者競剽掇而靡關於世務；侈藻績者或扶疏枝葉、闊畧本根，甚乃浸淫於諸子百家矣。即學術且淺駁繆鑿，又何建樹之足云！夫本所爲設科羅士與申飭廣厲者，固期得經明行修、出入不悖所聞者，爲國家用也。乃求以實，或應以虛…
translation_en: …home, and dedicated it at the court of the Son of Heaven; what they recited and discussed when living in obscurity, they applied in practice when meeting with opportunity—there were not two separate Ways. Today, scholars pore over a single classic, toiling tirelessly from dawn to dusk; in this they are indeed diligent. Yet those who engage in mere rote learning use it to fuel talk without applying its standard to their own bodies and minds; those who specialize in examination essays vie in plagiarizing and piecing together fragments with no relevance to the affairs of the world; and those who indulge in ornate embellishment sometimes spread out branches and leaves while neglecting the root and trunk, going so far as to steep themselves in the Non-Canonical Philosophers and Hundred Schools. If their very scholarship is already shallow, impure, erroneous, and forced, what achievements are even worth mentioning? Now, the fundamental purpose of establishing examination categories to gather scholars, and of issuing repeated injunctions and broad encouragement, is assuredly to hope to obtain men who understand the Classics and cultivate their conduct—who in public and private life do not betray what they have learned—to be of use to the State. Yet when sought with substance, some respond with emptiness…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
剽求以雅或應以頗僻則
國家奚賴焉臣爲此懼故甄士
必質文並茂稱引當物者必
會文切理精約質雅者而剽
掇緇綴者弗與焉誠欲得忠
實端亮之士備任使以稱
德意亦冀
輦轂之下敦雅尚以風四方或
於世教不無小補爾抑臣猶
有懼焉夫怔營夙夜因言考
衷者有司職也自獻成信立
德立功者士所効也有如士
飾樸售偽斵不失有司者之
尺寸而措諸用無當於功實

於世教不無小補爾抑〔臣〕猶

德立功者士所効也有如士
飾樸售僞蘄不失有司者之
尺寸而措諸用無當於功實
punctuated: 剽，求以雅或應以頗僻，則國家奚賴焉？臣爲此懼，故甄士必質文並茂、稱引當物者，必會文切理、精約質雅者，而剽掇緇綴者弗與焉。誠欲得忠實端亮之士，備任使以稱德意，亦冀輦轂之下敦雅尚以風四方，或於世教不無小補爾。抑臣猶有懼焉：夫怔營夙夜，因言考衷者，有司職也；自獻成信，立德立功者，士所効也。有如士飾樸售偽，斵不失有司者之尺寸，而措諸用無當於功實，
translation_en: … superficiality; when sought with elegance, some respond with perversity and eccentricity—then what can the State rely upon? Your servant is fearful of this. Therefore, in selecting scholars, I insisted on those in whom substance and refinement both flourish and whose citations suit the subject, and those whose compositions closely match moral principle and are concise, substantial, and elegant; whereas those who plagiarize and patch together fragments were not included among them. Truly I desired to obtain loyal, honest, upright, and clear-minded scholars to be ready for appointment and employment so as to fulfill Your virtuous intent; and I also hoped that beneath the imperial chariot-hubs [in the capital] we might foster refined tastes so as to influence the four quarters, which perhaps would not be without some small benefit to the moral instruction of the age. Yet your servant still has a fear: to labor anxiously from morning till night, examining inner sincerity through their words, is the duty of the authorities; to present oneself with established good faith, and to establish virtue and meritorious deeds, is what the scholars must render in service. Suppose a scholar disguises himself as simple while peddling falsehood, hewing his writing so as not to miss the measurements of the authorities, yet when put to practical use he proves unequal to real achievement—…

title: 萬曆七年順天府鄉試錄
text:
有司者又何所逭責邪諸士
勗矣夫修身致
主匡一寓內之道六籍備之士誠
通經學古參以時宜天下事
可考而鏡也誠偽淑慝此心
辨之倘設誠于內而致行焉
又何悖所聞之有若是則庶
幾哉植德效實之士可與藹
吉維使者倫矣有司以人事
君之義不藉是少稱塞哉不然士
豈惟上負
天子下負所學吏且奉三尺繩之
而主者亦以不適蒙罰吁諸
士重勗哉俾臣獲逭于罰也

punctuated: 有司者又何所逭責邪？諸士勗矣！夫修身致主、匡一寓內之道，六籍備之。士誠通經學古，參以時宜，天下事可考而鏡也。誠偽淑慝，此心辨之；倘設誠于內而致行焉，又何悖所聞之有？若是，則庶幾哉植德效實之士，可與藹吉維使者倫矣。有司以人事君之義，不藉是少稱塞哉？不然，士豈惟上負天子、下負所學，吏且奉三尺繩之，而主者亦以不適蒙罰。吁！諸士重勗哉，俾臣獲逭于罰也，
translation_en: …how then could the authorities evade their responsibility? Exert yourselves, scholars! Indeed, the Way of cultivating oneself, devoting oneself to the Sovereign, and rectifying and unifying all within the realm is fully set forth in the Six Classics. If a scholar truly masters the Classics and learns from antiquity, adapting them to what is appropriate for the times, the affairs of the empire can be examined and mirrored therein. Sincerity and falsehood, virtue and vice, are discerned by this very mind; if one establishes sincerity within and carries it out in practice, how could there be any betrayal of what one has learned? If it be thus, then one will come close to being a scholar who plants virtue and yields substantive results, worthy to be classed with the "many admirable officers, fit to be employed" [of the Book of Odes]. Would not the duty of the authorities to serve the Sovereign by recommending men of talent thereby be fulfilled in some small measure? Otherwise, not only will the scholars fail the Son of Heaven above and betray their own learning below, but the judicial officials will apply the three-foot statute book to restrain them, and the presiding examiners too will incur punishment for making unsuitable selections [in accordance with ancient rites]. Alas! Exert yourselves doubly, scholars, so that if your servant is enabled to escape punishment,…
